one_line: The optimal NMS IoU threshold is a hidden scene-density prior, and a per-image threshold predicted from a cheap pre-NMS density estimate recovers crowd recall without retraining
problem: Detectors ship with one global NMS threshold tuned on dataset-average density; crowded scenes lose true positives to suppression while sparse scenes keep duplicates, and practitioners treat this as an unavoidable trade-off.
core_hypothesis: The best NMS threshold per image is a monotone function of local instance density, so a single global threshold encodes the training set's density distribution rather than anything about the detector; density is estimable from pre-NMS score mass cheaply enough to adapt the threshold at inference.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping NMS thresholds per image and taking the oracle best threshold will show the oracle threshold correlates strongly with GT instance density, and a threshold predicted from pre-NMS score mass alone will recover a majority of the oracle-vs-global recall gap on crowded subsets.
why_important: If true, a zero-training inference-time change improves every anchor-based and anchor-free detector in crowded deployments (retail, traffic, sports) where suppression losses dominate.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive-NMS ideas exist as trained density heads inside specific architectures; treating density-adaptive suppression as a detector-agnostic post-hoc calibration problem driven by pre-NMS statistics, with an oracle-gap analysis, appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take any off-the-shelf detector, run per-image NMS threshold sweeps on a crowd-heavy split and a sparse split, record oracle thresholds, regress them on pre-NMS score mass and peak counts, then test the predicted-threshold pipeline against the global threshold.
main_risk: The oracle threshold may vary more within an image (per region) than across images, making a per-image scalar adaptation nearly useless.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: NMS thresholds are a fixed hyperparameter tuned once per dataset, and crowd losses require architectural fixes like set prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score miscalibration across images may corrupt the pre-NMS density estimate exactly in the scenes where adaptation matters most.
fastest_falsification: One day: 500 images stratified by GT count, per-image threshold sweep, plot oracle threshold vs density; a flat relationship kills the idea.

one_line: Many surviving duplicate detections are not noise but part-whole ambiguity, and suppressing them destroys recoverable hierarchical structure
problem: Duplicate detections are treated as a uniform nuisance to be suppressed, yet some duplicates are systematically located on objects with salient sub-parts, suggesting the detector is voting for two valid granularities.
core_hypothesis: Post-NMS surviving duplicates and near-threshold suppressed boxes concentrate on objects with part structure (person with backpack, cup with handle), because classification and box heads receive legitimate evidence at two granularities; the duplicate pattern is a free part-decomposition signal.
falsifiable_prediction: The rate of high-IoU duplicate pairs per object will be significantly higher for objects human annotators judge as having nameable sub-parts than for blob-like objects, controlling for size and class frequency.
why_important: If duplicates encode granularity, suppression should be replaced by structured output in applications needing parts (robotics grasping, fine-grained retrieval), and duplicate statistics become a cheap probe of what a detector has learned about part structure.
why_possibly_novel: Duplicate analysis in the literature focuses on suppression efficacy; interpreting the duplicate distribution itself as a semantic signal about part-whole structure appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a detector without NMS on a few hundred images, cluster raw boxes per GT object, have annotators label which objects have nameable parts, and test whether multi-cluster objects are enriched for part structure versus a size-matched control.
main_risk: Duplicates may instead track annotation ambiguity or aspect-ratio anchor coverage, confounding the part-structure interpretation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Duplicates are redundant predictions of the same object caused by dense anchors, carrying no useful information beyond the best box.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern one-to-one matched detectors produce few duplicates yet still detect parts, suggesting duplicates and part evidence are separable phenomena.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: 100 images, raw pre-NMS boxes clustered per object, quick manual part annotation, chi-square test on multi-mode rate vs part presence.

one_line: Score-ordered NMS keeps the most confident box, not the best-localized one, and the kept-vs-best localization gap is a measurable, correctable bias
problem: NMS uses classification confidence as the sort key, silently assuming the most confident box is also the best-localized; when confidence and IoU are imperfectly correlated, NMS systematically discards better boxes.
core_hypothesis: For a meaningful fraction of detections, a suppressed box has higher IoU with GT than the kept box, and this fraction grows with object aspect-ratio extremity and occlusion; re-ranking clusters by a localization-quality estimate before suppression recovers this gap without new training.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring per-cluster oracle IoU (best suppressed box) versus kept-box IoU will show a positive gap concentrated in occluded and elongated objects, and simple weighted box fusion within clusters will close a majority of that gap.
why_important: This is free localization accuracy for every deployed detector at high IoU thresholds where downstream tasks like tracking and measurement are most sensitive.
why_possibly_novel: IoU-prediction heads and box voting exist, but a systematic decomposition of exactly how much localization mAP is lost to score-ordered suppression, stratified by object geometry, has not been published as a diagnostic.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For an off-the-shelf detector on a val set, log all pre-NMS boxes with cluster assignments, compute kept-IoU vs cluster-max-IoU per GT object, stratify by aspect ratio and occlusion flags, then evaluate cluster-mean box fusion.
main_risk: Modern detectors with centerness or IoU-aware scores may already have made the gap negligible, leaving nothing to recover.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Confidence ordering in NMS is essentially harmless because confidence and localization quality are strongly correlated in trained detectors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The correlation between confidence and IoU may be strong precisely in the regimes where the gap would matter, making the recoverable fraction tiny.
fastest_falsification: A few hours: instrument NMS on one detector, compute the kept-vs-oracle IoU histogram on 1000 images; a near-zero gap kills the idea.

one_line: Per-class NMS lets visually similar class pairs double-count the same object because each class's box hides below the other's suppression, inflating count-based downstream tasks
problem: Standard per-class NMS never compares boxes across classes, so an object ambiguous between two classes (cup vs vase, van vs truck) can emit two surviving high-overlap boxes, corrupting object counting and tracking initialization.
core_hypothesis: Cross-class duplicate pairs are not uniformly distributed but concentrate on confusable class pairs whose confusion structure is predictable from classifier logit correlations, so a targeted cross-class suppression on high-confusion pairs removes double counts without harming legitimate containment cases like person-on-bicycle.
falsifiable_prediction: The rate of surviving box pairs with IoU above 0.7 but different class labels will exceed by an order of magnitude what independent errors predict, and will rank-correlate with the classes' logit confusion matrix measured on crops.
why_important: Counting applications (inventory, wildlife surveys, crowd estimates) silently over-count with per-class NMS, and the fix is a lookup table rather than retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Class-agnostic NMS is known as a blunt alternative, but a data-driven middle ground that suppresses only across confusable pairs, validated against containment relationships, appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run per-class NMS, extract all surviving cross-class pairs with IoU above 0.7, manually judge 300 pairs as same-object or containment, and test whether same-object pairs concentrate in high logit-confusion class pairs.
main_risk: Legitimate overlapping-class cases (clothing on person, food on plate) may dominate the high-IoU cross-class pairs, making any suppression harmful.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Per-class NMS is the correct default and cross-class overlaps are almost always distinct nested objects, not duplicates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmarks with fine-grained taxonomies may already show most high-IoU cross-class pairs are containment, in which case the double-count rate is negligible.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: extract cross-class high-IoU survivors from 2000 images and eyeball 100 of them; if under 10 percent are true duplicates, drop the idea.

one_line: Soft-NMS gains are a dataset-density artifact: the soft-vs-hard ranking flips as a function of occlusion statistics, so the community's default choice encodes COCO's density
problem: Soft-NMS is widely believed to be a safe drop-in improvement, but its decay function trades duplicate retention against crowd recall in a way that depends on how often true objects overlap, which varies enormously across deployment domains.
core_hypothesis: There is a crossover point in the distribution of GT-to-GT IoU beyond which soft-NMS beats hard NMS and below which it adds score noise that hurts precision; the crossover is estimable from unlabeled data via pre-NMS overlap statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing eval subsets binned by GT-pair overlap will show a monotone reversal: hard NMS wins on low-overlap bins, soft-NMS on high-overlap bins, with the crossover at a similar overlap statistic across different detectors.
why_important: Practitioners could choose the suppression scheme per domain from unlabeled statistics instead of copying benchmark defaults that may be wrong for their data.
why_possibly_novel: Soft-NMS ablations report aggregate mAP on standard benchmarks; a controlled decomposition by GT overlap structure with a domain-transfer prescription appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bin COCO-style val images by max GT-pair IoU, evaluate hard vs soft NMS per bin with fixed detections, check for a consistent crossover, then verify the crossover statistic predicts the winner on a held-out crowd dataset.
main_risk: The crossover may depend on the detector's score distribution as much as on data density, breaking the domain-statistic prescription.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Soft-NMS is a weakly dominant improvement over hard NMS that at worst does nothing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score-threshold interactions downstream may mask any density-dependent structure, making both schemes effectively equivalent at deployment operating points.
fastest_falsification: One day: fixed cached detections, evaluate both schemes across overlap bins on two datasets; no consistent crossover kills it.

one_line: A large share of reported gains from NMS variants are score-reranking effects on the mAP integral, not changes in which objects are found
problem: Papers report mAP gains from suppression variants, but mAP is sensitive to the ordering of detections; a method can gain mAP by reordering scores without changing the detected set, misleading practitioners who deploy at fixed thresholds.
core_hypothesis: Decomposing mAP deltas from NMS variants into (a) set-difference effects at deployment thresholds and (b) pure reordering effects will show reordering dominates for most published variants, implying negligible benefit for threshold-based deployments.
falsifiable_prediction: For several NMS variants applied to identical raw detections, the fixed-threshold F1 delta will be near zero while mAP deltas remain positive, and the mAP delta will shrink dramatically when scores are quantized to coarse bins.
why_important: It reframes a whole subliterature: if gains are reranking artifacts, deployment guidance should ignore them, and evaluation should report fixed-threshold metrics alongside mAP.
why_possibly_novel: The reranking-vs-set decomposition for suppression methods is a simple audit nobody appears to have published systematically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cache raw detections from one detector, apply hard NMS, soft-NMS, and box-fusion variants, compute mAP and fixed-threshold F1 at several operating points, then repeat with score quantization to isolate ordering effects.
main_risk: Some variants may genuinely change the detected set in crowded scenes, making the audit conclusion variant-specific rather than general.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: An mAP gain from a suppression variant reflects genuinely better detections.
why_it_might_be_wrong: mAP-vs-threshold-metric divergence may be small in practice because reordering also moves boxes across typical deployment thresholds.
fastest_falsification: Half a day with cached detections: compare mAP deltas against fixed-threshold F1 deltas for three variants; strong agreement kills the claim.

one_line: In crowded scenes most recall is lost inside the suppression stage, not the network: pre-NMS oracle recall stays high while post-NMS recall collapses
problem: Crowd detection failures are usually attributed to feature-level limitations, prompting expensive architectural work, but if the raw detection pool already covers most crowd instances, the bottleneck is suppression logic.
core_hypothesis: For dense same-class crowds, the pre-NMS box pool contains boxes matching most GT instances at IoU 0.5, and the recall gap opens almost entirely during suppression; therefore crowd-detection research should target assignment-aware suppression rather than backbone capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: Oracle matching of pre-NMS boxes to GT in heavy-crowd images will show recall far above post-NMS recall, with the gap growing monotonically in instance density, across at least three detector families.
why_important: It redirects effort: if suppression is the bottleneck, cheap inference-stage research beats retraining, and crowd benchmarks should report pre-NMS oracle recall as a standard diagnostic.
why_possibly_novel: Pre-NMS oracle recall is occasionally mentioned in passing; establishing it as the dominant crowd failure decomposition across architectures with density stratification would be a new empirical claim.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a crowd-heavy dataset, compute oracle pre-NMS recall vs post-NMS recall per density decile for an anchor-based, an anchor-free, and a set-prediction detector.
main_risk: Pre-NMS pools are huge, so oracle matching may flatter the network by counting low-score accidental overlaps that no realistic suppression could keep.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Crowd failures reflect representational limits requiring architectural innovation like set prediction or crowd-specific heads.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the accidental-overlap confound is controlled with score floors, the oracle gap may shrink to the point where features really are the bottleneck.
fastest_falsification: One day: oracle-vs-actual recall curves on one crowd dataset with a score floor at the deployment threshold; a small gap kills the redirection claim.

one_line: DETR-style decoders telegraph their duplicates: instability of query-to-object assignment across decoder layers at inference predicts which objects get duplicate or dropped predictions
problem: One-to-one matched detectors are advertised as NMS-free, yet they still emit duplicates and misses in hard scenes, and there is no inference-time signal for when the one-to-one property is about to fail.
core_hypothesis: When two queries swap or share responsibility for an object across successive decoder layers (measured by box-center trajectories and pairwise IoU between layer-wise predictions), the final output is far more likely to contain a duplicate or a miss, making layer-wise assignment stability a free reliability signal.
falsifiable_prediction: A simple instability score computed from intermediate decoder outputs will rank-order images by duplicate rate with strong correlation, and gating a light NMS only on unstable clusters will remove duplicates without hurting stable predictions.
why_important: It gives set-prediction detectors a principled self-diagnostic and a targeted fallback, avoiding the blanket reintroduction of NMS that negates their design.
why_possibly_novel: Auxiliary-layer predictions are used for training losses, but exploiting inter-layer assignment dynamics at inference as a duplicate predictor appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a pretrained DETR-family model to dump per-layer boxes, define an instability metric over layer trajectories, correlate with duplicate and miss events on val, then test instability-gated suppression.
main_risk: Instability may be ubiquitous in crowded scenes and rare elsewhere, adding no information beyond raw density.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: One-to-one matching makes suppression obsolete and intermediate decoder layers matter only as training-time auxiliaries.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Final-layer self-attention may already resolve most inter-layer instability, leaving the signal uncorrelated with output errors.
fastest_falsification: One day: dump per-layer outputs on 1000 images, compute instability vs duplicate incidence AUROC; chance-level AUROC kills it.

one_line: Detection flicker under numerically perturbed inference (fp16, quantization) partly traces to unstable NMS tie-breaking, not feature degradation
problem: Deployment teams observe detections appearing and disappearing between nearly identical runs or frames after quantization, and blame representation fragility, but suppression order depends on score comparisons that flip under tiny numeric perturbations.
core_hypothesis: Near-tie score pairs within NMS clusters are common, so sub-1e-3 score perturbations flip suppression order and cascade into different surviving sets; a deterministic tie-breaking rule keyed on box geometry rather than raw score order removes a measurable share of run-to-run output variance.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding Gaussian noise of magnitude comparable to fp16 rounding to raw scores will change the post-NMS detection set on a nontrivial fraction of images, and the changed cases will be concentrated where within-cluster score gaps are below the noise scale.
why_important: Reproducibility and video stability are deployment-critical; attributing flicker correctly avoids wasted effort on quantization-aware retraining when a suppression fix suffices.
why_possibly_novel: Quantization studies measure mAP deltas; the combinatorial instability of suppression under score noise, and geometry-keyed tie-breaking as a remedy, appear unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run identical images through fp32 and fp16 pipelines, isolate output differences attributable to suppression order by replaying both score sets through identical NMS, and measure variance reduction from deterministic tie-breaking.
main_risk: Feature-level numeric differences may dominate so thoroughly that suppression-order effects are a rounding error on the rounding error.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Quantization-induced output changes reflect degraded features, and NMS is a deterministic postprocess not worth auditing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Well-separated score distributions in trained detectors may make near-ties rare enough to ignore.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: perturb cached scores with tiny noise, re-run NMS, count changed detection sets across 5000 images; near-zero change rate kills it.

one_line: Test-time-augmentation box averaging geometrically shrinks elongated and rotated objects, so TTA helps blob-like classes while quietly hurting thin structures
problem: TTA with box voting is applied uniformly, but averaging axis-aligned boxes predicted under flips and scales is a geometric operation whose bias depends on object shape, which nobody stratifies.
core_hypothesis: For elongated or diagonal objects, the axis-aligned boxes from augmented views differ systematically, and their average is biased toward smaller, more central boxes; TTA therefore redistributes AP from thin classes to compact classes rather than improving uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-class TTA deltas will correlate negatively with mean object elongation, and replacing mean fusion with union-then-refit fusion will flip the sign of TTA's effect for the most elongated classes.
why_important: TTA is a standard competition and production trick; knowing it has a shape-dependent failure mode changes when to apply it and how to fuse.
why_possibly_novel: TTA ablations report aggregate gains; a geometric analysis of fusion bias as a function of object shape appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a detector with and without flip-scale TTA, compute per-class AP deltas, regress on annotation-derived elongation statistics, then swap in union-based fusion and re-test the most elongated classes.
main_risk: Class-level confounds (thin classes may also be rare or small) could mimic the geometric effect without the causal mechanism.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: TTA with box voting is a shape-agnostic, weakly positive ensemble trick.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern fusion schemes weight by confidence and may already suppress the geometric averaging artifact.
fastest_falsification: One day: per-class TTA delta vs elongation scatter on one benchmark; no negative trend kills it.

one_line: Detector confidence conflates presence and localization quality, and the two are separately calibratable with different temperature structure
problem: A single confidence scalar must express both whether an object exists and how well the box fits, so downstream users filtering on confidence cannot distinguish a certain-but-sloppy box from an uncertain-but-tight one.
core_hypothesis: The reliability diagrams for existence (does the box match any GT at IoU 0.1) and for localization (IoU conditional on existence) have different shapes and respond to different calibration transforms, so a two-channel calibrated output strictly dominates single-scalar calibration for threshold-based decisions.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting separate calibration maps for existence probability and expected IoU will yield lower joint negative log-likelihood than any single-temperature calibration of the combined score, and the improvement will concentrate in occluded and small objects.
why_important: Downstream systems make different decisions for presence errors vs localization errors (a tracker can fix a sloppy box but not a hallucination); giving them decomposed uncertainty is nearly free.
why_possibly_novel: IoU-aware scoring exists in training-time forms; a post-hoc, detector-agnostic decomposition of the confidence scalar into calibrated presence and localization channels with a dominance proof appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On cached detections from two detectors, fit existence calibration and conditional-IoU regression on half the val set, evaluate joint likelihood and decision-cost curves against single-scalar calibration on the other half.
main_risk: Presence and localization quality may be so correlated in practice that the decomposition adds parameters without adding usable information.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: One confidence scalar per detection, possibly temperature-scaled, is sufficient for downstream use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: IoU-aware trained detectors may already have merged the two signals optimally, leaving no post-hoc gain.
fastest_falsification: One day: fit both calibrations on cached detections and compare held-out likelihood; no gain over single temperature kills it.

one_line: Detection miscalibration is scale-structured: per-object-size temperature scaling fixes what global temperature cannot, because small and large objects sit on opposite sides of the reliability curve
problem: Calibration of detectors is usually done with one global transform, but the evidence available per object scales with its pixel area, suggesting confidence errors have systematic size dependence that a global transform cannot repair.
core_hypothesis: Small objects are overconfident relative to their precision (few pixels, high feature noise, but trained with the same loss targets), while large objects are underconfident, so reliability curves stratified by object area will show opposite-signed calibration errors, fixable with a size-conditional temperature.
falsifiable_prediction: Expected calibration error computed per size stratum will show a sign flip between the smallest and largest strata for most detectors, and size-conditional temperature will cut overall detection ECE substantially more than the best global temperature.
why_important: Threshold-based deployments implicitly favor whichever size regime the global calibration happens to fit, systematically dropping small objects or admitting large false positives.
why_possibly_novel: Calibration for detection is understudied relative to classification, and the specific claim of a size-driven sign flip with a conditional fix appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute reliability diagrams per area quartile for three detectors on standard val sets, fit size-conditional temperatures, compare ECE and fixed-threshold F1 across strata.
main_risk: The apparent size effect may be an artifact of matching-threshold geometry (IoU is harsher for small boxes), requiring careful metric design to avoid circularity.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Calibration is a per-model scalar property; size effects on AP are about features, not confidence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: IoU-threshold harshness for small boxes may fully explain the stratified ECE without any genuine confidence pathology.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: stratified reliability diagrams with center-distance matching instead of IoU to control the geometric confound; no sign structure kills it.

one_line: The optimal confidence threshold shifts predictably across domains as a function of simple unlabeled image statistics, enabling label-free threshold transfer
problem: Teams tune the confidence threshold on a labeled source validation set, deploy into a shifted domain, and silently operate far from the new optimum because re-tuning requires labels they lack.
core_hypothesis: The dominant effect of moderate domain shift on a fixed detector is a monotone shift of the score distribution rather than a reshuffle of ranking, so the optimal threshold moves in a way predictable from unlabeled statistics such as score histogram quantiles, mean edge density, or contrast, allowing a transfer rule fit once across a few shifted domains.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a suite of corrupted and cross-domain test sets, the labeled-optimal threshold will correlate strongly with unlabeled score-distribution quantiles, and a transfer rule fit on half the domains will recover most of the F1 lost by keeping the source threshold on the held-out domains.
why_important: This converts an ubiquitous silent deployment failure into a cheap unlabeled-statistics computation, applicable to every fielded detector.
why_possibly_novel: Unsupervised accuracy estimation exists for classification; a threshold-transfer rule specifically for detection operating points from unlabeled detection-score statistics appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 15 shifted variants of a val set (corruptions, other datasets), compute labeled-optimal thresholds and unlabeled statistics, fit and cross-validate the transfer rule.
main_risk: Severe shifts change ranking not just scale, in which case no threshold rule helps and the method gives false comfort.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Operating thresholds must be re-tuned with labeled data per domain; unlabeled transfer is unreliable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score distributions may shift heterogeneously per class, so a single global threshold rule could fail even when per-class rules would work.
fastest_falsification: One day: corruption suite, plot labeled-optimal threshold vs unlabeled score quantiles; weak correlation kills it.

one_line: High-confidence background hallucinations have a distinct logit signature (anomalous margin structure) that separates them from true detections without retraining
problem: The most damaging detector errors in deployment are confident false positives on textured background, and they are indistinguishable from true positives by the confidence scalar alone.
core_hypothesis: True-object detections activate a coherent set of class logits (target class plus semantically related runners-up), while texture-driven hallucinations show incoherent runner-up structure; a margin-and-entropy feature over the full logit vector therefore separates hallucinations from hits at equal confidence.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched top-1 confidence, a two-feature classifier on logit margin and runner-up entropy will separate verified false positives from true positives with AUROC well above chance across multiple detector families.
why_important: A post-hoc hallucination filter that needs no retraining would directly cut the error type practitioners care most about, and its failure would also be informative about how detectors encode evidence.
why_possibly_novel: Full-logit-vector forensics for detection false positives, as opposed to classification OOD scoring, appears rarely studied; detection adds localization context that may sharpen or break the classification-derived intuitions.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect high-confidence detections on val, label them as TP or background-FP by GT matching, extract logit-vector features, train a tiny classifier with cross-validation, and test transfer to a second dataset.
main_risk: Sigmoid-based multi-label heads in modern detectors may not produce meaningful runner-up structure, gutting the feature set.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: At equal confidence, false and true positives are not separable without extra models or extra data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hallucinations may be caused by genuinely object-like feature activations, in which case their logit structure is exactly as coherent as real objects.
fastest_falsification: One day: extract logit features for matched-confidence TP/FP sets on one detector; AUROC near 0.5 kills it.

one_line: A distinct mode of detector 'false positives' consists of correctly detected objects missing from GT, and its size is estimable without new annotation via cross-detector agreement
problem: Benchmarks count every unmatched detection as a false positive, but training sets with incomplete annotation teach evaluation to punish real detections; the community lacks a cheap way to estimate how much measured precision is annotation artifact.
core_hypothesis: Detections flagged as false positives that are independently reproduced by architecturally diverse detectors at consistent locations are enriched for missing GT rather than shared error, so cross-detector agreement provides an unbiased-enough estimator of the annotation-miss rate and a corrected precision metric.
falsifiable_prediction: Human re-annotation of agreement-clustered false positives will confirm a majority as real objects, while non-agreed false positives will confirm at a much lower rate, validating agreement as an enrichment signal with quantifiable purity.
why_important: It changes how precision is interpreted on every incompletely annotated benchmark and gives teams a labeled-data-free audit of their eval sets.
why_possibly_novel: Missing-annotation studies exist for specific datasets; an agreement-based estimator producing corrected precision with purity bounds, applicable to any dataset, appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three diverse detectors on a val set, cluster unmatched detections by cross-model agreement, sample 200 agreed and 200 non-agreed cases for human verification, compute enrichment and corrected precision.
main_risk: Diverse detectors share training data and thus share systematic hallucinations, which would contaminate the agreement signal in exactly the worst way.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: False positive counts on standard benchmarks are trustworthy measures of detector error.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-dataset-induced shared hallucinations may make cross-detector agreement a poor proxy for ground truth.
fastest_falsification: One day: agreement clustering plus quick human check of 100 agreed FPs; if under a third are real objects, the estimator is too impure.

one_line: The shape of a detector's calibration curve is determined by its loss family: rank-based and focal losses produce signature miscalibration profiles that dictate which post-hoc fix works
problem: Post-hoc calibration methods are chosen by habit (temperature scaling) regardless of how the detector was trained, yet losses like focal loss deliberately distort the probability semantics of scores in ways temperature cannot invert.
core_hypothesis: Detectors trained with focal loss, rank-based losses, and plain cross-entropy fall into distinct calibration-curve families (e.g., focal loss producing systematic underconfidence concentrated at high scores), so the correct post-hoc transform is predictable from the loss alone, without any reliability measurement.
falsifiable_prediction: Grouping many public detector checkpoints by training loss and overlaying their reliability diagrams will show tight within-group clustering and between-group separation, and the best post-hoc method per group will differ systematically (e.g., beta calibration beating temperature for focal-loss models).
why_important: It converts detection calibration from per-model measurement into a lookup by training recipe, and clarifies that loss choices silently pre-commit deployment behavior.
why_possibly_novel: Loss-dependent calibration shape is known anecdotally for classification focal loss; a systematic detection-side taxonomy with a prescription table appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a dozen public checkpoints spanning three loss families, compute detection reliability diagrams under a fixed matching protocol, cluster the curves, and evaluate three calibration methods per family.
main_risk: Backbone, schedule, and NMS differences across public checkpoints may swamp the loss signature, requiring controlled retraining that raises the cost.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Calibration is a per-model idiosyncrasy to be measured, and temperature scaling is a universal adequate fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The interaction of losses with detection-specific machinery (assignment, NMS) may destroy any clean loss-family signature that exists in classification.
fastest_falsification: One day: reliability curves for six checkpoints across two loss families; no visible family clustering kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab detectors multiply objectness and image-text similarity as if commensurable, and per-component temperature fixes rare-class ranking for free
problem: Open-vocabulary detection scores typically fuse a class-agnostic objectness with a text-region similarity via product or geometric mean, but the two components have wildly different dynamic ranges and miscalibration, distorting rankings especially for rare vocabulary.
core_hypothesis: The similarity component is systematically compressed for rare or long text queries while objectness is not, so a two-parameter recalibration (separate exponents per component) fit on a handful of classes transfers to unseen vocabulary and improves rare-class ranking without touching the model.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping the fusion exponents on a small class subset will find optima far from the default equal weighting, and applying them to held-out rare classes will improve their AP while leaving frequent-class AP within noise.
why_important: A two-scalar post-hoc fix that improves open-vocab rare-class detection would be immediately deployable everywhere these detectors run.
why_possibly_novel: Fusion weighting exists in specific systems as tuned constants; framing it as a calibration problem with transfer-to-unseen-vocabulary validation appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take an off-the-shelf open-vocab detector, grid-search fusion exponents on 20 classes, evaluate on disjoint rare classes, compare against default fusion and per-class oracle.
main_risk: Optimal exponents may be strongly class-dependent, in which case a global recalibration transfers nothing.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The published fusion formula of an open-vocab detector is part of the method and near-optimal as released.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detector authors may have already tuned fusion on broad vocabulary, leaving held-out gains negligible.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: exponent grid on one model and one benchmark split; flat response surface kills it.

one_line: Detector confidence is non-monotone in occlusion level: moderate occlusion hurts scores more than heavy occlusion, creating an unmonitored blind spot at mid-occlusion
problem: Occlusion robustness is reported as an average, but if confidence dips hardest at intermediate occlusion (where the object is visible enough to detect but distorted enough to score poorly), threshold-based systems will fail precisely in the common partial-occlusion regime while metrics dominated by extremes look fine.
core_hypothesis: As occlusion increases, detections transition from confident-correct to low-confidence-correct to confidently-absent (missed entirely, hence excluded from confidence stats), producing a U-shaped observed-confidence curve and a mid-occlusion recall cliff at deployment thresholds.
falsifiable_prediction: Using synthetic occluders swept from 0 to 90 percent coverage on real objects, the mean confidence of still-detected objects will be non-monotone with a minimum at intermediate coverage, and fixed-threshold recall will drop fastest in the middle band.
why_important: Safety-critical systems (driving, robotics) encounter mid-occlusion constantly; knowing the confidence curve shape dictates threshold policy and targeted augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion studies report detection rate vs occlusion; the selection-effect-corrected confidence curve and its threshold implications appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paste controlled occluders over GT objects at swept coverage ratios, record per-object confidence and detection outcome, plot the selection-corrected confidence and recall curves for two detectors.
main_risk: Synthetic occluders may introduce edge artifacts that detectors key on, making the curve an artifact of the paste operation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Confidence degrades monotonically with occlusion severity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With natural occluders the missed-detection selection effect may dominate so early that the observable curve is monotone after all.
fastest_falsification: One day: synthetic occlusion sweep on 300 objects, plot confidence vs coverage; a monotone curve kills it.

one_line: Cross-FPN-level self-agreement is a better correctness signal than confidence: objects detected consistently at adjacent pyramid levels are far more likely to be true positives
problem: Detectors assign each object to one pyramid level and read confidence there, discarding the information of whether neighboring levels also saw the object, which costs a free reliability signal.
core_hypothesis: True objects produce correlated responses at adjacent FPN levels (the evidence is scale-robust), while hallucinations tend to be single-level phenomena tied to a specific receptive-field texture resonance; an agreement score across levels therefore predicts correctness beyond confidence.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched confidence, detections with high adjacent-level response agreement will have substantially higher precision than single-level detections, and adding the agreement feature to a reranker will improve AP at high-precision operating points.
why_important: It is a free, architecture-native uncertainty signal for the entire FPN-based detector family, requiring only reading activations that are already computed.
why_possibly_novel: Level assignment research aims to pick the best level for training; using inference-time cross-level consistency as a confidence auxiliary appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument an FPN detector to record per-level class responses at each detection's location, compute an agreement score, stratify precision by agreement at fixed confidence bands on val.
main_risk: Small objects legitimately activate only one level, so the signal may just re-encode object size rather than correctness.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The assigned level's confidence contains all usable evidence; other levels are noise for that object.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Level-assignment training may actively decorrelate adjacent levels, destroying the agreement signal by design.
fastest_falsification: One day: log per-level responses on 2000 images, precision-vs-agreement curves within confidence bands, controlling for size; no stratification kills it.

one_line: Leaderboard mAP and deployed fixed-threshold performance diverge enough to reorder detector rankings, and the divergence is measurable as a 'deployment gap' statistic
problem: Model selection is done by mAP, which integrates over all thresholds, but deployment uses one threshold; if models differ in score-distribution shape, the mAP ranking can invert at operating points, and nobody reports how often.
core_hypothesis: Among detector pairs within a small mAP margin, a substantial fraction exhibit rank inversion in fixed-threshold F1 at common operating points, and the inversion probability is predictable from the difference in their precision-recall curve shapes near the operating region.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a pool of public checkpoints will find pairs with equal-or-worse mAP but better F1 at every practical threshold, and a curve-shape statistic will predict inversion pairs with useful accuracy.
why_important: If rankings invert regularly, the community's model-selection practice systematically picks worse deployment models, and papers should report operating-point metrics.
why_possibly_novel: The mAP-vs-threshold-metric tension is folklore; quantifying inversion frequency across a broad model pool and giving a predictive statistic would make it actionable.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 20 public checkpoints on one benchmark, compute mAP and F1 at five thresholds, count ranking inversions among close-mAP pairs, and fit the shape statistic.
main_risk: Inversions may be rare among well-trained models, making the finding a corner case rather than a practice-changing result.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Higher mAP means a better detector for deployment, up to negligible exceptions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score distributions of modern detectors may be similar enough that PR curves rarely cross in the operating region.
fastest_falsification: One day: mAP vs threshold-F1 tables for a dozen checkpoints; zero inversions kills the significance claim.

one_line: Confidence is a poor proxy for downstream utility: detections equally confident are unequally useful to trackers and planners, and utility-calibrated scores change system behavior
problem: Perception stacks threshold on detection confidence, implicitly assuming confidence ranks detections by their value to downstream modules, but a confident box with slightly wrong extent can be worse for a tracker than a hesitant but tight box.
core_hypothesis: Downstream utility (tracking continuity, planning safety margins) is a function of localization error structure and temporal stability that confidence does not capture; a utility model trained on downstream outcomes reranks detections differently from confidence and improves end-to-end metrics at equal detection budget.
falsifiable_prediction: In a detector-plus-tracker pipeline, replacing confidence thresholding with a learned utility score (features: confidence, box stability, size, edge contrast) will improve MOT-style association metrics at matched detection count, with the gain concentrated in partially occluded targets.
why_important: It challenges the universal interface between detection and downstream modules, suggesting the scalar handed over should be task-conditional.
why_possibly_novel: Detection-for-downstream evaluation exists piecemeal; learning an explicit utility recalibration and demonstrating reranking gains at fixed budget appears uncommon.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a public tracker on a video benchmark, define per-detection utility labels from association outcomes, train a small reranker, and A/B the pipeline at matched detection counts.
main_risk: Utility may be dominated by confidence after all, making the reranker a complicated identity function.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Optimizing and thresholding detection confidence is the right interface to downstream tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: End-to-end trained perception stacks may make the handoff moot before this line of work matures.
fastest_falsification: Two days: train the reranker on one tracking benchmark and A/B association metrics; no improvement kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab detection AP per category is driven more by the category name's text-corpus frequency than by visual difficulty, and renaming to a frequent synonym changes AP
problem: Open-vocabulary detectors are evaluated as if the class name were a neutral handle for a visual concept, but the text encoder's representation quality varies enormously with how often the name appears in pretraining text, confounding what benchmarks measure.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed set of test images, swapping a category's query string to a more corpus-frequent synonym or a less frequent one will move AP substantially and systematically in the direction of frequency, demonstrating that a large share of measured open-vocab difficulty lives in the text side, not the visual side.
falsifiable_prediction: Across dozens of categories with attested synonyms, AP under the frequent synonym will exceed AP under the rare synonym for a large majority of categories, with the gap correlating with an independent estimate of term frequency.
why_important: It reframes open-vocab evaluation (name choice is a hidden hyperparameter), suggests free AP via synonym selection, and separates text-representation failure from visual failure for targeted fixes.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity is known qualitatively; a controlled synonym-swap study isolating name frequency as the causal variable with fixed imagery appears missing for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 50 categories with clean synonym pairs, run one open-vocab detector on a fixed test set under both names, plot AP deltas against frequency estimates from a public corpus.
main_risk: Synonyms are rarely perfectly co-extensive (every 'sofa' vs 'couch' pair carries slight sense differences), which could contaminate the frequency effect.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Category AP measures visual detectability; the specific query string is a minor implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern text encoders may represent moderately rare object names well enough that frequency effects are second-order to visual difficulty.
fastest_falsification: One day: 20 synonym pairs, one model, AP deltas vs frequency; no correlation kills it.

one_line: Size and position words in text prompts act as geometric priors in open-vocab detectors, shifting which boxes are retrieved independently of semantics
problem: Practitioners engineer prompts like 'a small distant traffic light' assuming semantic refinement, but the geometric adjectives may directly bias box size and location selection, a mechanism nobody has isolated from the semantic content.
core_hypothesis: Appending size or position words to an otherwise identical query systematically shifts the size and position distribution of retrieved boxes even when the scene content is held fixed, because the text encoder embeds geometric words along directions the region-text alignment reads as scale and location preferences.
falsifiable_prediction: On fixed images, queries differing only in size adjectives will produce box-area distributions shifted in the adjective's direction, including retrieving different physical objects, and the shift magnitude will be consistent across unrelated noun categories.
why_important: If geometric words are usable control knobs, prompt-based scale steering becomes a free deployment tool; if they are ignored, prompt engineering folklore needs correction.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt ablation studies focus on synonym or template variation; the isolation of geometric adjectives as box-statistics controllers appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a matrix of noun-times-adjective queries, run an open-vocab detector on a fixed image set, compare retrieved-box area and position distributions across adjectives with the noun held constant.
main_risk: Effects may exist but be so noisy across scenes that they cannot function as a reliable control knob, landing the result in an uninteresting middle.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Adjectives in prompts refine semantics; box geometry is determined by the image, not the query wording.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Region-text alignment training may have squeezed out non-nominal information, making geometric words inert padding.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: three size adjectives times ten nouns on 200 images, compare area distributions; no shift kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab detectors detect the head noun and largely ignore compositional modifiers, so 'red valve wheel' style queries silently degrade to 'wheel' with a measurable modifier-compliance rate
problem: Industrial users query compositional phrases expecting the detector to bind attributes to objects, but region-text similarity may collapse to the head noun, returning all instances of the noun regardless of the modifier, without any signal that the modifier was ignored.
core_hypothesis: For compositional queries, the ranking of retrieved boxes is nearly identical to the head-noun-only ranking (rank correlation close to 1), except for lexicalized compounds frequent in pretraining text; a modifier-compliance metric (fraction of retrieved boxes actually satisfying the modifier) will be low and predictable from compound frequency.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes containing both modifier-satisfying and modifier-violating instances of the same noun, the detector's top-k will include violating instances at a rate close to their base rate, demonstrating near-zero modifier binding for non-lexicalized compounds.
why_important: It defines and measures a failure mode that users currently discover only through deployment incidents, and gives a metric (modifier compliance) that future methods must report.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute-binding failures are documented for CLIP classification; porting this to detection with a compliance metric on controlled contrast scenes appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or synthesize 200 scenes with contrastive object pairs (same noun, different attribute), query with composed phrases, compute modifier compliance and rank correlation to head-noun queries.
main_risk: Contrastive scene curation is labor-intensive and synthetic scenes may not transfer to natural imagery conclusions.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Open-vocab detectors understand the full query phrase; longer more specific queries give more specific detections.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection-tuned text encoders trained on grounding data with rich referring expressions may bind modifiers far better than CLIP-style encoders.
fastest_falsification: One day: 50 contrast pairs, compliance rate for composed vs head-noun queries; high compliance kills it.

one_line: Negative vocabulary is the underused half of open-vocab detection: adding confusable distractor class names cuts false positives more than any tuning of the positive prompt
problem: Practitioners tune positive prompts endlessly but query the detector with only the classes they want, leaving the score normalization without competitive alternatives, so near-miss concepts absorb into the target class as false positives.
core_hypothesis: Open-vocab scores are effectively contrastive against the provided vocabulary, so explicitly querying likely confusers (for 'wolf', adding 'dog', 'coyote') redistributes score mass and lowers false-positive rates at fixed recall more than positive-prompt engineering, with the best negatives predictable from text-embedding neighborhoods.
falsifiable_prediction: Adding a handful of embedding-neighbor distractor names to the query vocabulary will improve precision at fixed recall on categories with natural confusers, while adding random distractors will not, and the gain will exceed the best-of-N positive prompt variants.
why_important: It is a zero-training deployment technique with a principled selection rule, directly attacking the confident-false-positive problem in open-vocab systems.
why_possibly_novel: Some benchmarks query full vocabularies implicitly; the deliberate, minimal, embedding-guided negative set as a tuning knob with head-to-head comparison against prompt engineering appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pick 20 categories with known confusers, evaluate precision-recall with and without embedding-selected negatives and with random negatives, compare against a positive-prompt tuning baseline of equal effort.
main_risk: Score fusion in some architectures may not be vocabulary-contrastive at all (per-query sigmoids), nullifying the mechanism.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Query only what you want to find; improving detection means improving the positive prompt or the model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sigmoid-scored open-vocab heads score each query independently, in which case negatives change nothing and the idea dies on architecture choice.
fastest_falsification: Two hours: check whether adding a distractor changes target-class scores on one sigmoid-head and one softmax-head model; no interaction on both kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab detectors pay a vocabulary-size tax: AP on a fixed class degrades as unrelated query classes are added, quantifying an unreported interference effect
problem: Deployments grow query vocabularies over time assuming class additions are free, but score normalization and attention over queries can make classes compete, silently degrading previously working detections.
core_hypothesis: Per-class AP is a decreasing function of total vocabulary size even when added classes are semantically unrelated, with the decay rate depending on architecture (softmax-normalized heads decaying faster than independent-sigmoid heads), implying vocabulary sharding at inference recovers the loss.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring AP for a fixed probe class while sweeping vocabulary from 1 to thousands of entries will show monotone degradation on normalization-based architectures and near-flat curves on independent-scoring ones, and sharded querying will match the small-vocabulary AP.
why_important: It gives deployment teams a concrete scaling law and a free mitigation, and gives architects a measurable design criterion for query independence.
why_possibly_novel: Vocabulary scaling is discussed for classification; a controlled per-class interference curve for detection architectures with the sharding mitigation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix five probe classes and their test images, sweep vocabulary size with random unrelated fillers, plot per-class AP vs vocabulary size for two architectures, then test sharded inference.
main_risk: Degradation may be negligible until extreme vocabulary sizes, making the tax real but irrelevant to practice.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Adding query classes to an open-vocab detector does not affect existing classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern grounding architectures may cap cross-query interaction by design, having already solved the interference privately.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: AP of one probe class at vocabulary sizes 1, 10, 100, 1000 on one model; flat curve kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab errors on rare classes are systematically superclass substitutions, because rare-class text embeddings collapse toward their frequent hypernyms
problem: Rare-class failures in open-vocab detection are reported as undifferentiated low AP, hiding whether the model fails to see the object or sees it but names it generically, which require different fixes.
core_hypothesis: Text embeddings of rare category names sit close to their frequent superclass in the encoder's space, so the detector localizes the object correctly but the similarity ranking prefers the superclass; error analysis will show rare-class misses re-emerge as correct-box wrong-label detections of the hypernym at high rates.
falsifiable_prediction: For rare classes with a frequent hypernym in vocabulary, a large fraction of missed GT will have an overlapping detection labeled with the hypernym, and the fraction will correlate with embedding distance between the class and its hypernym.
why_important: If rare-class failure is mostly naming, cheap fixes exist (hierarchical scoring, embedding correction) that are very different from collecting more rare-class images.
why_possibly_novel: Hierarchical error analysis exists for closed-set classification; connecting open-vocab rare-class AP to text-embedding hypernym collapse with a predictive distance measure appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a long-tail benchmark, match missed rare-class GT against detections of hypernym labels, compute the substitution rate, and regress it on text-embedding distances.
main_risk: Localization may genuinely fail for rare classes (never proposed at all), making substitution a minor mode.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Rare-class open-vocab failure means the model cannot detect the object, requiring more data or better features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-agnostic proposal stages may be the true bottleneck for rare objects, in which case no naming fix helps.
fastest_falsification: One day: substitution-rate analysis on one long-tail benchmark; low substitution rate kills it.

one_line: Querying part names in open-vocab detectors returns whole objects at a high rate because region-text alignment was trained object-centric, defining a measurable part-query failure mode
problem: Users query 'wheel', 'handle', or 'door' expecting part localization, but training pairs regions with object-level captions, so the model may have never learned sub-object alignment, and nobody reports part-query behavior systematically.
core_hypothesis: For queries naming canonical parts of common objects, a large fraction of top-ranked boxes will cover the whole containing object rather than the part, with the whole-object rate predictable from how often the part name co-occurs with the object name in captions; a box-size prior conditioned on the query partially corrects it.
falsifiable_prediction: On images with annotated parts, part-name queries will yield whole-object boxes at rates far above chance, and the rate will drop for parts that frequently appear detached in imagery (wheels lying alone) versus parts that never appear detached (noses).
why_important: Part queries are central to robotics and inspection use cases; quantifying and predicting this failure defines the gap for part-aware open-vocab training.
why_possibly_novel: Part-whole confusion is discussed in segmentation; a quantitative open-vocab detection study with a detachment-frequency predictor appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use a part-annotated dataset, query part names on an open-vocab detector, classify each top-k box as part, whole, or other, and correlate whole-rates with caption co-occurrence and detachment statistics.
main_risk: Part annotations are scarce and inconsistent across datasets, making the measurement itself noisy.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Open-vocab detectors can find anything nameable, including parts, just with lower accuracy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Grounding-style training data includes referring expressions about parts, which may have taught sub-object alignment better than the caption-centric account predicts.
fastest_falsification: One day: ten part queries on 200 part-annotated images, part-vs-whole box classification; low whole-object rate kills it.

one_line: Grammatical number in open-vocab queries steers instance grouping: plural queries bias toward group boxes and merged detections, singular toward instance boxes
problem: Query phrasing is assumed not to affect the fundamental individuation of objects, but caption supervision pairs plural phrases with multi-object regions, potentially teaching a grouping prior that activates on plural morphology.
core_hypothesis: For scenes with multiple instances, plural queries produce measurably more merged boxes covering several instances, and singular queries produce more per-instance boxes, because the text encoder's number feature aligns with region granularity learned from captions.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-instance scenes, the merged-box rate under plural queries will exceed the singular-query rate by a consistent margin across categories, and the effect will be stronger for categories that typically appear in groups in captions (birds, sheep) than for typically-solitary categories.
why_important: It reveals that individuation, a supposedly visual competence, is partially controlled by query morphology, which matters for counting applications and suggests a free control knob for group-vs-instance detection.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt sensitivity studies vary templates and synonyms; grammatical number as a granularity controller in detection appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select multi-instance scenes for 20 categories, query singular and plural forms, measure per-query merged-box rates via GT matching, compare across group-typical and solitary-typical categories.
main_risk: Tokenization may make singular and plural forms nearly identical embeddings for many nouns, diluting the effect below detectability.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Object individuation is determined by the image and the detector; query wording does not change what counts as one object.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection heads may operate on region proposals fixed before text fusion, structurally preventing morphology from affecting grouping.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: singular vs plural queries for five group-typical categories on 100 scenes; equal merged-box rates kills it.

one_line: Attribute words in open-vocab queries relocate boxes toward the attribute-bearing subregion instead of gating detection, producing systematically distorted boxes for attribute queries
problem: Queries like 'black dog' are assumed to select among objects, but if attribute evidence is spatially localized (a dark patch), similarity-driven localization may shift or shrink the box toward the evidence region, corrupting geometry in a way mAP-style evaluation on attribute datasets rarely isolates.
core_hypothesis: For objects with spatially non-uniform attributes, attribute-composed queries produce boxes measurably shifted or shrunk toward the attribute-bearing region compared to noun-only queries on the same object, because region-text similarity peaks where attribute and object evidence co-occur.
falsifiable_prediction: On objects with annotated attribute subregions (two-tone animals, partially painted vehicles), the centroid displacement between noun-query and attribute-query boxes will point toward the attribute region at rates far above chance, and box area will shrink correspondingly.
why_important: Attribute queries are a flagship use case of open-vocab detection; a systematic geometric distortion would matter for measurement applications and reveal how alignment arbitrates between object extent and evidence location.
why_possibly_novel: Attribute binding studies measure classification correctness; the geometric displacement signature of attribute evidence appears unmeasured in detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate 150 objects with localized attributes, run noun-only and attribute-composed queries, compute box displacement vectors relative to attribute-region centroids, test directionality against chance.
main_risk: The effect may exist only for weakly trained models and vanish in grounding-trained detectors, reducing the finding to a model-specific artifact.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Attributes in queries act as filters over candidate objects; box geometry comes from the object's visual extent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Box regression may be handled by a proposal head that never sees the text, structurally preventing query-conditional geometry.
fastest_falsification: One day: displacement analysis on 50 two-tone objects with one model; isotropic displacements kill it.

one_line: Closed-set fine-tuning of open-vocab detectors destroys open-vocabulary transfer in a predictable frequency order: abstract and rare concepts die first, and the decay is measurable per epoch
problem: Teams fine-tune open-vocab detectors on their closed target classes and later discover the model no longer detects anything else, but the community lacks a characterization of how and in what order open-vocab ability decays during fine-tuning.
core_hypothesis: Catastrophic forgetting under closed-set fine-tuning is not uniform: transfer AP for held-out vocabulary decays fastest for concepts distant from the fine-tuning classes in text-embedding space and for low-frequency concepts, following a predictable ordering that allows forecasting which capabilities survive a given fine-tune.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking held-out vocabulary AP across fine-tuning epochs will show decay rates that rank-correlate with embedding distance to the fine-tuning class set and inversely with concept frequency, consistently across fine-tuning datasets.
why_important: A decay forecast lets practitioners choose fine-tuning budgets and regularization deliberately, and turns anecdotal forgetting complaints into an engineering quantity.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting is studied for classification; a per-concept decay-ordering law for open-vocab detection with distance and frequency predictors appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune an open-vocab detector on a small closed set, evaluate a 200-concept probe vocabulary every epoch, fit decay curves, regress decay rates on embedding distance and frequency.
main_risk: Decay may be dominated by the vision side (proposal drift) rather than text alignment, in which case text-space predictors fail.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning trades generality for target performance in an unstructured way; if you want open-vocab ability, do not fine-tune.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decay may be abrupt and global (a phase transition when the text head is overwritten) rather than gradual and ordered, making forecasting impossible.
fastest_falsification: Two days: one fine-tune with per-epoch probe evaluation; unordered or cliff-like decay kills the forecasting claim.

one_line: Multilingual queries for the same concept yield systematically different detections, and cross-language ensembling is a free accuracy gain that also fingerprints text-encoder bias
problem: Open-vocab detectors with multilingual text encoders are queried in one language, assuming the concept representation is language-neutral, but training data imbalance across languages likely makes detection quality language-dependent in unmeasured ways.
core_hypothesis: Querying the same category in several languages produces detection sets with meaningful symmetric difference, the per-language quality tracks that language's share of pretraining data, and score-averaging across translations improves AP over the best single language for underrepresented concepts.
falsifiable_prediction: Across categories and languages, AP variance across translations of the same concept will be substantial, and the cross-language ensemble will beat the English-only query on a non-trivial share of categories, especially culture-specific ones.
why_important: It exposes a hidden fairness and robustness dimension (detection quality depends on the query language), and offers a zero-training ensemble trick for global deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Multilingual evaluation exists for retrieval and classification; language-conditional detection performance and translation ensembling for detection appear unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Translate 50 category names into six languages, evaluate a multilingual open-vocab detector per language on fixed imagery, measure AP spread and ensemble gain.
main_risk: Popular open-vocab detectors use English-dominant encoders where non-English queries fail trivially, making the study about tokenizer garbage rather than representation bias.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The query language is irrelevant as long as the text encoder nominally supports it; English is a safe default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For genuinely multilingual encoders the concept representations may be well-aligned across languages, leaving only noise-level differences.
fastest_falsification: One day: 20 concepts in four languages on one model; near-identical detection sets kill it.

one_line: Classification and localization errors are anti-correlated per detection because training assignment couples them, violating the independence assumption baked into error analyses
problem: Error decomposition tools treat classification and localization failures as independent categories, but the label assignment process during training (which samples get positive class labels depends on box overlap) mechanically couples the two heads' error patterns.
core_hypothesis: Detections with excellent localization are misclassified more often than an independence model predicts, because assignment rules train the classifier hardest on well-overlapping samples of frequent classes, leaving well-localized rare-class boxes under-supported; the joint error distribution deviates from the product of marginals in a direction predictable from the assignment rule.
falsifiable_prediction: The joint histogram of (IoU with GT, classification correctness) will show significant negative dependence in the high-IoU region for rare classes, and the dependence structure will differ between detectors using different assignment schemes but same backbone.
why_important: Error-analysis conclusions and downstream fixes (better boxes vs better labels) rest on an independence assumption that may be systematically wrong, misdirecting engineering effort.
why_possibly_novel: Error taxonomies count error types; testing the statistical dependence structure between subtask errors and tracing it to assignment rules appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two detectors differing only in label assignment, compute the joint (IoU, class-correctness) distribution per class-frequency bin on val, test independence, compare dependence signatures across assignment schemes.
main_risk: Dependence may be dominated by per-image difficulty (hard images hurt both heads), requiring careful conditioning to isolate the assignment-driven component.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Classification and localization errors are separate failure categories that can be counted and fixed independently.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-difficulty confounds may explain all observed dependence, leaving nothing attributable to assignment coupling.
fastest_falsification: One day: joint error histograms with image-difficulty conditioning on one detector pair; independence after conditioning kills it.

one_line: Box regression systematically under-covers extreme aspect ratios because residual parameterizations shrink toward prior shapes, measurable as an aspect-ratio-conditional coverage bias
problem: Regression targets are parameterized as offsets from anchors or priors with roughly normal aspect ratios, so extreme shapes require extreme regression outputs that L1-style losses discourage, but coverage bias is never reported as a function of GT aspect ratio.
core_hypothesis: Predicted boxes for very elongated objects are systematically shorter along the long axis than GT (regression shrinkage toward prior shapes), with the bias magnitude growing with the ratio between GT aspect ratio and the nearest prior, and largely fixable by aspect-ratio-conditional output rescaling.
falsifiable_prediction: Signed relative error of predicted long-axis extent will be negative on average for high-aspect-ratio objects across anchor-based detectors, near zero for square objects, and smaller in magnitude for anchor-free center-based detectors with distance regression.
why_important: Elongated objects (poles, vehicles side-on, tools) matter in robotics and infrastructure inspection; a one-line conditional rescale could fix a structural bias that mAP averages hide.
why_possibly_novel: Anchor design papers optimize coverage for training; the inference-time shrinkage bias as a measurable function of shape, with a post-hoc correction, appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bin val GT by aspect ratio, compute signed long-axis extent error per bin for three detectors, fit a conditional correction on half the data, verify high-IoU AP gains on the other half.
main_risk: Modern IoU-based losses may have removed the shrinkage, leaving the bias only in older architectures nobody deploys.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Box regression errors are symmetric noise around GT; aspect ratio affects difficulty but not error direction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: IoU-loss-trained detectors optimize overlap directly, which penalizes under-coverage and over-coverage symmetrically, plausibly eliminating directional bias.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: signed extent-error vs aspect-ratio plot on cached detections; zero-centered curves kill it.

one_line: Cross-dataset localization disagreement is substantially a modal-vs-amodal annotation convention mismatch, not a feature gap, and convention adapters recover most of the transfer loss
problem: Detectors transferred across datasets lose high-IoU AP, which is attributed to domain gap, but datasets silently differ in whether occluded object extents are boxed by visible pixels or inferred full extent, an unmodeled target-convention difference.
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of high-IoU transfer loss between dataset pairs is explained by a learnable global convention transform (how occluded extents are boxed), such that a small adapter fit on a few hundred boxes recovers most of the loss without touching features.
falsifiable_prediction: For occluded objects, transfer errors will be directionally consistent (systematically too small or too large depending on the dataset pair) rather than symmetric, and a per-class linear box adapter fit on 500 boxes will recover a large share of AP at IoU 0.75 while leaving AP at 0.5 unchanged.
why_important: It re-attributes a well-known transfer penalty from features to labels, changing the fix from expensive adaptation to a cheap calibration, and pushes dataset authors to document conventions.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation inconsistency is acknowledged qualitatively; decomposing cross-dataset AP loss into convention vs capability with a directional-error test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a detector trained on dataset A on dataset B, stratify errors by occlusion, test directional consistency, fit the box adapter on a small sample, re-evaluate.
