main_risk: Convention differences may vary by annotator batch within datasets, making a global transform too crude to show the effect cleanly.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Cross-dataset AP drops measure domain gap in features and appearance statistics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If most transfer loss sits at IoU 0.5 rather than high thresholds, conventions cannot be the story since they mostly perturb tightness.
fastest_falsification: One day: directional error analysis on occluded objects for one dataset pair; symmetric errors kill it.

one_line: Detectors inherit photographer framing bias as a spatial prior: predicted boxes are pulled toward image center and canonical thirds, measurable as signed center drift on off-center objects
problem: IoU-based metrics are direction-blind, so a systematic spatial pull in predictions would be invisible in standard evaluation while corrupting downstream geometry (distance estimation, gaze targets) that depends on unbiased box centers.
core_hypothesis: Training photos concentrate objects near composition-favored locations, teaching a spatial prior that manifests as predicted centers drifting toward those locations; the drift is largest for low-evidence detections (small, blurry, occluded) where the prior dominates the likelihood.
falsifiable_prediction: The signed displacement between predicted and GT centers, averaged over objects binned by image position, will point toward composition-favored regions with magnitude inversely related to detection confidence, consistently across detector families trained on web-photo datasets.
why_important: Downstream systems consume box centers as unbiased measurements; a documented prior-driven drift with a correction map improves geometric pipelines for free and demonstrates dataset bias becoming metric error.
why_possibly_novel: Center bias is documented in saliency research; its quantification as a localization drift in detection with confidence-dependence appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On val sets, compute signed center-error fields over image coordinates for several detectors, test alignment with the training set's object-position density gradient, check confidence dependence.
main_risk: The measured drift may be caused by evaluation matching asymmetries at image borders rather than a learned prior.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Localization errors are zero-mean; dataset composition bias affects which objects exist, not where boxes land.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fully convolutional detectors are translation-equivariant by construction, so any prior must enter via padding and border effects, which may be too weak to measure.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: signed center-error vector field on one detector, compare against position density gradient; no alignment kills it.

one_line: Class labels are less stable than boxes under sub-pixel input shifts: classification flips exceed localization jitter, revealing that the class head is the aliasing-sensitive component
problem: Detector instability under tiny translations is treated as a localization phenomenon (box jitter), but classification is read from coarse pooled features where aliasing may cause label flips even when boxes stay put, and nobody separates the two instabilities.
core_hypothesis: Under sub-pixel to few-pixel input translations, the rate of class-label flips at stable box positions exceeds the rate of significant box-geometry changes, because classification pools from lower-resolution maps with stronger aliasing; anti-aliased downsampling in the backbone reduces class flips more than box jitter.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring per-object label-flip rate and box-IoU-with-itself under a dense translation sweep will show label instability dominating for small and medium objects, and an anti-aliased backbone variant will cut label flips disproportionately.
why_important: Video and multi-frame systems suffer from label flicker more than box flicker; locating the instability in the class pathway redirects architectural fixes.
why_possibly_novel: Shift-invariance work measures classification accuracy or box jitter separately; the direct comparison of subtask instabilities within one detector under controlled shifts appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take crops allowing 8-pixel translation sweeps, run a detector at each offset, track per-object label and box across offsets, compare flip statistics; repeat with an anti-aliased backbone.
main_risk: NMS and score-threshold interactions may masquerade as label flips, requiring careful pre-threshold analysis.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Translation instability in detectors is primarily box jitter; class labels are the stable part of a detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class logits may be smoother than box regressions in practice because classification pools over larger receptive fields, averaging out aliasing.
fastest_falsification: One day: translation sweep on 200 objects with pre-NMS logging; box instability dominating everywhere kills it.

one_line: Localization-quality heads (centerness, IoU prediction) learn dataset-specific box statistics that anti-transfer: they hurt more than they help under dataset shift
problem: Quality-estimation heads improve in-distribution ranking by predicting how well a box fits, but what they actually learn may be the source dataset's annotation style, making their scores misleading exactly when transferring to differently annotated or differently distributed data.
core_hypothesis: Under cross-dataset evaluation, ablating the quality head's contribution to the final score improves transfer AP for a meaningful subset of dataset pairs, because the head's learned notion of a good box encodes source-specific priors (tightness style, typical aspect ratios) that misrank valid target boxes.
falsifiable_prediction: For detectors with decomposable quality scores, the score-fusion weight that maximizes AP will be substantially lower on shifted test sets than in-distribution, and the drop will correlate with annotation-style distance between datasets.
why_important: Quality heads are ubiquitous in modern detectors; knowing they anti-transfer changes deployment configuration (down-weight or drop them off-domain) at zero cost.
why_possibly_novel: Quality estimation is evaluated in-distribution; its transfer behavior and the annotation-style explanation appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take two detectors with separable quality scores, sweep the fusion weight in-distribution and on three shifted sets, compare optimal weights, correlate with a measurable annotation-style statistic.
main_risk: Quality heads may mostly encode geometry-feature relationships that are domain-general, showing no meaningful optimal-weight shift.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Localization-quality estimation is a domain-general improvement that helps wherever the detector runs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The head conditions on features, not raw statistics, so it may generalize exactly as well as the rest of the detector, no better and no worse.
fastest_falsification: One day: fusion-weight sweep on one detector across two shifted benchmarks; stable optima kill it.

one_line: Box edges are located by texture gradient evidence, so boundary error is predictable per edge from local contrast, enabling contrast-conditional uncertainty on each box side
problem: Box uncertainty is at best a single scalar per detection, but the four box edges have independent evidence quality (a car against sky on top, against shadow below), and no deployed system expresses per-edge reliability.
core_hypothesis: Per-edge localization error is strongly predicted by a simple local contrast statistic along that edge, because regression heads exploit gradient evidence; this yields a training-free per-edge uncertainty map, with low-texture boundaries (glass, smoke, shadow) showing predictably inflated error.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-edge absolute error against edge-local contrast measures on val data will show strong positive dependence for all detector families, and the fitted relation will transfer across datasets well enough to rank edges by reliability without labels.
why_important: Per-edge uncertainty is directly usable by downstream geometry (fusion, tracking, measurement) and requires no model change, just an image statistic.
why_possibly_novel: Box uncertainty research is head-centric (learned variance); an evidence-side, image-computable per-edge error model appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For cached detections on val, compute per-edge signed and absolute errors and local contrast statistics, fit and cross-validate the error model, test transfer to a second dataset.
main_risk: Context-driven localization (detectors placing edges from object shape priors rather than local evidence) may dominate for familiar classes, breaking the contrast relationship.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Localization error is a per-detection property; edge-level structure is noise not worth modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Strong shape priors in modern detectors may decouple edge placement from local contrast for most categories.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: per-edge error vs contrast scatter on one detector; weak correlation kills it.

one_line: L1-family and IoU-family regression losses produce different error distribution shapes (many-small vs few-large) that are invisible to mAP but decisive for tracking and measurement downstream
problem: Loss choice for box regression is settled by mAP comparisons, but two detectors with equal mAP can have very different error distributions, and downstream consumers care about the shape (outlier frequency) rather than the mean.
core_hypothesis: L1-style losses yield heavier-tailed localization error distributions (occasional gross failures, tight mode) while IoU-based losses yield lighter tails but a wider mode, so the loss family should be selected by downstream tolerance to outliers versus average precision of geometry, not by mAP.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-mAP detector pairs differing in regression loss will show statistically distinguishable error-distribution shapes (kurtosis, tail mass beyond fixed IoU deficits), and a tracking benchmark will prefer the light-tailed model while a mean-IoU metric prefers the other.
why_important: It gives system designers a principled loss-selection rule tied to their downstream error tolerance, replacing cargo-cult loss adoption.
why_possibly_novel: Loss comparisons report mAP and sometimes mean IoU; distribution-shape analysis tied to downstream task outcomes appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train (or obtain) matched detector pairs differing only in regression loss, compare error histograms and tail statistics, then A/B them inside one tracker and one measurement task.
main_risk: Matched pairs are hard to source publicly and expensive to train, and the shape difference may shrink with modern hybrid losses.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Regression loss choice is a solved question settled by benchmark mAP; remaining differences are negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hybrid losses used in practice may already blend the two families' behavior, leaving no clean shape dichotomy to exploit.
fastest_falsification: One day with public checkpoints of both loss families: error histogram comparison at matched mAP; indistinguishable shapes kill it.

one_line: Much of the small-object gain from higher input resolution is an assignment artifact, not better features: re-running assignment at high resolution with low-res features recovers a large share
problem: Raising input resolution is the standard costly remedy for small-object AP, justified as providing finer features, but resolution also changes which anchors and locations become positive samples, and the two mechanisms have never been decomposed.
core_hypothesis: A substantial fraction of the small-object AP improvement from resolution comes from more favorable label assignment geometry (more positive samples per small object) rather than from richer features, implying that assignment-side fixes at low resolution could capture much of the gain at a fraction of the compute.
falsifiable_prediction: A factorial experiment crossing feature resolution with assignment resolution will show the assignment factor explains a large share of small-object AP variance, and low-res features with high-res-style assignment will approach high-res performance for objects above a minimal pixel size.
why_important: Inference cost scales quadratically with resolution; if assignment is the real lever, small-object performance becomes affordable on edge hardware.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution ablations treat input size as atomic; decomposing it into feature-quality and assignment-geometry factors appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train detector variants crossing two feature resolutions with two assignment densities on one dataset, evaluate small-object AP per cell of the factorial, compute factor contributions.
main_risk: The factors may interact so strongly (assignment density useless without feature detail) that the decomposition yields no actionable low-cost recipe.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: High resolution helps small objects because small objects need fine-grained features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For truly tiny objects the feature information may be genuinely absent at low resolution, capping any assignment-side recovery at a low ceiling.
fastest_falsification: Three days including training: 2x2 factorial on a small dataset; feature factor dominating everywhere kills it.

one_line: FPN level-assignment boundaries create scale cliffs: objects near level-transition sizes have systematically worse AP, and soft assignment flattens the cliffs
problem: Objects are assigned to pyramid levels by size thresholds, so an object near a threshold is split between levels during training and served by whichever level wins at inference; per-size AP is reported in three coarse buckets that hide any structure at the transition sizes.
core_hypothesis: Fine-grained AP as a function of object size exhibits localized dips at the level-transition sizes of the specific FPN configuration, because near-threshold objects receive diluted training signal on both adjacent levels; smoothing assignment across levels removes the dips.
falsifiable_prediction: Plotting AP in fine size bins will reveal dips aligned with the architecture's transition sizes, the dip locations will move when the assignment thresholds are moved, and soft assignment will fill the dips without hurting mid-level sizes.
why_important: It identifies a purely architectural failure mode with a targeted fix, and explains cross-detector disagreement on which object sizes are hard.
why_possibly_novel: Level assignment research optimizes aggregate AP; the existence and alignment of size-localized dips as a fingerprint of assignment thresholds appears unreported.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate two off-the-shelf FPN detectors with different transition thresholds in 20 fine size bins, test for dips at the respective predicted sizes, then retrain one with shifted thresholds to confirm dip movement.
main_risk: Size-binned AP is noisy and dataset size distributions are lumpy, so dips may be statistically unresolvable without very large eval sets.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Size difficulty is smooth; the small-medium-large breakdown captures everything worth knowing about scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature pyramid fusion may share enough information across levels that near-threshold objects are effectively co-trained, preventing any dip.
fastest_falsification: One day: fine size-bin AP curves for two detectors with different thresholds; no aligned dips kills it.

one_line: Small-object detection is context-parasitic: randomizing context collapses small-object AP far more than large-object AP, quantifying how little pixel evidence detectors actually use for tiny instances
problem: Small-object AP is interpreted as measuring the detector's ability to read tiny pixel patterns, but small objects may be detected mostly from their context (a distant boat found by the water), and the two evidence sources are never separated in evaluation.
core_hypothesis: The ratio of context-derived to object-derived evidence increases sharply as object size shrinks, so context randomization (pasting the same object pixels into incongruent scenes) will degrade small-object recall multiplicatively more than large-object recall, and the crossover size where context dominates is measurable per class.
falsifiable_prediction: In paste-based experiments controlling object pixels exactly, recall for sub-32-pixel objects will drop by a much larger factor than for large objects under context randomization, and classes with strong scene priors (boats, birds) will show earlier crossover sizes than context-free classes.
why_important: It changes what small-object benchmarks measure and predicts brittle deployment behavior when context priors break (novel scenes, unusual viewpoints), guiding data collection toward context diversity.
why_possibly_novel: Context sensitivity is studied at whole-image level; the size-conditional decomposition of evidence sources with a per-class crossover size appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paste segmented objects at multiple sizes into congruent and incongruent backgrounds, measure recall as a function of size and context condition, fit the crossover model per class.
main_risk: Paste artifacts may themselves be size-dependent (blending is harder for small objects), confounding the size-context interaction.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Small-object difficulty is about limited pixel evidence; context is a secondary bonus that helps uniformly across sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may use context uniformly for all sizes, making the size interaction flat and the parasitism story wrong.
fastest_falsification: Two days including paste-set construction: recall-vs-size curves under two context conditions; parallel curves kill it.

one_line: Detection probability for small objects oscillates with sub-stride pixel phase due to downsampling aliasing, creating a spatial lottery that anti-aliasing fixes
problem: A small object's detectability should not depend on where it falls relative to the stride grid, but strided downsampling without proper filtering aliases high-frequency evidence, plausibly making detection depend on pixel phase in a way nobody measures or reports.
core_hypothesis: For objects near or below the effective stride of their assigned feature level, detection confidence varies periodically with sub-stride translation, with amplitude growing as object size shrinks; anti-aliased downsampling shrinks the oscillation and yields disproportionate small-object AP gains in video where phase drifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Translating test images in single-pixel steps will produce periodic confidence oscillation for small objects with period equal to the relevant stride, minimal oscillation for large objects, and reduced amplitude on anti-aliased backbone variants.
why_important: A phase lottery means reported small-object AP has an irreducible variance term and video applications see flicker; the fix is a known architectural change whose detection-side value is unquantified.
why_possibly_novel: Shiftability is studied for classification; the phase-dependence of detection confidence, its period structure, and its size scaling appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Single-pixel translation sweeps on crops containing small objects, record per-object confidence traces, Fourier-analyze for stride-periodic components, compare against an anti-aliased variant.
main_risk: Augmentation with random scales during training may have partially randomized the phase sensitivity, leaving oscillations too small to matter.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detection is effectively translation invariant; sub-pixel placement of objects is irrelevant noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern training pipelines' aggressive scale-jitter may act as implicit anti-aliasing, flattening the phase response.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: translation sweep on 100 small objects; no stride-periodic oscillation kills it.

one_line: Detectors learn pixel scale, not metric scale: they ignore depth cues that would predict object size, leaving a free consistency check for false positives
problem: A human sees that a car-sized blob at horizon distance cannot be a nearby pedestrian, using scene geometry to constrain object size; detectors trained with scale augmentation are explicitly encouraged to ignore absolute scale, potentially discarding physically informative signals.
core_hypothesis: Detector confidence is insensitive to violations of geometric size consistency (an object at the wrong size for its scene position), so false positives systematically violate depth-size consistency more than true positives, making a monocular-depth-based size prior an effective post-hoc false-positive filter that the detector itself provably does not implement.
falsifiable_prediction: Pasting objects at geometrically implausible sizes will produce confidences indistinguishable from plausible sizes (demonstrating insensitivity), while on natural data a depth-conditioned size-consistency score will separate FPs from TPs at matched confidence with meaningful AUROC.
why_important: It identifies an entire evidence channel deliberately destroyed by standard training, exploitable immediately as a filter and eventually as a training signal for driving and robotics scenarios.
why_possibly_novel: Geometry-aware detection exists for 3D tasks; the explicit demonstration that 2D detectors are scale-consistency-blind plus the post-hoc filter framing appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paste-based plausibility probe on one detector, then combine an off-the-shelf monocular depth model with per-class metric size priors to score val detections, measure FP-TP separation at matched confidence.
main_risk: Monocular depth errors on exactly the hard cases (unusual scenes) may make the consistency score too noisy to filter with.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Scale augmentation is purely beneficial; whatever geometry matters, the detector learns implicitly from data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may partially learn ground-plane priors despite augmentation, showing measurable sensitivity in the paste probe and closing the exploitable gap.
fastest_falsification: One day: implausible-size paste probe on 200 scenes; if confidence drops sharply for implausible sizes, the blindness claim dies.

one_line: Tiled inference for small objects fails in a structured border pattern, and the merge heuristics reintroduce exactly the NMS pathologies tiling was meant to avoid
problem: High-resolution imagery is processed in overlapping tiles, with detections merged by NMS across tile borders; practitioners know border effects exist but there is no quantitative anatomy of where and why tiled pipelines lose or duplicate objects.
core_hypothesis: Tiled-inference errors concentrate in predictable border zones and take two structured forms: truncation-induced misses (objects split across tiles score below threshold in both) and merge-induced errors (cross-tile NMS keeps misaligned fragments), with the balance controlled by overlap ratio in a way that admits an optimal-overlap prescription per object-size distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: Error density as a function of distance to tile border will show sharp elevation within an object-diameter-scaled band, and sweeping overlap will trade miss-type against duplicate-type errors with a computable optimum that differs across datasets by their size distribution.
why_important: Tiling is the default for aerial, medical, and industrial imagery; a principled overlap and merge prescription would replace folklore settings in thousands of pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: Tiling papers report end metrics; the border-zone error anatomy and the overlap-optimization framing appear unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run tiled inference on an aerial benchmark across five overlap settings, map errors by border distance, classify error types, fit and validate the optimal-overlap model on a second dataset.
main_risk: Modern merge schemes (soft merging, seam-aware fusion) in some libraries may already erase most of the structure.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Generous tile overlap plus cross-tile NMS makes tiling artifacts negligible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For sparse small objects the border zones may contain too few objects for the structured losses to matter in aggregate metrics.
fastest_falsification: One day: border-distance error histogram at one overlap setting; flat histogram kills it.

one_line: Below a size floor, small-object AP measures annotation noise, not detection: inter-annotator box IoU for tiny objects bounds achievable AP and reorders leaderboard conclusions
problem: Leaderboards celebrate small-object AP gains, but human annotators placing boxes on sub-16-pixel objects disagree with each other by margins comparable to the IoU thresholds used in scoring, raising the question of what the metric measures at those sizes.
core_hypothesis: There exists a size floor below which inter-annotator agreement IoU falls under the evaluation threshold, making AP at those sizes dominated by label noise; a noise-adjusted small-object metric (threshold scaled by measured annotator sigma per size) changes method rankings and deflates claimed progress.
falsifiable_prediction: A re-annotation study will show median inter-annotator IoU declining with size and crossing 0.5 near a measurable pixel floor, and re-scoring existing methods with size-adjusted thresholds will compress or reorder their small-object AP differences.
why_important: If tiny-object AP is noise-dominated, method development targeting it is optimizing randomness, and benchmarks need size-adaptive thresholds to restore signal.
why_possibly_novel: Annotator noise is documented in general; connecting the size-conditional noise floor to achievable AP bounds and re-scoring published methods appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Triple-annotate 500 small objects sampled by size decile, measure agreement curves, derive noise-adjusted thresholds, re-evaluate several public detectors under the adjusted metric.
main_risk: Professional annotation with zoom tooling may show much higher agreement than expected, moving the floor below sizes anyone cares about.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Small-object AP differences between methods reflect genuine capability differences at all annotated sizes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may make errors much larger than annotator sigma even at tiny sizes, keeping the metric informative despite label noise.
fastest_falsification: Two days including annotation: agreement-vs-size curve from 200 re-annotated objects; high agreement at all sizes kills it.

one_line: The upsampling operator in FPN top-down pathways imprints a grid artifact on small-object detection rates, making detector behavior depend on interpolation choice in a spatially periodic way
problem: Feature pyramids upsample coarse maps to fuse with fine maps using nearest or bilinear interpolation chosen by convention, and any positional non-uniformity this creates would show up as spatially periodic variation in small-object sensitivity, which standard evaluation cannot see.
core_hypothesis: Nearest-neighbor upsampling creates a checkerboard-like positional bias in fused features, so small-object detection probability varies periodically with position at the coarse-grid scale; bilinear or learned upsampling reduces the periodicity, and the artifact accounts for a measurable slice of small-object variance.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense positional sweeps of a fixed small object will show detection-rate periodicity matching the coarse-level grid for nearest-upsampled models, weaker periodicity for bilinear, and per-position variance will predict which GT objects in natural images are missed.
why_important: It ties a mundane implementation choice to a measurable detection lottery, informing architecture defaults for small-object-critical applications like aerial survey.
why_possibly_novel: Checkerboard artifacts are known for generative upsampling; their quantified effect on detection sensitivity fields appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Positional sweep protocol on two variants of one detector differing only in FPN upsampling, extract sensitivity maps, Fourier test for grid periodicity, correlate with natural-image miss locations.
main_risk: Subsequent convolutions in the head may smooth away the positional structure before it affects outputs.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Interpolation choice in FPN fusion is a negligible implementation detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The 3x3 convolutions after fusion are explicitly there to clean fusion artifacts and may fully succeed.
fastest_falsification: One day: positional sensitivity map for one nearest-upsampled detector; no grid periodicity kills it.

one_line: Detector false positives are context-conditioned hallucinations: the FP class distribution in a scene matches co-occurrence statistics of the training set, enabling context-debiased rescoring
problem: False positives are treated as unstructured noise, but if detectors hallucinate what usually accompanies the visible scene (a phantom fork near a plate), FP structure is predictable and correctable, yet no standard analysis conditions FP rates on scene content.
core_hypothesis: The probability that a false positive of class X appears in an image is strongly predicted by the training-set co-occurrence of X with the classes actually present, beyond what visual similarity of background patches explains; subtracting a co-occurrence-derived prior from scores reduces contextual FPs at fixed recall.
falsifiable_prediction: Regressing per-image FP class counts on co-occurrence with present classes will show strong positive coefficients across detector families, and prior-subtraction rescoring will improve precision specifically for high-co-occurrence class pairs while leaving isolated-object performance unchanged.
why_important: It converts the dominant real-world error type into a structured, correctable phenomenon and quantifies how much detectors rely on scene priors versus evidence.
why_possibly_novel: Context bias is known for recognition accuracy; the systematic study of FP generation as co-occurrence sampling with a debiasing fix appears missing for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On val sets, tabulate FPs by class conditional on GT-present classes, compare against co-occurrence matrices, implement prior-subtraction rescoring, evaluate precision-recall movement per class pair.
main_risk: Visual confusability (forks appear near plate-like textures) may explain most of the correlation, making the co-occurrence account redundant.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: False positives are caused by locally confusing textures; scene-level statistics are not a primary driver.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Co-occurrence and texture confusability are so entangled in natural images that no analysis can cleanly separate them without synthetic controls.
fastest_falsification: One day: FP-class vs co-occurrence regression on one detector with texture-similarity controls; no residual co-occurrence effect kills it.

one_line: Inpainting away one object changes the scores of remaining objects by class-pair-specific amounts, giving a causal map of inter-object dependence in detectors
problem: Detectors are evaluated object-by-object as if detections were independent, but features are shared and attention mixes evidence across the image, so each detection may causally depend on other objects in ways that determine failure cascades under occlusion or removal.
core_hypothesis: Removing an object via inpainting shifts the confidence of remaining detections with a magnitude and sign structured by class pair (removing a rider drops motorcycle-class confidence, removing a random car does not affect a distant dog), producing a reproducible inter-object dependence graph that predicts co-failure in natural scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across many removal interventions, confidence deltas for remaining objects will be far from zero for semantically linked pairs and near zero for unlinked pairs, and the measured dependence graph will predict which detections disappear together under natural occlusion in held-out video.
why_important: A causal dependence map explains cascade failures (one occlusion silently kills a neighboring detection), which matters for safety cases, and provides a new interpretability primitive for detectors.
why_possibly_novel: Context studies use image-level manipulations; a per-object causal intervention protocol producing a pairwise dependence graph appears new for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build an inpainting-intervention pipeline on a few hundred multi-object scenes, measure per-remaining-object confidence deltas across removals, test graph stability across seeds and inpainting models, validate co-failure predictions on video with natural occlusions.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts inject their own evidence changes, requiring careful controls (removing background patches of matched size) to isolate object-driven effects.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detections are approximately independent given the image; other objects matter only through occlusion geometry.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Receptive-field locality in some architectures may bound inter-object influence to near-zero beyond small distances, making the graph trivially sparse.
fastest_falsification: Two days: removal interventions on 100 scenes with matched background-patch controls; deltas indistinguishable from controls kill it.

one_line: Scene-gist anchoring: the same object patch pasted into different backgrounds receives predictably different scores, and the effect size is a measurable per-class context-dependence index
problem: Every claim about detector robustness implicitly assumes object evidence dominates context, but the community lacks a standardized per-class number stating how much a detector's score depends on the surrounding scene versus the object pixels themselves.
core_hypothesis: Pasting identical object pixels into congruent versus incongruent scenes shifts detection scores by class-specific amounts that are stable across images, defining a context-dependence index per class; the index predicts which classes will fail under domain shift (unusual contexts) and correlates with the class's contextual concentration in training data.
falsifiable_prediction: The per-class index measured on one paste set will replicate on a disjoint paste set with high rank correlation, and classes with high indices will show disproportionate AP drops on out-of-context benchmarks compared to low-index classes.
why_important: A standardized context-dependence index would let practitioners predict deployment brittleness per class before deployment, from a purely synthetic probe.
why_possibly_novel: Out-of-context studies exist as one-off demonstrations; packaging context dependence as a replicable per-class index with predictive validity for shift robustness appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct congruent and incongruent paste sets for 30 classes, compute score shifts and the index, replicate on disjoint scenes, correlate indices with AP drops on an out-of-context evaluation set.
main_risk: Paste blending quality may interact with background type, contaminating the index with compositing artifacts.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Context helps or hurts idiosyncratically; a stable per-class context number does not exist or would not predict shift behavior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Context dependence may be scene-specific rather than class-specific, making any per-class scalar too coarse to predict anything.
fastest_falsification: Two days: index computation for 10 classes on two disjoint paste sets; poor replication kills it.

one_line: Detectors learn spatial grammar between class pairs (ties below faces, shoes below legs), and violating the grammar suppresses detections even with perfect object evidence
problem: Co-occurrence bias is usually described as which classes appear together, but detectors may also encode where classes appear relative to each other, a stronger structural prior whose violation could veto detections in rearranged or unusual scenes.
core_hypothesis: For strongly co-structured class pairs, moving one object to a grammar-violating position (tie floating beside a head, hat below feet) reduces its detection score substantially more than equivalent moves of non-structured pairs, demonstrating a learned relative-position prior distinct from mere co-occurrence.
falsifiable_prediction: Paste experiments swapping relative positions will show score drops for grammar-violating placements that exceed matched-distance control moves, with the effect concentrated in pairs having low positional entropy in training data.
why_important: Spatial grammar violations occur in exactly the scenarios where detection matters most (accidents, falls, unusual configurations), so a veto-like prior is a safety-relevant failure mode worth quantifying.
why_possibly_novel: Relative-position priors are exploited in structured models of the pre-deep era; demonstrating and measuring them as implicit failure modes of modern detectors appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select ten low-positional-entropy class pairs and ten high-entropy controls, run placement-swap paste probes, compare score-drop distributions between groups.
main_risk: Positional priors may be mediated by pixel-level co-occurrence (skin adjacency for ties) rather than object-relative geometry, complicating interpretation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detectors use local evidence plus loose scene context; explicit relative-position grammar between classes is not part of what they learn.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern detectors' strong local features may dominate any positional prior, making violations cost little.
fastest_falsification: One day: placement-swap probe on three iconic pairs (tie-face, shoe-leg, hat-head); no differential drop kills it.

one_line: Text-supervised open-vocab detectors and box-supervised closed-set detectors have opposite context-dependence profiles, revealing that supervision type, not architecture, sets contextual reliance
problem: Context reliance is usually attributed to dataset statistics or architecture, but caption supervision (weak, scene-level) and box supervision (strong, object-level) plausibly teach different evidence weighting, and no controlled comparison isolates supervision type.
core_hypothesis: Holding backbone and test data fixed, caption-aligned detection heads rely more on scene context (larger score shifts under context randomization) than box-supervised heads, because caption supervision cannot localize credit and therefore rewards scene-consistent guessing.
falsifiable_prediction: A context-randomization probe applied to matched pairs (same backbone, one open-vocab head, one closed-set head) will show systematically larger context sensitivity for the caption-aligned head across classes, with the gap widening for classes whose captions rarely mention them without scene words.
why_important: If supervision type sets contextual reliance, the choice between open-vocab and closed-set deployment becomes a robustness decision, not just a flexibility decision.
why_possibly_novel: Comparisons between paradigms focus on accuracy and generality; a controlled context-reliance comparison isolating supervision appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one backbone with both an open-vocab alignment head and a fine-tuned closed-set head, run identical paste-based context probes on shared classes, compare sensitivity distributions.
main_risk: Truly matched pairs are hard to construct; pretraining differences beyond supervision type may leak into the comparison.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Open-vocab detectors are assumed more robust in general because of larger pretraining, including robustness to unusual contexts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Massive pretraining diversity may expose caption-supervised models to more context variety, actually reducing their contextual reliance below box-supervised models.
fastest_falsification: Two days: context probe on one matched pair over 15 classes; equal or reversed sensitivity kills it.

one_line: Detection recall is pose-and-placement conditional: objects in statistically rare orientations or positions (upside-down, ceiling-mounted) are missed at rates augmentation does not fix because the prior lives in context features
problem: Rotation and flip augmentation is assumed to grant orientation robustness, yet deployed systems still miss inverted or oddly placed objects, suggesting the miss is driven by scene-relational priors (objects belong on floors) that image-level augmentation never varies.
core_hypothesis: Recall conditioned on object orientation and scene-relative placement shows deficits for rare configurations even in heavily augmented detectors, because augmentation rotates object and context together, never teaching the model that objects can be unusually placed within a normal scene; targeted compositional augmentation (rotating objects within scenes) closes the gap where image-level augmentation cannot.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall for pasted objects rotated within an upright scene will be substantially lower than for the same objects in whole-image-rotated inputs, isolating the relational prior, and compositional augmentation will improve the former without affecting the latter.
why_important: Fallen people, overturned vehicles, and dropped objects are high-stakes rare configurations; understanding why augmentation fails to cover them redirects data strategy.
why_possibly_novel: Rotation robustness is studied via whole-image transforms; the decomposition into object-relative versus scene-relative orientation priors with compositional probes appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build probe sets contrasting whole-image rotation with object-within-scene rotation for shared instances, measure recall gaps on standard detectors, then fine-tune with compositional augmentation and re-measure.
main_risk: Paste realism for rotated objects (shadows, contact points) may be the true driver of measured deficits.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Standard rotation and flip augmentation provides orientation robustness for detection.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deficits for unusual placements may be mostly appearance-driven (unfamiliar viewpoints of the object itself), not relational, in which case whole-image augmentation is the right tool after all.
fastest_falsification: Two days: recall comparison between the two rotation protocols on 20 classes; equal recall kills it.

one_line: Detectors encode camera-height priors from eye-level training photos, and overhead-view failure is largely prior mismatch measurable by horizon manipulation rather than feature novelty
problem: Detectors transferred to drone or overhead imagery fail badly, universally attributed to viewpoint-novel appearance; but eye-level training also instills expectations about where the horizon sits and how object size scales with image height, a separable prior nobody has isolated.
core_hypothesis: Part of the overhead-transfer failure is caused by learned image-height-to-scale and horizon-position priors rather than unfamiliar object appearance, so synthetically manipulating horizon position and vertical size gradients in normal photos will degrade detection predictably, and prior-neutralizing fine-tuning (vertical cropping regimes) will recover overhead performance disproportionately to the small data used.
falsifiable_prediction: Detection performance on eye-level photos will degrade when images are vertically shifted or size gradients are inverted even though local object appearance is untouched, and the per-class degradation will correlate with that class's overhead-transfer deficit.
why_important: Aerial deployment currently assumes full retraining is needed; if a scene-geometry prior is a major factor, cheap prior-neutralization beats data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Viewpoint robustness work focuses on object appearance; isolating scene-geometry priors via horizon manipulation as a transfer-failure component appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct horizon-shifted and gradient-inverted variants of a val set, measure per-class degradation, correlate with measured overhead-benchmark deficits, then test vertical-cropping fine-tuning on a small overhead sample.
main_risk: Synthetic horizon manipulation may introduce unnatural compositions whose degradation reflects distribution shift generally, not the specific geometric prior.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Overhead-view failure is about unfamiliar object appearance from above; scene geometry priors are not a major separable factor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Object appearance changes from viewpoint are so dominant that even a confirmed geometric prior would explain only a trivial slice of the transfer gap.
fastest_falsification: One day: horizon-shift probe on one detector; no degradation kills the prior claim outright.

one_line: Training on incompletely annotated data teaches detectors confident-negative behavior on real objects, and the effect is dose-dependent: FP-labeled-as-background rate during training predicts deployment under-detection per class
problem: Benchmark training sets miss many true objects, so the loss actively penalizes correct detections during training; the community treats this as benign noise, but it may install systematic suppression of exactly the object appearances most often left unannotated.
core_hypothesis: The degree to which a class is under-annotated in training (estimable via cross-detector agreement or partial re-annotation) predicts that class's deployment under-detection beyond what training-sample count explains, because gradient pressure teaches the model to score real-but-unannotated appearances as background.
falsifiable_prediction: Classes with higher estimated annotation-miss rates will show recall deficits on fully re-annotated eval sets disproportionate to their nominal sample counts, and training with missing-aware losses (ignoring low-loss unmatched detections) will differentially recover those classes.
why_important: It quantifies a training-data pathology that no amount of architecture work fixes, and provides an estimator identifying which classes are silently sabotaged.
why_possibly_novel: Missing-label robustness has been studied with synthetic label dropping; connecting naturally occurring per-class miss rates to deployment deficits with an agreement-based estimator appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-class annotation-miss rates on a training set via detector-ensemble agreement plus spot re-annotation, train standard and missing-aware variants, compare per-class recall on a re-annotated eval set against miss-rate predictions.
main_risk: Miss-rate estimation itself relies on detectors trained on the same flawed data, risking circularity that must be broken with genuine re-annotation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Missing annotations are random noise that large datasets average away; standard training is robust to them.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loss functions with soft negative weighting may already blunt the suppression effect enough that dose-dependence is unmeasurable.
fastest_falsification: Two days: correlate agreement-estimated miss rates with recall deficits on an existing re-annotated benchmark subset; no correlation kills it.

one_line: Crowd-region labels teach detectors to ignore dense clusters wholesale: recall inside iscrowd-style regions collapses even for clearly separable instances, and the suppression transfers to unlabeled crowd-like textures
problem: Datasets mark dense groups with crowd flags that exclude them from matching, and training pipelines skip or ignore these regions; the behavioral consequence for the trained detector inside and near such regions has never been characterized.
core_hypothesis: Detectors trained with crowd-region conventions learn a texture-level suppression of dense same-class clusters, reducing recall for separable instances inside crowd-like arrangements even in new images without crowd labels, with the suppression triggered by periodicity and density cues rather than instance ambiguity.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall for instances placed within synthetic dense arrangements will be substantially below recall for the same instances in sparse arrangements at matched local appearance, and models trained on crowd-flag-free datasets will show a smaller gap.
why_important: Crowd scenarios (audiences, flocks, parking lots) are common deployment targets; if the training convention itself installs blindness, dataset design and loss handling need revision.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd flags are treated as an evaluation nicety; their causal effect on learned detector behavior appears uninvestigated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose paste-based density sweeps with fixed instance appearance, evaluate recall vs density for detectors trained with and without crowd-region conventions, compare gap sizes.
main_risk: Density-driven recall loss also arises from NMS and feature collision, requiring pre-NMS analysis to isolate the trained-suppression component.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Crowd flags are a labeling convenience with no effect on what detectors learn.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The pre-NMS analysis may show all density loss comes from suppression mechanics, leaving nothing attributable to training conventions.
fastest_falsification: Two days: density-sweep recall curves with pre-NMS logging on two detectors with different training conventions; identical curves kill it.

one_line: Annotator-batch style drift is learnable and fingerprintable: detectors partially encode which annotation team labeled which portion of training data, and the mixture explains bimodal tightness errors
problem: Large datasets are annotated by multiple teams over years with drifting guidelines, so box tightness and inclusion rules vary by batch; detectors trained on the mixture must reconcile inconsistent targets, but how they resolve the conflict (averaging vs context-dependent mimicry) is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Detector localization errors on val data are bimodal or multimodal in tightness, matching the mixture of annotation styles in training rather than centering on a single convention, and the mode weights track the batch proportions; a style-conditional output head trained with batch metadata would collapse the modes.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting mixture models to signed tightness errors will find multiple modes aligning with independently identified annotation-batch styles, and images visually similar to a given batch's collection period will receive boxes biased toward that batch's style.
why_important: It reveals that a chunk of measured localization error is actually target inconsistency, bounding achievable AP and motivating style metadata in dataset releases.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation inconsistency is discussed at dataset level; showing that detectors internalize the mixture and produce context-dependent style mimicry appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify annotation batches in a public dataset via metadata or clustering of GT statistics, fit tightness-error mixtures for a detector, test alignment between error modes and batch styles.
main_risk: Batch metadata is often unavailable, forcing indirect batch identification that could manufacture the very structure being tested.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detectors learn an averaged annotation convention; annotator variation washes out as zero-mean noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The network may genuinely average styles, producing unimodal errors and leaving no fingerprint to find.
fastest_falsification: One day: mixture fit on signed tightness errors for one dataset-detector pair; a clean single mode kills it.

one_line: Cross-dataset AP drops decompose into taxonomy-convention mismatch versus capability gap, and a small relabeling experiment quantifies how much transfer failure is definitional
problem: When a detector trained on one dataset scores poorly on another, the gap is read as generalization failure, but datasets disagree on category boundaries (what counts as a chair vs stool, truck vs van), and the definitional component has never been separated from the capability component.
core_hypothesis: A significant, quantifiable fraction of cross-dataset AP loss for taxonomically ambiguous classes disappears when target-set labels are re-mapped by annotators using the source dataset's definitions, providing a decomposition of transfer loss into convention mismatch and true capability gap that varies dramatically by class.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating a sample of the target dataset under source conventions will recover a large share of AP for boundary-ambiguous classes and almost nothing for visually distinctive classes, and the recovered share will correlate with independently measured definitional ambiguity.
why_important: Transfer benchmarks drive research priorities; if a chunk of the measured gap is definitional, effort aimed at features is partly wasted and label-space alignment tools deserve investment.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-dataset evaluation is common; the convention-vs-capability decomposition via targeted re-annotation appears not to have been done systematically.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select ten ambiguous and ten distinctive classes across a dataset pair, re-annotate 200 target images per class group under source definitions, recompute transfer AP, report the recovered fraction per group.
main_risk: Re-annotation under another dataset's guidelines is itself noisy, and annotator interpretation of written guidelines may not reproduce the original convention.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Cross-dataset AP drops measure generalization capability of the detector.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For most classes the definitional overlap may be near-perfect, making the decomposition a footnote rather than a reframing.
fastest_falsification: Two days: convention re-mapping for three ambiguous classes; negligible AP recovery kills it.

one_line: Near-duplicate scenes between train and test splits inflate detection benchmarks: deduplicated evaluation shrinks measured progress and reorders methods by their memorization reliance
problem: Web-collected detection datasets contain visually near-duplicate scenes across splits (same landmarks, similar compositions, repeated venues), so some measured performance may be scene memorization; the size of this inflation and its method-dependence are unknown for detection.
core_hypothesis: Partitioning test sets by embedding-based similarity to training scenes will reveal a performance gap between near-duplicate and novel-scene strata, the gap will be larger for higher-capacity models, and method rankings on the novel-scene stratum will differ from the full-set rankings, exposing differential memorization.
falsifiable_prediction: AP on the most-similar test stratum will exceed AP on the least-similar stratum by a substantial margin for all models, with the stratified gap growing in model capacity, and at least some method pairs will swap ranks between strata.
why_important: If leaderboard gains partly reflect memorization headroom, the community is over-crediting capacity and under-crediting genuine generalization mechanisms.
why_possibly_novel: Duplicate-contamination audits exist for classification benchmarks; a scene-similarity-stratified audit of detection benchmarks with capacity analysis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute train-test scene similarity with an off-the-shelf embedder for one benchmark, stratify test AP for five detectors spanning capacities, test gap-capacity correlation and rank stability.
main_risk: Similarity strata correlate with scene difficulty (common scene types are both duplicated and easy), requiring difficulty controls to avoid overclaiming.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Standard split protocols make train-test contamination negligible for detection benchmarks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection performance depends on object-level factors that may swamp scene-level memorization, leaving strata gaps within noise.
fastest_falsification: One day: similarity stratification and AP gap for two detectors; no stratified gap kills it.

one_line: Rare-class AP in long-tail detection benchmarks primarily measures annotation agreement, not model capability: label noise on rare classes bounds and scrambles the metric that the field optimizes
problem: Long-tail detection research optimizes rare-class AP, but rare classes are exactly where annotators disagree most (unfamiliar categories, ambiguous boundaries), so the metric may be dominated by label noise rather than detection quality, misleading a whole subfield.
core_hypothesis: Per-class annotation agreement (measurable by re-annotation) declines with class rarity, and rare-class AP differences between competing long-tail methods are largely within the noise band implied by that agreement, meaning many published improvements are not distinguishable from label-noise lottery.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating a sample of rare-class instances will show significantly lower inter-annotator agreement than frequent classes, and injecting agreement-level label perturbations into the eval will produce AP fluctuations comparable to the gaps between published long-tail methods.
why_important: If true, the field needs agreement-aware metrics or cleaned eval subsets before further method development on long-tail benchmarks means anything.
why_possibly_novel: Label noise is studied in training; its role in bounding the discriminative power of rare-class evaluation appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dual-annotate 50 instances each for 20 rare and 20 frequent classes, quantify the agreement-rarity relationship, simulate label perturbation at measured levels, compare induced AP variance against published method gaps.
main_risk: Some long-tail method gaps may be large enough to survive the noise band, making the critique partial rather than field-reframing.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Rare-class AP is a valid measure of long-tail detection capability, and improvements on it represent real progress.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rare classes in curated benchmarks may have been annotated with extra care, breaking the assumed rarity-noise link.
fastest_falsification: Two days: dual-annotation of 10 rare classes; high agreement kills the premise.

one_line: Saturated headline classes hide structured failure: person-class AP conceals pose- and attire-conditional recall deficits that stratified evaluation exposes and that transfer learning silently inherits
problem: The most-used class in detection (person) reports near-saturated AP, so it receives no research attention, yet aggregate AP can hide severe recall deficits for specific poses, attire, and activities that matter in deployment and propagate into every fine-tuned derivative model.
core_hypothesis: Stratifying person detection by pose (lying, crouching, climbing), attire (high-visibility gear, robes, costumes), and activity context will reveal recall strata differing by large margins under the same headline AP, with deficits stable across architectures because they trace to shared training data, and inherited nearly unchanged by models fine-tuned from common checkpoints.
falsifiable_prediction: Pose-stratified evaluation on re-annotated subsets will show lying and crouching recall far below standing recall across all tested detectors, the deficit profile will correlate strongly between architecturally unrelated models, and fine-tuned downstream models will exhibit the same profile.
why_important: Fallen-person detection is safety-critical in driving, eldercare, and industrial monitoring; a shared inherited blind spot in the ecosystem's most-used class is a systemic risk worth documenting rigorously.
why_possibly_novel: Pose-conditional person detection deficits are known anecdotally in applications; a systematic cross-architecture inheritance study tying the deficit to shared data lineage appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble pose and attire strata via existing keypoint annotations plus targeted collection, evaluate five unrelated detectors and three fine-tuned derivatives, compute deficit profiles and inter-model correlations.
main_risk: Strata assembly may itself be biased (unusual poses come from unusual imagery), confounding pose with photographic conditions.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Person detection is a solved problem, as evidenced by saturated benchmark AP.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern web-scale pretraining may have already diversified pose coverage enough that stratified deficits are modest.
fastest_falsification: One day using keypoint-derived pose strata on an existing benchmark: recall by pose for two detectors; flat profiles kill it.

one_line: Corruption robustness decomposes by subtask: image corruptions degrade classification while boxes persist (or vice versa per corruption family), so robustness interventions should be subtask-targeted
problem: Detection robustness under corruption is reported as a single mAP drop, hiding whether the detector stopped finding objects, stopped naming them correctly, or stopped localizing them tightly, which are different failures needing different fixes.
core_hypothesis: Corruption families act selectively: noise-like corruptions primarily destroy classification (texture evidence) while boxes on found objects remain accurate, whereas blur-like corruptions primarily degrade localization and recall (edge evidence); a per-subtask robustness profile is stable across architectures and dictates which augmentation to deploy.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing corrupted-set errors into recall, classification-given-found, and IoU-given-found will show corruption-family-specific signatures reproducible across detector families, and augmenting training with a corruption will repair chiefly its signature subtask.
why_important: Robustness engineering currently applies blanket augmentation; a subtask map would cut the cost and explain why some augmentations do not move deployment metrics.
why_possibly_novel: Corruption benchmarks for detection report aggregate deltas; the subtask decomposition with family signatures and targeted-repair validation appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three detectors on a corruption suite, compute the three-way error decomposition per corruption family, test signature stability, then fine-tune with single-family augmentation and verify targeted repair.
main_risk: Recall and classification failures are entangled through score thresholds, requiring careful matched-threshold analysis to keep the decomposition meaningful.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Corruption robustness is a scalar property of the detector; augmentation improves it globally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Subtask degradations may be strongly correlated within each corruption, leaving no exploitable selectivity.
fastest_falsification: One day: three-way decomposition on one detector across two corruption families; identical signatures kill it.

one_line: Box supervision forces more shape reliance than classification training: detectors are measurably less texture-biased than classifiers sharing the same backbone, revising the texture-bias narrative for localization tasks
problem: The texture-bias literature, built on classification, is casually extrapolated to detection, but predicting box extents requires shape information that classification does not, so the bias profile of detectors may be fundamentally different and the extrapolated conclusions wrong.
core_hypothesis: Training a detection head on top of a backbone shifts feature reliance toward shape (measured by cue-conflict stimuli adapted to detection), so a detector and classifier sharing initialization will diverge in texture bias, with the detector's classification-of-detected-objects relying more on shape than the standalone classifier.
falsifiable_prediction: On detection-adapted cue-conflict images (objects with swapped textures), detectors will label detected objects by shape at a higher rate than matched classifiers label whole images, and the shape reliance will increase with the localization loss weight used in training.
why_important: Robustness interventions imported from classification (style augmentation) may be mis-targeted for detection; knowing the actual bias profile redirects them.
why_possibly_novel: Texture-bias measurement has not been properly ported to detection with cue-conflict stimuli that preserve localizable shape, and the loss-weight dependence is a new causal handle.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build cue-conflict detection stimuli, evaluate matched backbone-classifier and detector pairs, compare shape-reliance indices, retrain the detector with varied localization loss weights to test causality.
main_risk: Cue-conflict synthesis at object level may produce unnatural boundaries that both models handle idiosyncratically, muddying the comparison.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: CNN-family models are texture-biased; detection inherits the classification bias profile unchanged.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The classification head inside a detector may remain just as texture-biased, with shape used only by the box head, making the aggregate story unchanged.
fastest_falsification: Two days including stimulus synthesis: shape-reliance comparison for one matched pair; identical bias kills it.

one_line: Low-light detection failure begins at normalization, not features: detectors degrade before human-visible darkness because input statistics leave the trained regime, and simple statistic-matching recovers a predictable fraction
problem: Low-light robustness is treated as a feature-learning problem requiring specialized training or enhancement networks, but a mundane candidate cause, input normalization statistics drifting far from the training regime, has not been cleanly separated from genuine evidence loss.
core_hypothesis: A measurable share of low-light detection degradation occurs while object evidence is still recoverable, caused by activation-statistics drift; per-image statistic matching (adaptive gamma or histogram alignment to training statistics) recovers that share, and the residual unrecoverable part defines the true photon-limited failure point.
falsifiable_prediction: Along a controlled exposure-reduction sweep, detection performance will fall significantly before pixel-SNR-based information limits, and cheap statistic-matching preprocessing will shift the failure curve toward the information limit by a consistent margin across detectors.
why_important: It separates fixable-by-preprocessing degradation from genuine sensing limits, potentially replacing heavy enhancement networks with one-line corrections in many deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Low-light benchmarks compare enhancement pipelines; the decomposition into statistics-drift versus information-loss components with an information-theoretic reference curve appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Create synthetic exposure sweeps with calibrated noise from well-lit images, evaluate detectors with and without statistic matching, compare failure curves against a patch-level information proxy (trained low-level discriminability).
main_risk: Synthetic darkening may not reproduce real sensor noise structure, limiting external validity of the decomposition.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Low-light failure reflects missing training data for dark conditions; the fix is enhancement networks or low-light training sets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern detectors trained with strong photometric augmentation may already be statistics-robust, leaving nearly all degradation on the information side.
fastest_falsification: One day: exposure sweep with and without gamma matching on one detector; no recovery gap kills it.

one_line: Motion blur degrades detection anisotropically: blur direction interacts with class-specific edge-orientation statistics, so horizontal camera pans selectively erase classes defined by vertical edges
problem: Motion blur is treated as an isotropic difficulty knob in robustness suites, but real blur has direction, and object classes have characteristic edge-orientation profiles, implying a structured interaction nobody measures.
core_hypothesis: Per-class detection degradation under directional blur is predicted by the overlap between blur direction and the class's discriminative edge-orientation distribution, so a deployment's dominant motion axis makes a predictable subset of classes fragile, and orientation-diverse blur augmentation fixes exactly the predicted classes.
falsifiable_prediction: Applying horizontal versus vertical synthetic blur will produce class-level degradation profiles that swap according to each class's edge-orientation histogram, with the interaction effect large for elongated or striped classes and near zero for isotropic-texture classes.
why_important: Vehicles and drones have dominant motion axes; predicting which classes fail under a platform's characteristic blur enables targeted augmentation and risk assessment.
why_possibly_novel: Blur robustness is benchmarked isotropically; the class-by-direction interaction with an edge-statistics predictor appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute class edge-orientation histograms from GT crops, apply directional blur sweeps to a val set, fit degradation against the predicted overlap, validate on a held-out class set.
main_risk: Blur simultaneously destroys context and small-object evidence, potentially swamping the orientation-specific signal.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Motion blur is a severity-parameterized corruption whose direction is irrelevant to which classes fail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deep features may be orientation-pooled early enough that directional evidence loss homogenizes before classification.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: horizontal vs vertical blur on ten classes; uncorrelated degradation profiles kill it.

one_line: Weather shifts damage specific FPN levels (haze kills high-frequency levels first), so level-targeted adaptation beats whole-network fine-tuning at a fraction of the parameters
problem: Domain adaptation for weather retrains whole detectors, but atmospheric effects have characteristic spatial-frequency signatures that should map to specific pyramid levels, suggesting most of the network is fine and adaptation is being over-applied.
core_hypothesis: Per-level feature-distribution drift under haze, rain, and snow is strongly non-uniform and predictable from each corruption's frequency signature, and adapting only the most-drifted levels (normalization parameters or light adapters) recovers most of the full fine-tuning gain with far fewer trainable parameters.
falsifiable_prediction: Feature-drift metrics computed per FPN level will rank levels consistently within each weather type across architectures, and level-targeted adaptation on the top-drifted levels will achieve a large share of full fine-tuning recovery while adapting under a tenth of the parameters.
why_important: Cheap targeted adaptation matters for on-device weather robustness, and the level-drift map gives an interpretable account of what weather actually does to detectors.
why_possibly_novel: Domain adaptation treats the backbone monolithically; a frequency-to-pyramid-level analysis with targeted parameter-efficient repair appears new for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-level drift on synthetic and real weather sets for two detectors, run adaptation ablations per level subset, compare recovery-vs-parameters curves against full fine-tuning.
main_risk: Drift metrics may not predict repair value (the most-drifted level may not be the most performance-critical), breaking the targeting logic.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Weather adaptation requires adapting the whole feature extractor since domain shift pervades all layers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Compound real weather (haze plus droplets plus contrast loss) may spread drift across all levels, erasing the targeting advantage.
fastest_falsification: One day: per-level drift profile for haze on one detector; uniform drift kills the premise.

one_line: Backbone-feature domain-gap metrics fail to predict detection transfer loss because transfer is head-limited: a detection-head-specific gap measure predicts what backbone metrics cannot
problem: Practitioners estimate deployment risk with feature-space domain distances computed on backbone embeddings, but detection loss under shift may be dominated by head-level failures (assignment geometry, score calibration) invisible to backbone statistics, making current risk estimates misleading.
core_hypothesis: Across many source-target pairs, backbone-level distribution distances correlate weakly with detection AP drop, while a head-aware gap measure (distribution shift of head inputs at matched proposal quality, plus score-distribution divergence) correlates strongly, revealing that the transfer bottleneck usually sits above the backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: On a matrix of detectors and shifted test sets, the head-aware measure will explain substantially more AP-drop variance than backbone distances, and interventions that repair only head inputs (recalibration, proposal-statistics matching) will recover a larger share than backbone-only adaptation at equal budget.
why_important: Unsupervised risk estimation guides deployment decisions; pointing it at the right layer changes both the metric and the cheapest repair.
why_possibly_novel: Unsupervised accuracy estimation exists mostly for classification; a detection-specific decomposition locating the predictive gap at the head appears fresh.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 20 shift scenarios, compute backbone and head-aware gap measures, regress AP drops on both, then run matched-budget head-only versus backbone-only repairs on the worst cases.
main_risk: Head-aware measures require careful matched-proposal protocols; sloppy matching would trivially inflate their apparent predictive power.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Domain gap lives in features; backbone-level distances are the right proxy for detection transfer risk.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For severe appearance shifts the backbone may genuinely dominate, restricting the head-limited claim to mild shifts only.
fastest_falsification: Two days: correlation comparison on ten shift scenarios with one detector; backbone metric winning kills it.

one_line: Synthetic-to-real transfer fails asymmetrically by subtask: synthetic training teaches transferable localization but non-transferable classification, so sim data should be spent on box supervision, not labels
problem: Synthetic data pipelines render both boxes and class labels at equal cost, and transfer failure is reported as one gap; if the gap decomposes asymmetrically by subtask, the optimal use of synthetic data changes fundamentally, but the decomposition has not been established.
core_hypothesis: Geometry (where objects are, their extents) transfers from synthetic to real far better than appearance-based classification, so a detector trained with synthetic boxes but real-image classification supervision (via unlabeled real data and pseudo-labels or contrastive alignment) will approach real-data performance, while the reverse split will not.
falsifiable_prediction: Factorial experiments splitting supervision sources by subtask will show sim-boxes-real-classes retaining most of full-real performance and real-boxes-sim-classes losing much more, consistently across rendering qualities.
