why_important: Synthetic data budgets are large in industrial detection; knowing which subtask sim can safely supervise redirects rendering effort and hybrid training design.
why_possibly_novel: Sim-to-real detection is studied as a monolithic gap; the subtask-asymmetric supervision-splitting experiment appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a sim-real dataset pair, train four detectors crossing box-supervision source with classification-supervision source, evaluate on real, compare retention per cell.
main_risk: Cleanly splitting supervision sources requires careful architectural separation of the heads' gradients, and leakage would blur the cells.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The sim-to-real gap is an appearance-domain problem affecting the whole detector uniformly; the fix is better rendering or domain randomization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Localization may depend on low-level texture statistics as much as classification does, making geometry transfer equally fragile.
fastest_falsification: Three days including training runs on a small benchmark: the 2x2 supervision factorial; symmetric losses kill it.

one_line: Compression artifacts create block-aligned phantom detections: small-object false positives cluster on 8-pixel JPEG grid boundaries, and grid-aware filtering removes them without touching true positives
problem: Deployed detectors consume compressed streams whose block-transform artifacts introduce artificial edges at fixed grid positions; whether detectors hallucinate small objects anchored to this grid is unknown because evaluation imagery is usually high quality.
core_hypothesis: Under moderate-to-heavy compression, small-object false positives are spatially enriched at block-boundary positions and their box edges align with the compression grid at rates far above chance, providing a forensic signature that separates artifact-driven FPs from evidence-driven detections and enables a targeted filter.
falsifiable_prediction: The distribution of FP box-edge positions modulo the block size will be strongly non-uniform for compressed inputs and uniform for uncompressed inputs, and filtering grid-aligned low-confidence small detections will improve precision on compressed streams with negligible recall cost.
why_important: Video-analytics systems run almost exclusively on compressed feeds; a free forensic filter and a characterization of compression-induced hallucination have direct deployment value.
why_possibly_novel: Compression robustness is measured as aggregate mAP; the grid-alignment forensic analysis of false positives appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-encode a val set at several compression levels, collect small-object FPs, test edge-position uniformity modulo block size, implement and evaluate the grid-aware filter.
main_risk: Modern codecs use variable block sizes and deblocking filters that may smear the grid signature below detectability.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Compression degrades detection by removing information; its artifacts are not a structured source of false positives worth modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors trained on web images have seen abundant compression artifacts and may have learned to ignore block edges entirely.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: FP edge-position histogram modulo 8 on heavily compressed val images; uniformity kills it.

one_line: DETR queries tile a latent position-size space with coverage gaps: objects falling in gap regions are systematically missed, and the gap map is extractable from the trained model without any test data
problem: Set-prediction detectors allocate a fixed set of learned queries, and misses are attributed to image difficulty; if queries tile position-size space unevenly, some misses are structural (no query is responsible for that region), a model-intrinsic failure map nobody extracts.
core_hypothesis: Each query's matched-object statistics concentrate in a compact position-size cell, the union of cells leaves gaps (rare corner-size combinations), and GT objects falling into gaps are missed at much higher rates independent of appearance difficulty; the gap map predicts misses on new data from model weights and matching statistics alone.
falsifiable_prediction: Deriving a coverage density from per-query matching distributions on training data will predict held-out per-object miss probability with meaningful discrimination after controlling for size and class, and artificially shifting objects into gap regions will raise their miss rate.
why_important: A weights-derived structural failure map enables pre-deployment risk audits and principled query re-initialization, turning an opaque architecture into an auditable one.
why_possibly_novel: Query specialization has been visualized qualitatively; a quantitative coverage-gap model with predictive validation and intervention appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract per-query matched-object distributions for a pretrained DETR variant, build the coverage map, validate miss prediction on held-out data with confound controls, then test translation interventions moving objects into and out of gaps.
main_risk: Decoder iterations may let queries migrate far from their prior cells at inference, making static coverage maps poor predictors.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Query sets are flexible enough that misses reflect image difficulty, not structural coverage holes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Deformable and dynamic-anchor variants explicitly redistribute queries per image, likely closing static gaps.
fastest_falsification: One day: coverage map plus miss-prediction AUROC on one DETR checkpoint; chance-level prediction kills it.

one_line: Early-training Hungarian assignment instability predicts final crowd performance: the flip rate of GT-query matching in early epochs is a cheap early-stopping-style diagnostic for set-prediction detectors
problem: Set-prediction training is known to converge slowly with unstable bipartite matching early on, but instability is treated as a transient nuisance; whether early instability leaves permanent capability scars (especially for crowded scenes) is unknown, and practitioners lack early predictors of final weaknesses.
core_hypothesis: The per-object matching flip rate integrated over early training predicts final recall deficits on dense scenes at the per-image-type level, because objects whose assignments oscillate receive diluted contradictory gradients precisely when representations form; interventions that stabilize early matching (assignment smoothing) differentially repair crowd recall.
falsifiable_prediction: Across training runs, early flip-rate statistics computed on a fixed probe set will rank-correlate with final dense-scene recall, and matched runs with early-phase assignment smoothing will beat controls on crowd metrics while tying on sparse-scene metrics.
why_important: A cheap early diagnostic saves full training runs during architecture search, and the causal link would redirect stabilization research toward the early phase specifically.
why_possibly_novel: Matching instability is documented as a convergence problem; its role as a predictor and cause of final crowd-specific deficits appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument DETR training to log matching flips on a probe set, train several seeds and variants, correlate early flip statistics with final crowd recall, then run the smoothing intervention.
main_risk: Flip rate may just proxy general convergence speed, predicting everything and explaining nothing crowd-specific.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Early matching instability is a transient optimization nuisance fully cured by convergence and modern denoising tricks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Denoising-based training may already eliminate meaningful early instability, leaving no variance to correlate.
fastest_falsification: Three days: instrument two training runs, test flip-rate versus final crowd recall across seeds; no correlation kills it.

one_line: Per-object best-layer oracles reveal recoverable AP inside DETR decoders: hard objects peak at intermediate layers and are degraded by later refinement, motivating per-object layer selection at inference
problem: Set-prediction detectors output only final-layer predictions, assuming monotone refinement across decoder layers; if a subset of objects is best predicted at intermediate layers and later layers overwrite them, the architecture discards accuracy it already computed.
core_hypothesis: For a non-trivial fraction of objects (concentrated in small, occluded, and boundary-ambiguous cases), intermediate-layer predictions have higher IoU or correct labels where the final layer fails, and a lightweight selector using per-layer agreement features can harvest a meaningful share of this oracle gap without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise oracle analysis will show final-layer-suboptimal objects at a consistent rate across DETR variants with the affected population enriched in hard-case categories, and a selector trained on layer-agreement features will capture a usable fraction of the oracle AP at negligible inference cost.
why_important: Free accuracy from computation already performed is the best kind of gain, and the phenomenon would revise the refinement narrative of decoder stacks.
why_possibly_novel: Auxiliary losses make intermediate predictions exist, but per-object layer-oracle analysis and inference-time layer selection appear unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Dump per-layer predictions for two DETR variants on val, compute per-object oracle layer and the oracle-vs-final gap, train a small selector on half the data, verify harvested gain on the other half.
main_risk: The oracle gap may consist of near-ties where selection noise cancels the theoretical gain.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Decoder layers monotonically refine predictions; the final layer is the best readout for every object.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training with auxiliary losses at every layer may make the final layer weakly dominant everywhere, leaving an oracle gap too small to harvest.
fastest_falsification: One day: per-layer oracle gap on one checkpoint; a negligible gap kills it.

one_line: DETR content queries are nearly inert at inference: replacing them with their dataset means barely moves outputs, showing these models are learned anchor grids and enabling aggressive query compression
problem: The query mechanism is described as dynamic content-dependent probing, but if content embeddings converge to static values that act like anchors, the community's mental model of these architectures is wrong and the query machinery is compressible.
core_hypothesis: For trained DETR-family models, ablating content-query variation (freezing to means, shuffling across images, or low-rank projecting) changes detection outputs marginally, because positional structure plus image features carry the load; the information content of query dynamics is measurable and small, licensing distillation into lighter fixed-probe architectures.
falsifiable_prediction: Mean-replacement of content queries will preserve the vast majority of AP across DETR variants, with degradation concentrated in the same hard cases where set prediction already struggles, while positional-query perturbation of matched magnitude will be far more damaging.
why_important: It corrects the field's understanding of what queries do and opens a straightforward path to cheaper inference by removing machinery that computes little.
why_possibly_novel: Query visualization studies exist; a controlled information-ablation quantifying the causal contribution of content-query dynamics appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run mean-replacement, cross-image shuffle, and rank-k projection ablations on three pretrained variants, chart AP degradation versus ablation strength, compare against positional-query controls.
main_risk: Two-stage variants that initialize queries from encoder proposals genuinely use dynamic content, so the claim may hold only for the vanilla family.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Learned queries perform image-conditional content probing that is essential to set-prediction performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Apparent inertness under mean replacement could hide redundant distributed coding, where the same information rides in multiple pathways and single ablations mislead.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: mean-replacement ablation on one checkpoint; large AP loss kills it.

one_line: Early decoder layers herd all queries toward the most salient object, and the model's crowd performance is determined by how fast attention de-collapses across layers, a measurable de-herding rate
problem: Attention analyses of DETR decoders average over scenes; the dynamics of how queries initially cluster on salient content and then disperse to cover remaining objects has not been quantified, though it may be the mechanistic bottleneck for multi-object scenes.
core_hypothesis: In the first decoder layer, query attention mass concentrates on a small salient subset of objects, and a de-herding rate (how quickly attention spreads to cover remaining GT across layers) varies across models and predicts their dense-scene recall better than aggregate attention statistics; salience-flattening input transforms causally improve crowd recall by accelerating de-herding.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-model comparison will show de-herding rate rank-correlates with crowd recall at matched sparse-scene performance, and reducing salience contrast (photometric flattening) will improve recall of low-salience objects in crowded scenes while slightly hurting the most salient object's localization.
why_important: A mechanistic dial for crowd performance suggests both architectural fixes (attention diversity regularizers) and cheap input-side interventions, plus a new model-selection statistic.
why_possibly_novel: Attention collapse is mentioned anecdotally; formalizing de-herding as a measurable rate with predictive and causal tests appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define attention-coverage curves over decoder layers against GT objects for several checkpoints, correlate rates with crowd metrics, then run the salience-flattening intervention on high-density scenes.
main_risk: Attention maps are an unreliable proxy for information flow, so coverage curves may not reflect the actual computation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Decoder attention allocation is an implementation detail; crowd performance is set by query count and training data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Value-pathway mixing may distribute object information regardless of attention concentration, making herding cosmetically alarming but functionally irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: One day: coverage curves for two models with different crowd performance; indistinguishable de-herding kills it.

one_line: Denoising-style DETR training installs an over-trust of near-prior boxes: models refine plausible-looking priors instead of reading evidence, measurable as inflated confidence on prior-consistent phantom boxes
problem: Denoising training accelerates convergence by teaching the decoder to reconstruct GT from noised boxes, but this auxiliary task may teach the model that box-like priors near plausible positions are usually real, a bias with no current measurement.
core_hypothesis: Denoising-trained models assign systematically higher confidence than non-denoising counterparts to injected phantom queries placed at scene-plausible positions with no object evidence, because the reconstruction task rewarded completing priors rather than verifying evidence; this manifests in deployment as context-plausible false positives resistant to score thresholds.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting synthetic near-plausible boxes into the query stream at inference will elicit higher completion confidence from denoising-trained checkpoints than matched non-denoising ones, and their natural false positives will skew toward context-plausible locations by a measurable margin.
why_important: Denoising is now default in state-of-the-art detectors; a systematic evidence-versus-prior imbalance would be an unrecognized cost shipping in every deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Denoising ablations report convergence and AP; behavioral probes of what the auxiliary task teaches about evidence weighting appear absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a phantom-query injection probe, compare completion-confidence distributions across matched checkpoints differing in denoising, then classify natural FPs by contextual plausibility and compare skews.
main_risk: Matched checkpoint pairs differing only in denoising are scarce, and retraining to create them adds cost and possible confounds.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Denoising training is a pure optimization aid with no behavioral side effects on the trained detector.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The denoising branch is isolated by attention masking during training, which may fully prevent behavioral leakage into the inference pathway.
fastest_falsification: One day: phantom-injection probe on one denoising and one vanilla checkpoint; identical completion confidence kills it.

one_line: The NMS-free property of set-prediction detectors is distribution-bound: duplicate rates climb under domain shift, and deployed DETR pipelines silently need an emergency suppression stage nobody ships
problem: One-to-one prediction is validated in-distribution, and practitioners remove NMS from DETR pipelines permanently; whether the learned mutual-exclusion behavior survives distribution shift is untested, and duplicate re-emergence would corrupt downstream counting silently.
core_hypothesis: Query mutual exclusion is a learned in-distribution behavior implemented by self-attention patterns tuned to familiar feature statistics, so under appearance shift (corruption, new domains) duplicate detection rates rise disproportionately compared to CNN-plus-NMS baselines whose suppression is structural, creating a shift-fragility unique to the set-prediction family.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring duplicate rates (post-hoc IoU clustering of confident outputs) across a corruption suite will show set-prediction models' duplicate rates growing with shift severity while NMS-based pipelines stay flat, with the growth concentrated in texture-shifted rather than geometry-preserving corruptions.
why_important: Counting and tracking systems built on NMS-free stacks would inherit an invisible failure mode; a cheap conditional suppression stage could be recommended as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: Robustness benchmarks report mAP under shift; duplicate-rate dynamics as a shift-fragile learned behavior appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched set-prediction and NMS-based detectors over a corruption ladder, compute duplicate-rate curves via IoU clustering against GT matching, compare growth slopes.
main_risk: mAP-oriented duplicate definitions may undercount perceptual duplicates, requiring careful metric design before the comparison means anything.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: One-to-one matching eliminates duplicates as an architectural property that holds wherever the model runs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mutual exclusion may be implemented by robust geometric attention patterns that survive appearance shift just fine.
fastest_falsification: One day: duplicate-rate curve over five corruption severities for one DETR variant; flat curve kills it.

one_line: Query count acts as a hidden density prior with a soft ceiling well below its nominal value: performance degrades once GT count exceeds a small fraction of queries, and the usable fraction is a stable architecture constant
problem: Set-prediction models ship with hundreds of queries, suggesting capacity for hundreds of objects, but self-attention repulsion and training-time object-count distributions may cap usable slots at a much lower effective number that nobody reports.
core_hypothesis: Recall as a function of GT object count shows an inflection at an effective capacity far below nominal query count, the effective-to-nominal ratio is roughly stable within an architecture family across datasets, and training on artificially dense data moves the inflection, proving the ceiling is learned from count statistics rather than architecturally fixed.
falsifiable_prediction: Recall-vs-count curves will show inflections at similar effective ratios for same-family checkpoints trained on different data mixes, dense-data fine-tuning will shift the inflection rightward without adding queries, and simply adding queries without dense data will not.
why_important: Deployments in dense domains (retail shelves, aerial crowds) select models by nominal query count; an effective-capacity law with a data-side remedy prevents systematic mis-selection.
why_possibly_novel: Query-count ablations exist for aggregate AP; the effective-capacity framing with its learned-versus-architectural disambiguation appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several checkpoints on count-stratified data to locate inflections, fine-tune one on synthetically densified scenes, re-locate the inflection, and contrast with a query-count-increase control.
main_risk: Count stratification confounds with object size and overlap (denser scenes have smaller objects), requiring synthetic density control to isolate count.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: A model with N queries can detect up to N objects; query count is the capacity spec.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The apparent ceiling may be entirely explained by size-overlap confounds rather than slot capacity, vanishing under proper controls.
fastest_falsification: One day: recall-vs-count on synthetic paste scenes with size held fixed; no inflection below nominal count kills it.

one_line: Grounding-data-trained detectors carry a single-referent bias: they under-return exhaustive instances because referring expressions taught one-answer-per-query, measurable as an instance-count saturation curve
problem: Foundation detectors trained partly on grounding data (phrase-to-one-region pairs) are deployed for exhaustive detection, but their training objective often rewarded finding the referent, not all instances, and the resulting bias on multi-instance scenes is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: For queries matching many instances, grounding-heavy detectors return a saturating number of detections (concentrated on the most prototypical instances) while detection-supervised models scale linearly with true count, and the saturation level correlates with the fraction of single-referent data in the training mix.
falsifiable_prediction: Detected-count versus GT-count curves on multi-instance scenes will show early saturation for grounding-heavy models and linear behavior for detection-supervised baselines at matched single-instance accuracy, with saturation onset predictable from training-mix composition where documented.
why_important: Exhaustive detection is the default industrial expectation; a hidden single-referent bias breaks counting and inventory tasks in ways single-object benchmarks never show.
why_possibly_novel: Grounding-versus-detection training tradeoffs are discussed for vocabulary; the instance-exhaustiveness axis with saturation-curve measurement appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble multi-instance test scenes with counts from 1 to 50, evaluate several foundation and classic detectors, fit saturation curves, relate saturation parameters to known training mixes.
main_risk: Score-threshold conventions differ across model families, requiring matched-calibration protocols before count curves are comparable.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Foundation detectors are general-purpose detectors; training-data task mix does not leave task-shaped biases in output cardinality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection-format data in the training mixes may dominate behavior, making grounding-induced saturation negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification: One day: count-curves for one grounding-heavy model versus one classic detector on paste-controlled scenes; parallel linear curves kill it.

one_line: Foundation and classic detectors fail differently in kind: foundation-model false positives are semantically coherent (plausible object, wrong image) while classic FPs are texture-driven, demanding different downstream guards
problem: Error budgets treat false positives as one category, but systems built on foundation detectors may face hallucinations that pass semantic sanity checks (a plausible bicycle where none exists) while classic detectors produce incoherent texture FPs easily caught by secondary classifiers, a difference with direct safety implications.
core_hypothesis: Classifying FPs by whether an independent recognition model endorses the crop will show foundation detectors' FPs endorsed at far higher rates (semantically coherent hallucinations), meaning the standard mitigation of cascade verification loses effectiveness exactly on the model family assumed to be more reliable.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched FP rates, the fraction of FPs endorsed by independent verifiers will be substantially higher for foundation detectors, the endorsed FPs will concentrate in context-plausible locations, and cascade-verification pipelines will show smaller precision gains on foundation stacks.
why_important: Verification cascades are the standard industrial guardrail; quantifying their differential effectiveness across detector families changes system design for safety-critical uses.
why_possibly_novel: FP taxonomies exist per model; the cross-family comparison of FP semantic coherence and its consequence for cascade guards appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect matched-rate FP sets from both families on shared imagery, score them with independent verifiers and human raters for coherence, then measure cascade precision gains per family.
main_risk: Verifier models may share pretraining with the foundation detector, inflating endorsement through correlated blind spots rather than genuine coherence.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: More capable detectors have strictly better-behaved errors; verification cascades remain equally effective as detectors improve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Foundation detectors may produce so few FPs overall that the coherence difference, even if real, is operationally irrelevant.
fastest_falsification: One day: verifier endorsement rates on 200 FPs per family; equal rates kill it.

one_line: Multi-class text queries interact inside grounding detectors: a class's AP depends on which other classes are queried alongside it, violating the independence assumption of every deployment
problem: Grounding-style detectors concatenate queried class names into one text sequence processed jointly, so cross-attention lets query terms influence each other, yet users assume querying more classes is free and evaluation always uses a fixed vocabulary, leaving the interaction unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Per-class detection performance shifts measurably with the composition of co-queried classes (semantically close co-queries suppressing or absorbing detections, unrelated ones diluting attention), so the effective behavior of a deployed detector depends on the full query set, and optimal deployment requires query-set design or per-class isolation.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating a probe class under systematically varied co-query sets will show AP variation well beyond resampling noise, with the largest effects from confusable co-queries, and single-class querying will differ measurably from full-vocabulary querying for the same class and images.
why_important: Every user of grounding detectors composes query lists ad hoc; documented interaction effects would establish query-set design as a necessary engineering step with concrete guidelines.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-set effects are studied in classification; systematic co-query interaction measurement in grounding detection appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix probe classes and images, sweep co-query sets across semantic-distance strata, chart AP variation per stratum, compare isolated versus joint querying overheads and accuracy.
main_risk: Sequence-length changes confound co-query composition effects, requiring padding controls to separate attention interaction from length artifacts.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Queried classes are processed effectively independently; vocabulary composition is a user convenience with no accuracy consequence.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Architectures that encode each phrase separately before fusion may exhibit no interaction, restricting the finding to joint-sequence designs.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: probe-class AP under five co-query compositions on one model; variation within noise kills it.

one_line: Vision-language detectors inherit bag-of-words relational blindness: spatial-relation queries retrieve the right objects with near-chance relational correctness, quantifiable as a relation-compliance metric
problem: Users query relations (cup on shelf, person holding tool) expecting relational filtering, but contrastive text encoders are known to underrepresent word order and relations, and detection pipelines add localization without necessarily adding relational grounding; the compliance rate is unreported.
core_hypothesis: For queries of the form X-relation-Y evaluated on scenes containing both relation-satisfying and relation-violating configurations, foundation detectors will select the correct configuration at rates near the base-rate of X prominence, demonstrating that relational words function as bag-of-words context rather than constraints, with compliance improving only for relations lexicalized as compound activities in pretraining.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled contrast benchmark (same objects, flipped relations) will show relation compliance close to chance for spatial prepositions across current grounding detectors, substantially below their object-retrieval accuracy on the same scenes.
why_important: Relational queries are the natural next interface for detection systems in robotics and retrieval; establishing the baseline failure and a compliance metric defines the problem for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Relational failures are documented for CLIP-style classification and image-text retrieval; porting the contrast-pair methodology into open-vocab detection with box-level compliance scoring appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate or synthesize 300 contrast-pair scenes for six spatial relations, query grounding detectors, score box-level compliance against GT configurations, compare to object-retrieval accuracy.
main_risk: Synthetic contrast scenes may be out-of-distribution enough that failures reflect scene weirdness rather than relational blindness.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Grounding detectors understand full referring expressions including spatial relations, as suggested by referring-expression benchmark scores.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Referring-expression training data may have taught genuine relational grounding that transfers to the contrast setting, yielding high compliance.
fastest_falsification: One day: 50 contrast pairs for two relations on one model; high compliance kills it.

one_line: Most localization ability is already latent in self-supervised foundation backbones: frozen-feature probes localize objects nearly as well as fine-tuned detectors, and the residual gap is concentrated in classification-region binding
problem: Detection fine-tuning is assumed to teach localization, justifying expensive detector training on top of foundation backbones, but if localization is largely present in frozen features, the actual contribution of detection training is misattributed and the training could be radically lighter.
core_hypothesis: Linear or shallow probes on frozen self-supervised features can recover object boxes at high agreement with fine-tuned detectors for most object categories, while the fine-tuning gain concentrates in binding class identity to regions and in calibration, implying detection training mainly teaches readout and binding, not localization.
falsifiable_prediction: Frozen-probe box quality (class-agnostic) will reach a large fraction of fine-tuned localization quality across backbone scales, the fraction will grow with backbone scale, and the per-category residual gap will correlate with classification difficulty rather than shape complexity.
why_important: If binding is the bottleneck, parameter-efficient detection adaptation should target the binding pathway specifically, potentially collapsing detector training costs.
why_possibly_novel: Frozen-feature detection probes exist in isolated papers; the decomposition of fine-tuning gains into localization versus binding components across scales appears unsynthesized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train shallow class-agnostic box probes on frozen features of two backbone scales, compare localization metrics against fully fine-tuned detectors, decompose remaining errors into localization and binding categories.
main_risk: Probe architecture choices can smuggle in capacity, making the frozen-versus-fine-tuned comparison sensitive to arbitrary decisions.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detection fine-tuning teaches the backbone to localize; frozen features are insufficient for accurate boxes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-IoU localization may specifically require fine-tuned edge-sensitive features that no shallow probe on frozen features can recover.
fastest_falsification: Two days: class-agnostic probe on one frozen backbone versus its fine-tuned detector; a large localization gap kills it.

one_line: Detection fine-tuning erodes a foundation model's rare-concept knowledge in frequency order, and the erosion is measurable mid-training as an early-warning signal for capability loss
problem: Teams fine-tune foundation detectors on domain data and later find that rare or fine-grained recognition silently degraded; the dynamics of what is lost, in what order, and how to detect the loss cheaply during training are uncharacterized for detection fine-tuning specifically.
core_hypothesis: Concept-recognition ability degrades during detection fine-tuning in inverse order of pretraining frequency (rarest first), the decay follows measurable curves visible within the first fraction of training, and a small probe-vocabulary evaluation run periodically during fine-tuning forecasts final capability loss accurately enough to trigger early stopping or regularization.
falsifiable_prediction: Probe-vocabulary AP tracked across fine-tuning will show decay rates ordered by concept frequency, early-decay slopes will predict final losses with usable accuracy, and frequency-stratified replay of tiny data amounts will selectively flatten the steepest decay curves.
why_important: A cheap early-warning protocol turns capability preservation from a post-hoc discovery into a controllable training-time quantity, directly useful to every team fine-tuning foundation detectors.
why_possibly_novel: Forgetting curves exist for classification continual learning; the frequency-ordered decay law and mid-training forecasting protocol for detection fine-tuning appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one foundation detector on a mid-size domain dataset, evaluate a 300-concept frequency-stratified probe every few hundred steps, fit decay curves, test slope-based forecasting and minimal-replay mitigation.
main_risk: Frequency estimates for pretraining corpora are rough proxies, potentially scrambling the predicted ordering enough to obscure a real effect.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Fine-tuning loss of generality is an accepted lump-sum cost, discovered after training and mitigated by ad hoc data mixing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Decay may be driven by embedding-space geometry rather than frequency, making the ordering unpredictable from corpus statistics.
fastest_falsification: Two days: one fine-tune with periodic probes; unordered decay kills the law, unpredictable decay kills the forecasting.

one_line: Foundation detectors fail on non-photographic imagery at the proposal stage, not classification: regions are never proposed on x-ray and sketch inputs even though crops classify correctly, inverting the assumed bottleneck
problem: Zero-shot transfer of foundation detectors to sketches, x-ray scans, and thermal imagery is poor, and the failure is generally attributed to unfamiliar appearance defeating recognition; if instead the class-agnostic proposal machinery is the failing stage, the standard fixes (recognition-side adaptation) are aimed at the wrong component.
core_hypothesis: On non-photographic modalities, the recall of the proposal or region-scoring stage collapses (objects never become candidates), while the recognition pathway classifies ground-truth crops of the same objects with comparatively high accuracy, so modality transfer is proposal-limited and proposal-stage adaptation (edge-statistics normalization, low-level adapters) yields outsized gains.
falsifiable_prediction: Stage-wise evaluation will show GT-crop classification accuracy far exceeding end-to-end recall on sketch and x-ray sets, oracle-proposal injection will recover most of the end-to-end gap, and small proposal-stage adapters will outperform recognition-stage adapters of equal size.
why_important: Modality transfer is a major promise of foundation detection (medical, security, industrial); locating the true bottleneck redirects adaptation research and deployment budgets.
why_possibly_novel: Transfer studies report end-to-end numbers; the stage-wise bottleneck decomposition with oracle-injection on non-photographic modalities appears rare or absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public sketch and x-ray detection sets, run stage-wise probes (GT-crop classification, oracle-box injection, proposal recall) for two foundation detectors, compare bottleneck attributions, then A/B stage-targeted adapters.
main_risk: Stage boundaries are blurry in single-stage grounding architectures, requiring careful operationalization of what counts as the proposal stage.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Modality transfer fails because unfamiliar appearance defeats recognition; better visual adaptation of the recognition pathway is the fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For heavily abstracted modalities like schematic sketches, recognition of crops may fail just as badly, making the bottleneck genuinely joint.
fastest_falsification: One day: GT-crop classification versus end-to-end recall on one sketch benchmark; matched failure rates kill it.

one_line: Supervised and self-supervised pretraining produce detectors with complementary failure profiles: SSL-initialized detectors hallucinate less from context but lose more small objects, and the profiles persist through identical fine-tuning
problem: Backbone pretraining choice is made by aggregate AP comparisons, but if pretraining paradigms leave distinct failure-mode signatures that survive fine-tuning, model selection should depend on which errors a deployment can tolerate, and ensembling across paradigms should target complementary failures.
core_hypothesis: Detectors fine-tuned identically from supervised-classification versus self-supervised initializations retain measurably different error compositions (context-driven false positives versus small-object misses, respectively), because pretraining objectives instill different feature reliance that fine-tuning reshapes but does not erase.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-taxonomy decompositions of paradigm-paired detectors will differ significantly in composition at matched mAP across datasets, the differences will replicate across architecture families, and cross-paradigm ensembles will outperform same-paradigm ensembles at equal compute.
why_important: It converts pretraining choice from a leaderboard decision into a failure-profile decision and gives a principled basis for heterogeneous ensembling in high-stakes systems.
why_possibly_novel: Pretraining comparisons report AP and transfer speed; persistent failure-mode signatures at matched aggregate performance appear undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune matched detector pairs from both initializations on two datasets, run error-taxonomy analysis at matched mAP, test profile replication and the ensemble prediction.
main_risk: Matched-mAP pairing may require unequal training that itself changes error profiles, confounding the pretraining attribution.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: After sufficient fine-tuning, pretraining paradigm differences wash out except for a small AP offset.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Long fine-tuning schedules on large detection data may genuinely converge feature reliance, erasing any signature worth acting on.
fastest_falsification: Three days including two fine-tunes: error decomposition at matched mAP; indistinguishable profiles kill it.

one_line: Caption-supervised detection inherits salience bias: objects that captions mention get detected, background instances of the same class get missed, measurable as a mention-likelihood recall gradient
problem: Caption and grounding supervision only labels what people bother to mention, which skews toward large, central, unusual, or action-relevant instances; detectors distilled from such supervision may systematically under-detect unmentionable instances, a bias invisible in benchmarks whose test annotation shares the same salience skew.
core_hypothesis: For a fixed class, per-instance recall of caption-supervised detectors is predicted by the instance's caption-mention likelihood (modeled from size, centrality, and scene role), with a much steeper gradient than box-supervised detectors show, and fully annotated evaluation sets expose a background-instance recall deficit that mention-skewed benchmarks hide.
falsifiable_prediction: Scoring instances by a mention-likelihood model will reveal recall declining sharply with lower mention likelihood for caption-supervised detectors, a flatter decline for box-supervised ones, and the gap will widen on exhaustively annotated test sets versus standard ones.
why_important: Exhaustive detection of unremarkable instances is precisely what industrial applications need; documenting a structural salience bias in caption-supervised pipelines warns against the cheapest scaling path and motivates mention-debiased training.
why_possibly_novel: Reporting bias is a known concept in vision-language; a quantitative per-instance recall gradient tied to modeled mention likelihood, contrasted across supervision types, appears new for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a mention-likelihood model on public caption data, stratify instance recall for caption-supervised and box-supervised detectors on an exhaustively annotated set, compare gradient slopes.
main_risk: Mention likelihood correlates with detection difficulty (small peripheral objects are also visually harder), demanding difficulty-matched controls to isolate the supervision effect.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Web-scale caption supervision produces broadly capable detectors whose recall structure mirrors visual difficulty, not caption pragmatics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Pseudo-labeling stages in modern pipelines may re-inject exhaustive box supervision that overwrites the salience skew.
fastest_falsification: Two days: recall-versus-mention-likelihood curves for one caption-supervised model with size-matched controls; flat gradient kills it.

one_line: Open-set detectors produce confident boxes for absent queried classes at rates predictable from embedding proximity to present objects, defining a measurable and correctable query-hallucination law
problem: Users query classes that are absent from the scene and expect empty results, but open-vocab detectors tend to return their best-matching region regardless; when and how strongly absent-class queries hallucinate is unquantified, though it determines reliability of the primary use case (searching for things that may not be there).
core_hypothesis: The hallucination rate for an absent query scales with the text-embedding similarity between the queried class and the classes actually present (absent 'wolf' hallucinates on scenes with dogs far more than scenes with furniture), following a smooth law that enables scene-conditional score correction subtracting the predicted hallucination propensity.
falsifiable_prediction: Querying absent classes across scenes with controlled present-class composition will show hallucination rates rising monotonically with maximum query-to-present embedding similarity, the fitted law will transfer across datasets, and similarity-conditional thresholds will cut absent-query false alarms at fixed present-query recall.
why_important: Search-and-alert deployments (find weapons, find spills) live on absent-query behavior; a quantitative hallucination law with a correction turns anecdotal distrust into an engineered property.
why_possibly_novel: Open-set false positives are reported in aggregate; the embedding-similarity-conditional hallucination law and its use for scene-adaptive thresholds appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct absent-query evaluations over scenes binned by present-class composition, fit hallucination rate versus embedding similarity for two open-vocab detectors, validate transfer and the corrected-threshold gains.
main_risk: Visual similarity may diverge from text-embedding similarity for many pairs, making the text-side law noisy where the vision side actually governs.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Absent-query false alarms are unstructured noise controlled by a global confidence threshold.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hallucinations may be driven mostly by localized texture accidents rather than class-level similarity, flattening the proposed law.
fastest_falsification: One day: absent-query FP rates across three present-class scene groups for five queries; no similarity ordering kills it.

one_line: Detection ability emerges later in model scale than recognition: small foundation models recognize what they cannot bind to regions, making binding, not recognition, the scaling bottleneck for detection
problem: Scaling studies for vision-language models track classification and retrieval, and detection capability is assumed to scale in tandem; if region-binding lags recognition in scale, small deployed models fail in a specific diagnosable way and scaling budgets should target the binding pathway.
core_hypothesis: Across a model-scale ladder with matched training recipes, crop-level recognition of a concept appears at smaller scales than the ability to localize that same concept in cluttered scenes, with the recognition-to-binding gap widest for small objects and semantically similar distractors, indicating that binding is a distinct later-emerging capability.
falsifiable_prediction: Per-concept scale curves will show recognition thresholds systematically below binding thresholds, the ordering will hold across concept categories, and binding-targeted architectural additions at small scale (explicit region-text alignment layers) will close more of the gap than equivalent parameter increases elsewhere.
why_important: Edge deployments must use small models; knowing that binding is the bottleneck defines what to distill and where to spend parameters, and reframes detection scaling laws.
why_possibly_novel: Emergent-capability analysis exists for language and classification; a recognition-versus-binding emergence comparison for detection across scale appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a public scale ladder of open-vocab detectors on paired tasks (crop recognition versus in-scene localization of identical concepts), chart emergence thresholds, test the binding-targeted intervention at one small scale.
main_risk: Public scale ladders confound scale with data and recipe changes, weakening the causal reading of emergence ordering.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detection performance scales smoothly with model size as recognition does; there is no distinct binding bottleneck.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Binding may emerge simultaneously with recognition once localization supervision is present, making the observed lag an artifact of training mixes rather than capability structure.
fastest_falsification: Two days: paired crop-versus-scene evaluation on three scales of one model family; no threshold gap kills it.

one_line: mAP integrates over recall regimes no deployment uses, and an operating-region-weighted metric reorders detector leaderboards in a way that predicts deployment satisfaction better
problem: The community's headline metric averages precision over all recall levels including regimes (very low precision tails) that no real system operates in, so leaderboard ordering may diverge from deployed usefulness, but the size and structure of that divergence is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Restricting the precision-recall integral to operationally relevant regions (high-precision band for alerting, high-recall band for screening) changes detector rankings for a meaningful fraction of model pairs, and the operating-region metric correlates better with task-level outcomes in downstream pipelines than full-integral mAP does.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of public detectors, rank correlation between full mAP and region-restricted AP will be visibly below 1 with concrete rank flips, and an end-to-end task benchmark (counting or alerting) will side with the region-restricted ordering in the flipped pairs more often than not.
why_important: Model selection across the industry defaults to mAP; demonstrating systematic rank divergence with a better-aligned alternative would change evaluation practice cheaply.
why_possibly_novel: Criticisms of mAP exist qualitatively; a quantitative flip-rate study tied to downstream task validation of the alternative ordering appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 20 public checkpoints, compute full and region-restricted metrics, count rank flips, then run flipped pairs through one alerting-style downstream task to see which ordering predicts task success.
main_risk: Region boundaries are a free parameter; conclusions could be sensitive to arbitrary band choices unless swept and reported honestly.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: mAP is a robust summary; detectors better in mAP are better in practice for essentially all uses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PR curves of modern detectors may rarely cross, making all reasonable weightings produce the same order.
fastest_falsification: One day: full-vs-banded metric ranking for a dozen checkpoints; near-perfect rank agreement kills it.

one_line: High-IoU evaluation thresholds measure annotation-style agreement rather than perceived localization quality: beyond the annotator-consistency ceiling, AP@0.9 stops correlating with human preference
problem: The strict end of the IoU threshold sweep is presumed to reward precise localization, but if GT boxes themselves carry style variance near that precision, the strictest thresholds may score agreement with an arbitrary convention, not quality, misdirecting method development toward convention-fitting.
core_hypothesis: There exists an IoU level (measurable from inter-annotator statistics) beyond which method-ranking by AP diverges from human side-by-side preference of boxes, because differences past that level are within annotation noise; below the level rankings agree, defining a principled maximum useful threshold per dataset.
falsifiable_prediction: Human preference studies comparing boxes from method pairs will agree with AP ordering at moderate thresholds and become uncorrelated at thresholds beyond the measured inter-annotator ceiling, consistently across datasets with different annotation rigor.
why_important: Threshold sweeps drive both evaluation and loss design (IoU-based losses chase strict thresholds); knowing where measurement turns to noise recalibrates both.
why_possibly_novel: Annotator variance is documented; connecting it to a divergence point between AP and human preference to derive dataset-specific maximum informative thresholds appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure inter-annotator IoU distributions on a dataset sample, collect human pairwise preferences on method outputs stratified by threshold band, locate the divergence point, compare with the annotator ceiling.
main_risk: Human preference for boxes is itself noisy and may not be the right gold standard for localization quality in task contexts.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Stricter IoU thresholds always measure finer localization quality; AP averaged to 0.95 is strictly more informative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern annotation tooling may produce boxes consistent enough that even 0.9 sits below the noise ceiling, leaving the sweep fully informative.
fastest_falsification: Two days: annotator-consistency measurement plus a small preference study at two threshold bands; sustained correlation kills it.

one_line: Benchmark mAP differences between adjacent leaderboard entries are often within bootstrap confidence intervals, and the field's progress narrative at the top end is partly statistical noise
problem: Detection papers claim superiority over prior work by fractions of an mAP point without reporting uncertainty, but mAP is a complicated statistic of a finite test set whose variance across resamples and rare-class contributions has never been made a standard part of comparisons.
core_hypothesis: Image-level bootstrap of standard test sets yields mAP confidence intervals wide enough to overlap many published adjacent-method gaps, with the variance dominated by rare-class AP terms, implying that a meaningful fraction of claimed state-of-the-art transitions are not statistically distinguishable.
falsifiable_prediction: Bootstrap intervals computed for a set of public checkpoints will overlap for a substantial share of consecutive leaderboard pairs, and the interval width will shrink dramatically when rare classes are excluded, localizing the noise source.
why_important: It would install uncertainty reporting as a norm and redirect attention from sub-noise leaderboard steps toward changes that survive statistical scrutiny.
why_possibly_novel: Variance concerns are voiced informally; a systematic bootstrap audit of leaderboard gaps with a decomposition of variance sources appears rare in the detection literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap test sets at the image level for a dozen checkpoints, compute interval widths and pairwise overlap rates, decompose variance by class-frequency strata.
main_risk: Image-level bootstrap may misrepresent the sampling process of benchmark construction, requiring careful justification of the resampling unit.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: A higher benchmark mAP, however small the margin, indicates a better method.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large test sets may make intervals tight enough that most published gaps clear them, deflating the critique.
fastest_falsification: Half a day: bootstrap intervals for five checkpoints; consistently non-overlapping intervals kill it.

one_line: mAP's duplicate penalty is weaker than its miss penalty in common regimes, so validation-tuned models systematically learn to over-detect, a bias measurable as deployment precision shortfall
problem: The matching rules of AP-style metrics penalize a duplicate as one false positive among many detections but a miss as a permanent recall loss, and every hyperparameter and threshold tuned against val mAP inherits this asymmetry; whether it audibly biases deployed model behavior is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: Optimizing detection pipelines against mAP drives score thresholds and NMS settings toward over-detection relative to what balanced deployment costs would choose, so mAP-tuned configurations sit systematically on the high-recall side of cost-optimal operating points, and the displacement is predictable from the metric's penalty structure.
falsifiable_prediction: Comparing mAP-optimal configuration choices against cost-curve-optimal choices across detectors will show a consistent directional displacement toward over-detection, growing when tuning uses lower IoU thresholds and shrinking under metrics with explicit FP costs.
why_important: Thousands of deployed systems inherit their operating character from val-mAP tuning; documenting a systematic displacement gives a correction recipe (tune against cost curves) with immediate effect.
why_possibly_novel: Metric critiques focus on ranking validity; the behavioral bias that metric asymmetry imprints on tuned configurations appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For three detectors, tune thresholds and NMS against val mAP and against several explicit cost ratios, measure the displacement of mAP-tuned configurations along the cost-optimal frontier.
main_risk: Displacement direction may vary by dataset density, complicating the clean directional story.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Tuning on val mAP produces balanced, deployment-appropriate configurations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Practitioners already re-tune thresholds for deployment, so the imprint may exist but be routinely corrected in practice.
fastest_falsification: One day: mAP-tuned versus cost-tuned thresholds for one detector across three cost ratios; no consistent displacement kills it.

one_line: The small-medium-large size buckets are misaligned with actual failure structure: data-driven size strata reveal different method rankings and hidden regressions that the standard buckets average away
problem: Size-stratified reporting uses fixed pixel-area cutoffs inherited from one benchmark's history, but failure modes cluster at architecture-specific sizes (assignment boundaries, stride effects), so the fixed buckets may hide exactly the strata where methods differ or regress.
core_hypothesis: Deriving size strata from the data (clustering per-object error profiles across models) produces bucket boundaries far from the conventional cutoffs, and re-reporting existing method comparisons under derived strata exposes rank changes and regressions invisible in the standard three buckets.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-profile clustering will yield stable boundaries that differ from conventional cutoffs, method pairs with identical bucket-level conclusions will show significant divergences in at least one derived stratum, and the divergent strata will align with architectural transition sizes of the compared models.
why_important: Size breakdown is the main diagnostic lens for detection progress; if its bins are wrong, the community routinely miscommunicates where methods actually improve.
why_possibly_novel: Bucket arbitrariness is acknowledged in passing; a principled derivation of strata from cross-model error structure with re-evaluation of published comparisons appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-object errors for six detectors, cluster error profiles over size, derive strata, re-evaluate three published-style comparisons under both stratifications, catalog conclusion changes.
main_risk: Derived strata may vary across datasets and model pools, undermining the goal of a standardized reporting improvement.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The conventional size buckets adequately capture scale-dependent behavior for reporting purposes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failure structure may be smooth in size for modern detectors, making any bucketing roughly equivalent.
fastest_falsification: One day: error-vs-size curves for three detectors; smooth structureless curves kill it.

one_line: Error-taxonomy attribution in detection is order-dependent: the sequence in which error types are fixed changes their measured contributions enough to reverse published conclusions about what limits detectors
problem: Popular error-analysis toolkits attribute mAP loss to error categories by fixing them sequentially, but the attribution of interacting errors depends on fixing order (a duplicate may also be a localization error), and the community reads the outputs as order-free truths.
core_hypothesis: Recomputing error attributions under permuted fixing orders (or Shapley-style averaging over orders) will change category shares substantially for typical detectors, sometimes reordering the top-ranked limiting factor, meaning conclusions drawn from single-order taxonomies are artifacts at a measurable rate.
falsifiable_prediction: Across detectors and datasets, the variance of category attribution across fixing orders will be large relative to between-model attribution differences, and specific published-style conclusions (which error dominates) will flip between plausible orders in a non-trivial fraction of cases.
why_important: Error taxonomies steer research investment; if their outputs are order artifacts, the field's map of what limits detection needs redrawing with interaction-aware attribution.
why_possibly_novel: Order dependence is a known caveat mentioned in fine print; quantifying it and providing an order-free Shapley alternative for detection error analysis appears undone.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement taxonomy analysis with permutable fixing order, run all orders (or sampled Shapley) for five detectors on two datasets, report attribution variance and conclusion-flip rates.
main_risk: Full order enumeration is combinatorial; sampling noise in Shapley estimates must be smaller than the effects claimed.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Error-taxonomy outputs are stable descriptions of a detector's limiting factors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Error-type interactions may be small in practice, making single-order attributions nearly identical to order-free ones.
fastest_falsification: One day: two extreme fixing orders on one detector; near-identical attributions kill it.

one_line: Frame-wise video detection metrics hide temporal flicker: models with equal per-frame mAP differ hugely in detection persistence, and a flicker-penalizing metric would reorder method preference for video deployments
problem: Video detection is evaluated frame-by-frame, so a model whose detections blink on and off scores identically to one with stable detections, while every downstream consumer (tracking, alerting, human review) strongly prefers stability; the size of the hidden stability differences across models is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Per-object detection persistence (run-length statistics of matched detections across frames) varies widely among models with matched frame-wise mAP, the variation is driven by score-threshold crossings rather than feature instability, and a metric combining frame accuracy with persistence changes model rankings for video use cases.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating several detectors on video with both frame-wise mAP and persistence-aware metrics will find matched-mAP pairs with large persistence gaps, and human raters reviewing alert streams will prefer the persistence-favored model in a majority of matched pairs.
why_important: Video is the dominant deployment medium; a validated stability-aware metric would realign evaluation with actual utility at near-zero adoption cost.
why_possibly_novel: Tracking metrics measure identity persistence with trackers attached; a detector-intrinsic flicker metric validated against human preference, without any tracker, appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run five detectors on annotated video, compute frame-wise and persistence metrics, identify matched-mAP divergent pairs, run a small human preference study on alert visualizations.
main_risk: Persistence depends on video content difficulty; normalization across sequences must be careful for the metric to be comparable.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Good frame-wise detection implies good video detection; stability is the tracker's job.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern detectors may all flicker similarly at matched mAP, leaving the new metric without discriminative power.
fastest_falsification: One day: persistence statistics for three detectors on one video set; near-identical persistence at matched mAP kills it.

one_line: Open-vocab benchmarks with static base-novel splits have been community-overfit: years of method development tuned on the same 'novel' classes inflates novel-class AP relative to genuinely fresh splits
problem: Open-vocabulary detection progress is measured on fixed benchmark splits whose novel classes have been public for years, so hyperparameters, prompt templates, and architecture choices have been implicitly selected against the supposedly held-out classes, and no one measures how much of the reported novel-class gain survives on fresh splits.
core_hypothesis: Re-running representative open-vocab methods on newly randomized base-novel splits (or on classes introduced after the methods were developed) will show systematically smaller base-to-novel generalization gaps than reported, with the shrinkage largest for methods with many split-tuned design choices, quantifying community-level overfitting to static splits.
falsifiable_prediction: The ranking of methods by novel-class AP will compress and partially reorder under fresh splits, the per-method shrinkage will correlate with the number of design decisions tuned on the original split, and time-stratified evaluation (classes unavailable during method development) will show the largest drops.
why_important: If novel-class progress is partly split memorization at the community level, the field's central claim of open-vocabulary generalization needs re-grounding with rotating or time-stratified splits.
why_possibly_novel: Community overfitting is documented for classification test sets; a split-rotation audit specifically for open-vocab detection generalization claims appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select four open-vocab methods with public code, generate five random base-novel splits plus one time-stratified split, re-evaluate, compare gap distributions against published-split gaps.
main_risk: Re-training on new splits is compute-heavy, and method reimplementations may not faithfully reproduce original tuning.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Static base-novel splits provide valid measurement of open-vocabulary generalization across the literature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Method designs may be genuinely split-agnostic, in which case fresh splits reproduce published gaps and the audit vindicates the benchmarks.
fastest_falsification: Three days: re-evaluate two methods on two fresh splits; reproduced gaps kill the overfitting claim.

one_line: Label-assignment strategy is the primary determinant of a detector's failure-mode profile: assignment swaps reshape error taxonomies more than backbone or loss swaps at matched mAP
problem: Detector components are compared by aggregate AP, treating architecture as the main axis of variation, but which samples get positive labels during training plausibly decides which situations the detector handles, and no study ranks components by their influence on error composition rather than error total.
core_hypothesis: In a factorial study swapping label assignment, loss family, and backbone at matched final mAP, assignment will explain the largest share of variance in error-taxonomy composition (crowd misses versus duplicates versus localization slop), because assignment directly shapes the training distribution each head sees.
falsifiable_prediction: Variance decomposition over the factorial will attribute more error-profile variance to assignment than to backbone or loss, and detectors sharing assignment but differing otherwise will have more similar error profiles than detectors sharing backbones but differing in assignment.
why_important: It would redirect failure-mode engineering from architecture search toward assignment design, a cheaper and more targeted lever, and explain why same-mAP detectors behave so differently in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: Assignment methods are compared on AP; their causal signature on error composition, ranked against other components, appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 2x2x2 factorial (two assignments, two losses, two backbones) to matched mAP on one dataset, run taxonomy analysis per cell, decompose profile variance by factor.
main_risk: Matching mAP across cells requires unequal training budgets, which could itself influence error profiles and muddy the attribution.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Backbone and loss choices dominate detector behavior; assignment is an optimization detail affecting convergence speed and a few AP points.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Error profiles may be dominated by data statistics that all training setups inherit equally, leaving little variance for any component to explain.
fastest_falsification: Four days including training: reduced 2x2 factorial (assignment x backbone) on a small dataset; backbone dominating profile variance kills it.

one_line: Focal-loss gamma is a hidden operating-point selector: it trades rare-class recall against background FP suppression in a smooth, predictable way that mAP hides but fixed-threshold deployment feels
problem: The focusing parameter of focal loss is treated as a converged default from early papers, but by reweighting easy negatives it implicitly chooses how aggressively the detector suppresses uncertain detections, a behavioral choice that never appears in mAP-based ablations because mAP averages over thresholds.
core_hypothesis: Sweeping gamma at fixed architecture traces a smooth frontier between rare-class recall and background false-positive rate at deployment thresholds, with mAP nearly flat along the frontier, meaning the community default silently picks one deployment character and applications should select gamma by cost ratio rather than convention.
falsifiable_prediction: Gamma-swept detectors will show near-constant mAP but monotone movement of fixed-threshold rare-class recall and FP rates in opposite directions, and the frontier position will be predictable enough to choose gamma from a target cost ratio without retraining twice.
why_important: A training-time scalar that sets deployment character without hurting benchmarks is a free control knob practitioners currently do not know they have.
why_possibly_novel: Gamma ablations report mAP; the fixed-threshold behavioral frontier interpretation and cost-driven selection recipe appear unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train five gamma variants of one detector on one dataset, evaluate mAP plus fixed-threshold recall and FP profiles per class-frequency stratum, chart the frontier.
main_risk: Gamma may interact with score calibration such that post-hoc recalibration erases the behavioral differences, making the knob redundant with thresholding.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: The standard gamma value is a solved hyperparameter; deviation is pointless since mAP is flat around it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flat mAP may reflect genuinely identical behavior rather than a hidden frontier, with threshold effects fully correctable by calibration.
fastest_falsification: Three days: three gamma variants on a small dataset with fixed-threshold profiling; identical profiles after recalibration kill it.

one_line: Copy-paste augmentation teaches boundary shortcuts: detectors learn to key on compositing edge statistics, detectable as inflated performance on pasted objects versus photometrically matched natural ones
problem: Copy-paste is a standard augmentation credited with large gains, but pasted objects carry subtle boundary artifacts (blending halos, context mismatch), and if detectors exploit these as shortcuts, some measured gains are artifact detection rather than object learning, with unknown consequences on natural data.
core_hypothesis: Detectors trained with heavy copy-paste develop measurable sensitivity to compositing signatures: they detect pasted instances more readily than appearance-matched natural instances, attention concentrates anomalously on paste boundaries, and their natural-data gains are smaller than mixed-eval suggests, with harder blending during training shrinking all three effects.
falsifiable_prediction: A probe set pairing pasted and natural instances of matched appearance will show a detection-rate gap favoring pasted instances for copy-paste-trained models but not for baseline models, and the gap will shrink monotonically with blending quality used during training.
why_important: Copy-paste is in most modern training recipes; quantifying its shortcut component recalibrates how much of reported gains transfer to deployment and dictates blending standards.
why_possibly_novel: Copy-paste ablations measure benchmark AP; the shortcut-learning audit with matched pasted-versus-natural probes appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched detectors with and without copy-paste, build the paired probe set, compare detection-rate gaps and boundary-attention statistics, sweep blending quality in a follow-up run.
main_risk: Constructing truly appearance-matched natural-versus-pasted pairs is hard, and residual mismatches could produce the gap without any shortcut learning.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Copy-paste gains reflect genuine data diversification; blending artifacts are too subtle to be exploited.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may generalize past boundary artifacts because object interiors dominate the receptive fields that drive detection.
fastest_falsification: Two days: probe-set gap measurement on one public copy-paste-trained checkpoint versus a baseline; no gap kills it.

one_line: Detection subtasks converge at different speeds: classification keeps improving while localization plateaus early, so single-criterion early stopping systematically ships suboptimal boxes
problem: Training is stopped by aggregate validation mAP, assuming subtasks improve in lockstep, but the classification and box-regression heads face different optimization landscapes and data richness, and their separate convergence trajectories are never monitored or exploited.
core_hypothesis: Localization quality (mean IoU of matched detections) saturates substantially earlier in training than classification accuracy, so late training mostly reshuffles scores; consequently per-subtask checkpointing (freezing or snapshotting the box head early, letting classification continue) yields better joint models than single-checkpoint selection.
falsifiable_prediction: Tracking subtask metrics across training will show localization plateaus at a consistent fraction of total schedule across datasets and architectures, and a composite model using an earlier box head with a later classification head will beat the best single checkpoint on high-IoU metrics without losing classification AP.
why_important: A free improvement from checkpoint composition plus a diagnosis of wasted late-training compute would matter to every detector training pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Training-dynamics studies chart aggregate loss; per-subtask convergence asymmetry and cross-checkpoint head composition appear untried for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument two training runs with per-epoch subtask metrics, locate plateaus, assemble composite checkpoints across epochs, evaluate against standard selection.
main_risk: Head compatibility across checkpoints may fail because features drift, breaking naive composition and requiring adapters that complicate the story.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Subtasks converge together; the best validation-mAP checkpoint is the best available model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared-backbone coupling may force subtask trajectories to move together, eliminating the asymmetry the idea depends on.
fastest_falsification: Two days: per-subtask training curves for one run; parallel trajectories kill it.

one_line: Gradient influence in detection training scales with per-image object count, so crowded images dominate learning and flat per-object reweighting measurably shifts detector behavior toward sparse-scene competence
