problem: Detection losses sum over objects, so a fifty-object image contributes fifty times a one-object image's gradient, silently reweighting training toward dense-scene statistics; whether this hidden weighting helps or hurts, and what per-object normalization would change, has not been isolated.
core_hypothesis: The implicit count-proportional weighting biases learned representations toward crowded-scene appearance and suppression behavior, and retraining with per-image gradient normalization trades crowd AP for sparse-scene AP along a controllable frontier, revealing scene-density balance as an unmanaged training choice.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched runs with count-proportional versus normalized weighting will show opposite-signed AP deltas on density-stratified eval subsets, with the effect size largest for classes appearing in both sparse and dense contexts.
why_important: Deployments differ enormously in density (surveillance versus product photography); exposing and controlling the density bias in standard training gives a free specialization knob.
why_possibly_novel: Loss normalization choices are discussed for optimization stability; their effect as a scene-density prior on final behavior appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train paired models under both weighting schemes on one dataset, evaluate on density-stratified splits, chart the trade-off frontier across a weighting interpolation.
main_risk: Batch composition and sampler interactions may dwarf the loss-weighting effect, requiring joint control.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Loss summation conventions are optimization details without systematic behavioral consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adaptive optimizers may partially neutralize scale differences between images, shrinking the density bias below relevance.
fastest_falsification: Three days: two matched runs with opposite weighting on a small dataset; identical density-stratified profiles kill it.

one_line: Frozen-backbone detectors are systematically better calibrated but less accurate than fine-tuned ones, revealing a plasticity-calibration trade-off exploitable by hybrid freezing schedules
problem: Fine-tuning the whole detector maximizes benchmark accuracy, and freezing backbones is framed purely as a compute compromise; the possibility that backbone plasticity is causally linked to deployment miscalibration (features co-adapting to the head's overconfident shortcuts) has not been tested.
core_hypothesis: At matched training data, frozen-backbone detectors produce reliably lower calibration error and better out-of-domain score transfer than end-to-end fine-tuned counterparts, because feature co-adaptation during fine-tuning inflates in-distribution confidence structure that does not travel; partial-freezing schedules trace a smooth frontier between the regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: Across matched pairs on multiple datasets, frozen variants will have lower detection ECE in-distribution and smaller optimal-threshold shift out-of-distribution despite lower mAP, and progressive-freezing variants will interpolate both properties monotonically.
why_important: For systems that prize predictable confidence over the last few AP points (medical triage, safety monitors), the freezing decision becomes a principled reliability choice rather than a compute compromise.
why_possibly_novel: Freezing ablations report accuracy and cost; the calibration and threshold-transfer consequences of backbone plasticity appear unmeasured for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train frozen, partially frozen, and fully fine-tuned variants of one detector on two datasets, evaluate ECE and OOD threshold shift alongside mAP, chart the frontier.
main_risk: Calibration differences may stem from effective capacity rather than co-adaptation, requiring capacity-matched controls to interpret.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Freezing is a compute-saving compromise that costs accuracy and offers nothing in return.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Post-hoc recalibration may equalize the calibration gap cheaply, leaving fine-tuning strictly dominant after a temperature fit.
fastest_falsification: Two days: ECE and OOD threshold-shift comparison for one frozen-versus-fine-tuned pair; equal calibration after temperature scaling kills it.

one_line: A chunk of reported EMA gains in detection is calibration artifact: weight averaging smooths score distributions in ways that flatter mAP without changing which objects are found
problem: Exponential moving average of weights is a default trick credited with consistent mAP improvements, but mAP is sensitive to score-distribution smoothness (fewer ties, better-spread ranks), so EMA could gain benchmark points by reshaping scores rather than detections, misleading the community about its mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Comparing EMA and non-EMA endpoints of identical runs will show that a substantial fraction of the mAP delta survives detection-set matching (same found objects, different scores), meaning the gain is score-shape improvement; the detection-set component concentrates in unstable late-training classes, and score-recalibration of the non-EMA model recovers much of the gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Set-level analysis will attribute a large share of EMA's mAP delta to reordering effects at matched detected sets, and per-class attribution will show detection-set differences only where late-training loss oscillates.
why_important: Understanding whether a universal trick improves representations or just score cosmetics changes how it should be used (or replaced by explicit calibration) and how ablations crediting EMA should be read.
why_possibly_novel: EMA is ablated as a scalar mAP delta; the set-versus-score decomposition of its detection gains appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Save paired EMA and raw checkpoints from several runs, match detection sets at fixed thresholds, decompose mAP deltas into set and ordering components, test post-hoc recalibration of raw checkpoints.
main_risk: The decomposition depends on threshold conventions for defining the matched set, and sloppy choices could manufacture either conclusion.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: EMA improves the learned representation, producing genuinely better detections.
why_it_might_be_wrong: EMA's smoothing may truly stabilize feature learning, with score effects a minor byproduct, in which case the decomposition confirms the standard story.
fastest_falsification: One day with paired checkpoints: set-versus-ordering decomposition on one run; ordering share near zero kills it.

one_line: Multi-dataset detection co-training suffers quantifiable taxonomy interference: identical concepts with mismatched labels across sources split score mass, and label-space unification recovers a predictable share of the lost AP
problem: Training detectors on merged datasets is standard for robustness, but sources disagree on names and boundaries for the same visible concept (sofa versus couch, differing vehicle splits), and the performance cost of forcing one model to satisfy conflicting taxonomies has not been isolated from the benefits of extra data.
core_hypothesis: For concept groups with cross-source label conflicts, co-trained models exhibit score splitting (probability mass divided between sibling labels), depressing per-label AP below what a unified-label retraining achieves on identical images, and the AP loss per group is predictable from a label-conflict statistic computed on the merged annotation sets.
falsifiable_prediction: Conflict-heavy concept groups will show sibling-label score anti-correlation and depressed AP in co-trained models, unification will recover AP proportionally to the measured conflict statistic, and conflict-free groups will show no such recovery.
why_important: Merged-data training is the default scaling path for detection; a conflict-audit tool plus predictable unification gains would improve every such pipeline at low cost.
why_possibly_novel: Label-space merging heuristics exist in engineering practice; the quantitative interference law linking conflict statistics to AP loss and recovery appears unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify conflicted and clean concept groups across a two-dataset merge, train co-trained and unified variants, measure score splitting and AP recovery, fit the conflict-to-loss relationship.
main_risk: Unification itself requires judgment calls; a poorly unified taxonomy could under- or over-state the recoverable share.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: More data helps; label mismatches across merged datasets are minor noise the model averages over.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Language-embedded label spaces in modern detectors may already absorb synonym conflicts, leaving interference only for genuinely contradictory boundary conventions.
fastest_falsification: Two days: score-splitting analysis on one co-trained public model for three conflicted groups; no anti-correlation kills it.

one_line: Occlusion robustness is memorized pairwise, not geometric: detectors handle frequent occluder-occludee pairs and fail on rare pairs with identical geometry, exposing lookup-table occlusion handling
problem: Occlusion performance is assumed to reflect general amodal competence, but training data contains highly repetitive occlusion pairings (person-behind-person, car-behind-car), so detectors may have learned pair-specific completions that masquerade as general occlusion reasoning until a rare pairing appears.
core_hypothesis: Recall under occlusion depends on the training-set frequency of the specific occluder-occludee class pair, beyond what occlusion geometry (coverage fraction, boundary complexity) explains, so geometry-matched rare pairs will show substantially lower recall, and synthetic training with randomized pairings will flatten the pair-frequency dependence.
falsifiable_prediction: A paste-based benchmark controlling occlusion geometry while varying pair identity will show recall differences of large magnitude between frequent and rare pairs, and the per-pair recall will regress strongly on pair co-occurrence counts in training data.
why_important: Safety cases assume occlusion handling generalizes; if it is pair-memorized, rare-event scenarios (unusual object stacked configurations) are systematically riskier than benchmarks suggest.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion studies vary coverage level; holding geometry fixed while varying pair identity to expose memorization appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct geometry-matched occlusion pairs across frequency strata via segmentation-based compositing, evaluate three detectors, regress recall on pair frequency with geometry covariates.
main_risk: Compositing realism differences across pair types could correlate with pair rarity, confounding the frequency effect.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Occlusion robustness is a general geometric capability that transfers across object pairings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may rely on occludee-local evidence alone, making the occluder's identity irrelevant and the pair-frequency effect nil.
fastest_falsification: Two days: geometry-matched frequent-versus-rare pair probe on one detector; equal recall kills it.

one_line: Amodal completion emerges unevenly and without supervision in standard detectors: some architectures silently regress boxes past occluders while others truncate, an unmanaged behavioral fork with downstream consequences
problem: Modal-versus-amodal box behavior under occlusion is set by dataset convention, but detectors interpolate when conventions are inconsistent, and different architectures may have settled on different implicit behaviors that nobody documents, breaking downstream assumptions about what a box means.
core_hypothesis: Probing detectors with progressive synthetic occlusion will reveal architecture-family-specific completion signatures (some extending boxes toward hidden extents, others tracking visible pixels), stable across datasets, implying that the semantic meaning of a box under occlusion is an uncontrolled architectural property rather than a data property.
falsifiable_prediction: Under monotonic occlusion sweeps, predicted-box extent curves will bifurcate into completion-type and truncation-type families aligned with architecture rather than training data, and the same architecture trained on different datasets will keep its signature.
why_important: Downstream geometry (distance from box bottom, size-based reasoning) silently depends on completion behavior; documenting the fork prevents category errors in system design and defines a property future benchmarks should specify.
why_possibly_novel: Amodal detection is studied with explicit supervision; the characterization of emergent, unsupervised completion behavior as an architectural signature appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build occlusion sweeps over segmented objects, measure predicted-extent-versus-coverage curves for six detectors spanning three families and two training sets each, cluster the curves.
main_risk: Within-family variation (losses, assignment) may dominate, making the signature architectural story too clean to be true.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Box behavior under occlusion follows training annotation convention; architecture is irrelevant to what boxes mean.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Convention in the dominant training sets may be strong enough to override any architectural inclination, homogenizing behavior.
fastest_falsification: One day: occlusion sweeps for two architectures sharing a training set; identical curves kill it.

one_line: Crowding failures have an architecture-specific feature-collision cliff: recall versus instance-overlap curves show sharp breakpoints where pooled representations of neighbors merge, and the cliff location is a measurable model constant
problem: Detection in crowds degrades with overlap, but the degradation is assumed gradual; if internal representations of adjacent instances collide abruptly past a spacing threshold (features pooled over overlapping receptive fields becoming indistinguishable), each architecture has a characteristic density cliff that deployment planners should know.
core_hypothesis: Recall as a function of controlled inter-instance overlap exhibits a breakpoint (not smooth decline) whose location is stable per architecture across object classes, predictable from receptive-field and pooling geometry, and movable by architectural changes (dilated context, higher-resolution heads) in the predicted direction.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetic spacing sweeps will show piecewise recall curves with statistically identifiable breakpoints, breakpoint locations will cluster by architecture family and correlate with computed receptive-field overlap statistics, and a resolution-increased variant will shift its breakpoint accordingly.
why_important: A model constant that predicts the density at which detection collapses lets planners match architectures to deployment densities a priori instead of empirically failing.
why_possibly_novel: Crowd degradation is benchmarked on natural datasets with entangled factors; controlled spacing sweeps isolating the collision threshold as an architectural constant appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate paste-based spacing sweeps at fixed instance appearance, fit piecewise regressions to recall curves for four architectures, test breakpoint stability across classes and correlation with receptive-field statistics.
main_risk: NMS and assignment effects overlay the representational collision, requiring pre-suppression analysis to locate the true cliff.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Crowd degradation is smooth and data-driven; there is no sharp architecture-determined density limit.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention-based architectures may separate overlapping instances adaptively, yielding genuinely smooth curves with no breakpoint to find.
fastest_falsification: One day: spacing sweep on one CNN detector with pre-NMS logging; a smooth curve kills the cliff claim for that family.

one_line: Hand occlusion is a privileged pattern: objects habitually held (phones, cups, tools) survive hand occlusion far better than geometry-matched occlusion by other objects, revealing learned occluder-specific robustness
problem: Occlusion is modeled as information loss parameterized by coverage, but the occluder's identity carries information too (hands imply held objects), and whether detectors exploit occluder identity, and for which patterns, has never been systematically mapped.
core_hypothesis: Detectors have learned occluder-conditional priors from frequent interaction patterns, so recall for handheld-class objects occluded by hands will exceed recall under geometry-matched occlusion by neutral objects, while classes never held will show no hand advantage, mapping which interaction priors detection models have internalized.
falsifiable_prediction: A compositing benchmark crossing occluder type (hand versus matched neutral occluder) with object class (habitually held versus not) will show a significant interaction: hand occlusion advantage exists only for held-class objects, and its size correlates with hand-object co-occurrence in training data.
why_important: Occluder-conditional robustness means benchmark occlusion numbers built from arbitrary occluders mispredict real-world performance where occlusion patterns are highly structured; it also reveals an unappreciated pathway by which detectors encode interaction knowledge.
why_possibly_novel: Hand-object interaction is studied for pose and affordance; its role as an occlusion prior inside plain object detectors appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Composite hand and neutral occluders at matched coverage over held and non-held object classes, evaluate recall interactions on three detectors, correlate advantages with co-occurrence statistics.
main_risk: Hands are visually distinctive, so a hand advantage might reflect general contextual cueing (a hand predicts an object nearby) rather than occluder-conditional completion, needing control probes with hands adjacent but not occluding.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Occlusion difficulty is determined by coverage geometry; the occluder's identity is irrelevant to detection robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The adjacency control may show the entire effect is contextual cueing, reducing the finding to known context effects.
fastest_falsification: Two days: hand-versus-neutral occlusion probe with adjacency controls for five classes; no interaction kills it.

one_line: Fence-like periodic occluders cause duplicate-fragmentation failure rather than recognition failure: detectors see stripes of one object as multiple objects, a failure signature distinct from opaque occlusion
problem: Transparent and periodic occluders (fences, railings, blinds) are common in surveillance and wildlife imaging, but occlusion research treats occlusion as contiguous information loss; periodic interruption may cause a categorically different failure (one object fragmenting into several detections) that aggregate metrics record misleadingly as localization error.
core_hypothesis: Behind periodic occluders, detectors emit multiple fragment detections whose boxes align with visibility stripes, at rates far above opaque-occlusion baselines of matched total coverage, because continuity cues that bind fragments into one object are architecture-dependent and weak in feedforward detectors; the failure signature (fragment count, stripe alignment) cleanly separates from recognition failure.
falsifiable_prediction: Compositing periodic versus contiguous occlusion at matched coverage will show fragmentation (multiple high-IoU-with-stripe detections per GT) dominating the periodic condition, minimal fragmentation in the contiguous condition, and fragment merging by simple continuity post-processing recovering a large share of the lost single-object detections.
why_important: The failure type dictates the fix (fragment merging or continuity modeling, not more occlusion augmentation), and the affected settings are high-value deployments where fences are ubiquitous.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion severity studies use contiguous masks; the periodic-occlusion fragmentation signature and its post-processing remedy appear undocumented.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched periodic and contiguous occlusion probes over animal and person imagery, quantify fragmentation statistics per condition on three detectors, test a continuity-based merge heuristic.
main_risk: Fragmentation may be entangled with NMS settings, requiring suppression-stage controls before attributing it to representation.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Occlusion difficulty scales with covered fraction; the spatial pattern of coverage is secondary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern detectors with large receptive fields and global attention may bind stripes effortlessly, making fragmentation a legacy-architecture artifact.
fastest_falsification: One day: fence-composite probe on 200 images with one detector; no excess fragmentation kills it.

one_line: The minimum visible fraction needed for detection is class-structured by part informativeness: objects with discriminative localized parts are detectable from slivers, and the visibility threshold is predictable from part-level recognition data
problem: Visibility thresholds for detection are reported, if at all, as global averages, but classes differ in whether identity concentrates in localized parts (faces, wheels, labels) or diffuses across extent, implying structured per-class visibility floors that risk models and annotation policies should know.
core_hypothesis: Per-class detection-versus-visible-fraction curves have inflection points predictable from the spatial concentration of discriminative evidence (measurable by occlusion-sensitivity mapping on unoccluded examples), so a cheap sensitivity analysis on clean data forecasts which classes survive heavy occlusion and which collapse early.
falsifiable_prediction: Classes with concentrated sensitivity maps will show low visibility floors when the informative part is visible and near-total failure when it is hidden (strong part-position dependence), while diffuse classes will show smooth coverage-dependence without part-position sensitivity, and the clean-data sensitivity statistic will predict the occlusion behavior with useful accuracy.
why_important: Forecasting occlusion behavior from clean-data analysis eliminates expensive occlusion benchmarking per class and informs sensor placement (ensuring informative parts stay visible).
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion sensitivity maps exist as interpretability tools; using them to predict per-class visibility floors and part-position-conditional detection appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute occlusion-sensitivity concentration per class on clean images, run part-aware occlusion sweeps (hiding versus revealing the concentrated region), test prediction of visibility floors across 20 classes.
main_risk: Sensitivity maps reflect the probing occluder's statistics as much as the model's reliance structure, risking circularity in the prediction.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detection under occlusion degrades with visible fraction roughly uniformly across classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contextual evidence may dominate for many classes, decoupling occlusion behavior from any object-internal part structure.
fastest_falsification: Two days: sensitivity concentration versus visibility-floor comparison for eight classes; no relationship kills it.

one_line: Detector-based counting saturates predictably in dense scenes, and the undercount is recoverable from pre-NMS score mass: a hybrid detector-regressor readout corrects counts without any new training
problem: Counting by detection undercounts once scenes densify (suppression and assignment limits), forcing teams to switch to density-regression models that lose localization; a signal inside the detector that tracks the true count past the detection ceiling would give both localization and accurate counts from one model.
core_hypothesis: Pre-suppression score mass (integrated objectness over the image) continues to scale with true instance count beyond the density where discrete detection saturates, so a per-class mapping from score mass to count, calibrated on sparse scenes, extrapolates to dense scenes and corrects the detector's undercount with quantifiable accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: On density-swept data, discrete counts will saturate while score mass stays near-linear in true count over a substantially wider range, and the hybrid readout will cut counting error in dense scenes by a large factor relative to detection-only counts, using no density-map supervision.
why_important: One-model counting-plus-localization would simplify retail, wildlife, and crowd systems that currently run two model families in parallel.
why_possibly_novel: Density regression and detection are separate literatures; extracting a latent count signal from an unmodified detector's pre-suppression mass appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep density with paste-composited scenes and natural crowd data, measure discrete-count saturation and score-mass linearity, fit and validate the hybrid mapping across classes.
main_risk: Score mass may saturate almost as early as discrete counts because feature collision suppresses raw activations too, not just suppression-stage outputs.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Dense counting requires density-map models; detectors fundamentally cannot count past their suppression ceiling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The linear range of score mass may extend only marginally past detection saturation, making the hybrid gain too small to justify complexity.
fastest_falsification: One day: score-mass-versus-count curve on one density sweep; early saturation kills it.

one_line: Video detection flicker is mostly threshold-crossing of smoothly varying scores, not representational instability: hysteresis thresholding eliminates the majority of flicker at negligible accuracy cost
problem: Detection flicker across consecutive frames is blamed on unstable features and motivates heavy temporal architectures, but if underlying scores vary smoothly and flicker is manufactured by binary thresholding near the operating point, the fix is a two-line change, and the field is over-engineering.
core_hypothesis: Per-object score time series in video are predominantly smooth (high lag-1 autocorrelation) with flicker events concentrated where scores hover near threshold, so dual-threshold hysteresis (enter high, exit low) removes most binary flicker without the latency or compute of temporal feature aggregation, and the residual flicker isolates the truly unstable cases worth architectural attention.
falsifiable_prediction: Instrumented score traces will show most flicker events occurring within a narrow score band around threshold with smooth underlying trajectories, and hysteresis will cut flicker rates by a large factor at under a point of frame-wise AP cost, while genuinely discontinuous score traces will account for only a small minority.
why_important: If flicker is a thresholding artifact, video deployments get an immediate free fix, and temporal-architecture research can refocus on the genuinely unstable residual.
why_possibly_novel: Hysteresis is standard in signal processing but its systematic evaluation against detection flicker, with the smooth-versus-discontinuous decomposition, appears missing from the video detection literature.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log per-object score traces for three detectors on annotated video, classify flicker events by underlying trace smoothness, evaluate hysteresis variants against frame-wise and stability metrics.
main_risk: Object association across frames (needed to define per-object traces) may itself be error-prone at exactly the flicker events, biasing the decomposition.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Flicker reflects unstable per-frame representations, requiring temporal feature aggregation or video-specific training to fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Score traces may be genuinely discontinuous under real motion and lighting, making hysteresis a cosmetic fix that hides misses rather than preventing them.
fastest_falsification: One day: score-trace autocorrelation and flicker-band analysis on one video benchmark; discontinuous traces dominating kills it.

one_line: Temporal feature aggregation helps only below a motion-speed threshold set by receptive-field geometry: past it, aggregation actively hurts, and the breakeven is computable per architecture
problem: Video detectors aggregate features across frames assuming temporal context helps, but fast-moving objects displace across receptive fields between frames, so aggregation may blend unrelated content; the speed regime where aggregation flips from helpful to harmful is neither measured nor reported.
core_hypothesis: Per-object gains from temporal aggregation are positive below an image-plane speed threshold and negative above it, with the threshold predictable from the aggregation window and effective receptive-field size, so speed-adaptive gating (bypassing aggregation for fast objects) dominates both pure per-frame and pure aggregated inference.
falsifiable_prediction: Speed-stratified evaluation of aggregation-based video detectors against their per-frame backbones will show a sign-flipping gain curve with a threshold matching the geometric prediction, and gated inference will beat both baselines on mixed-speed video.
why_important: Video architectures are chosen on aggregate benchmarks dominated by slow objects; a speed-conditional analysis changes both architecture selection and gives an immediate gating improvement.
why_possibly_novel: Motion-conditioned evaluation exists as difficulty binning; the sign-flip claim tied to receptive-field geometry with a predictive threshold appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-object image-plane speeds on a video benchmark, stratify aggregation gains for two video detectors, fit thresholds, compare with geometric predictions, then implement speed-gated inference.
main_risk: Speed correlates with size and blur, requiring careful covariate control to isolate the aggregation-specific effect.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Temporal aggregation is broadly beneficial for video detection; more temporal context is better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Alignment modules (flow or deformable offsets) in modern aggregators may already compensate for displacement, flattening the gain curve.
fastest_falsification: One day: speed-stratified gain curve for one aggregating detector; no sign flip kills it.

one_line: Static-image detectors have absorbed a motion-blur-mediated speed prior: sharp renderings of fast-context objects score lower than blurred ones, showing detectors expect fast things to be blurry
problem: Training photos encode a physical correlation (fast objects are motion-blurred), so detectors may treat blur as evidence for certain classes and poses; as global-shutter and high-framerate sensors deliver sharp images of fast motion, this hidden prior would misfire in unmeasured ways.
core_hypothesis: For classes photographed predominantly in motion (balls in play, birds in flight), detectors score sharp instances in dynamic contexts lower than appropriately blurred instances of matched geometry, revealing a learned blur-speed prior that penalizes sharp fast objects delivered by modern sensors.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled probes adding or removing motion blur on objects in dynamic scenes will show blur increasing confidence for motion-typical classes and decreasing it for static-typical classes, and detectors evaluated on high-framerate sharp footage will underperform their blurred-footage scores on motion-typical classes specifically.
why_important: Sports analytics, drone tracking, and industrial inspection increasingly use fast sharp capture; a prior that penalizes sharpness would systematically degrade exactly these premium pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: Blur is studied as corruption (hurting detection); the reverse direction, blur as expected evidence whose absence hurts, appears uninvestigated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched sharp-versus-blurred probes for motion-typical and static-typical classes in dynamic contexts, measure confidence deltas on three detectors, validate on real high-framerate footage.
main_risk: Synthetic blur realism may drive results; real optical blur has depth and motion structure that filters approximate poorly.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Sharper images are always at least as good for detection; blur only removes information.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detectors may key on shape and context so heavily that blur statistics contribute negligible evidence either way.
fastest_falsification: One day: sharp-versus-blurred confidence deltas for five motion-typical classes; no positive blur effect kills it.

one_line: Post-occlusion re-detection latency is a score warm-up artifact, not a memory requirement: detectors take measurable frames to re-fire on reappeared objects, and score-prior propagation eliminates the latency without any temporal architecture
problem: Objects reappearing after occlusion are re-detected with a delay that tracking systems paper over with motion models, and the delay is assumed to require temporal memory to fix; but if it stems from conservative score dynamics (the detector fires immediately but below threshold), a scoring fix suffices and memory architectures are overkill for this failure.
core_hypothesis: Upon reappearance, sub-threshold detection responses exist at the correct location several frames before the first threshold-crossing detection, so the latency is a thresholding artifact; propagating a location-conditional score prior from pre-occlusion frames (a simple Bayesian bump, no learned memory) removes most re-detection latency at negligible false-alarm cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Frame-by-frame analysis of reappearance events will find correct-location sub-threshold responses in the majority of latency frames, and the score-prior mechanism will cut median re-detection latency substantially while leaving false re-detections near baseline.
why_important: Re-acquisition speed matters for safety and for tracking identity preservation; a training-free scoring fix would be immediately deployable and would deflate one argument for expensive temporal models.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion handling research jumps to memory architectures; the decomposition of re-detection latency into sub-threshold response versus true representational absence appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate reappearance events from tracking benchmarks, log pre-threshold responses at GT locations across the latency window, implement the prior-propagation readout, evaluate latency and false-alarm deltas.
main_risk: Sub-threshold responses may be present but so weak that boosting them to detection also fires on background, making the false-alarm cost prohibitive.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Re-detection latency after occlusion reflects missing temporal memory that only recurrent or memory-augmented architectures can provide.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For long occlusions the representation may genuinely need re-establishment, restricting the scoring fix to short-occlusion cases only.
fastest_falsification: One day: sub-threshold response audit on 100 reappearance events; absent responses kill it.

one_line: Video benchmarks annotated on keyframes overstate detector performance: keyframe selection favors canonical poses and sharp frames, so all-frame evaluation reveals a hidden performance gap
problem: Video detection ground truth is often annotated on sampled keyframes chosen or influenced by human annotation workflows that favor clear, canonical views; if the unannotated frames are systematically harder, benchmark scores overstate real per-frame performance, but the gap has not been quantified.
core_hypothesis: Frames selected for annotation differ measurably from unselected frames in blur, pose canonicality, and occlusion, and detector performance on densely re-annotated segments will be systematically lower on the previously unannotated frames, with the gap size predicting deployment complaints that benchmarks fail to explain.
falsifiable_prediction: Dense re-annotation of video segments will show per-frame AP on originally unannotated frames falling below keyframe AP by a consistent margin, and the margin will correlate with measurable keyframe-selection bias statistics (sharpness, pose typicality) per benchmark.
why_important: Video benchmarks guide architecture choices for deployed per-frame systems; a quantified keyframe bias would recalibrate expectations and motivate all-frame or bias-corrected evaluation.
why_possibly_novel: Annotation cost bias is acknowledged; measuring its effect as a performance overstatement with dense re-annotation appears rare for video detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Densely annotate 50 video segments from a keyframe-annotated benchmark, compare detector AP on original keyframes versus interstitial frames, quantify selection-bias statistics.
main_risk: Dense annotation is expensive, and interstitial-frame ground truth is harder to produce accurately, risking noise that mimics the hypothesized gap.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Keyframe-annotated benchmarks representatively sample video difficulty; per-frame scores generalize to all frames.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some benchmarks sample keyframes uniformly by timestamp, which would eliminate selection bias and the predicted gap for those benchmarks.
fastest_falsification: Two days: dense annotation of ten segments; no keyframe-versus-interstitial gap kills it.

one_line: Temporal-consistency losses trade single-frame accuracy for stability along an unmeasured Pareto frontier: the exchange rate varies by class and is often worse than post-hoc smoothing achieves for free
problem: Video detectors add consistency objectives assuming stability gains come free or cheap, but any constraint spends capacity; without measuring the accuracy-stability exchange rate, the community cannot say whether trained consistency beats trivial post-hoc smoothing at the same stability level.
core_hypothesis: Sweeping consistency-loss weights traces a Pareto frontier between frame-wise AP and stability metrics, and for a substantial region of that frontier simple post-hoc smoothing of per-frame outputs (score EMA, box interpolation) reaches equal stability at lower accuracy cost, confining the genuine value of trained consistency to a narrow high-stability regime.
falsifiable_prediction: Frontier comparison will show post-hoc smoothing dominating trained consistency at low and moderate stability targets across at least two video detector families, with trained consistency winning only where smoothing's latency or lag costs bind.
why_important: It disciplines a popular design choice with a cost-benefit frontier, potentially replacing training complexity with two lines of inference code in many systems.
why_possibly_novel: Consistency losses are ablated as scalar improvements; the frontier framing with post-hoc smoothing as the null hypothesis appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train three consistency-weight variants of one video detector, evaluate frame-wise AP and stability, compare against a smoothing-parameter sweep applied to the zero-weight baseline.
main_risk: Stability metrics differ in what they reward; conclusions may flip across metric choices unless several are reported.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Temporal-consistency training meaningfully improves video detection beyond what output smoothing can achieve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Trained consistency can fix representation-level instability that no output smoothing can reach, potentially dominating everywhere once measured properly.
fastest_falsification: Three days: one consistency-trained model versus smoothed baseline at matched stability; trained model dominating everywhere kills it.

one_line: Open-world detectors mostly re-rank class-agnostic objectness rather than recognize unknowns: their unknown-recall gains vanish when proposal sets are equalized, exposing a field-wide evaluation confound
problem: Open-world detection methods claim to detect unknown objects, but their gains are measured end-to-end where proposal coverage and unknown-scoring are entangled; if the gains come from proposal-stage differences rather than any unknown-recognition capability, the field is optimizing the wrong component under the wrong name.
core_hypothesis: Equalizing candidate-proposal sets across open-world methods (feeding all methods identical class-agnostic proposals) will collapse most published unknown-recall differences, showing that what varies is proposal generosity, not unknown recognition, and that a trivial baseline (generous proposals plus simple objectness thresholding) matches sophisticated unknown-detection machinery.
falsifiable_prediction: Under matched-proposal evaluation, unknown-recall rankings of open-world methods will compress dramatically, and the generous-proposal baseline will land within the compressed pack, while known-class metrics retain their original spread.
why_important: If the confound holds, years of open-world detection comparisons need re-reading, and progress requires separating proposal coverage from unknown scoring as explicit, separately measured stages.
why_possibly_novel: Individual papers note strong class-agnostic baselines; a systematic matched-proposal re-evaluation across the open-world literature appears not to have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement three open-world methods with a shared proposal interface, evaluate unknown recall under native versus matched proposals, compare against the generous-proposal baseline.
main_risk: Some methods integrate proposal and scoring inseparably, forcing approximations that proponents can contest.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Open-world detection methods differ meaningfully in their ability to recognize unknown objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some methods may retain clear unknown-scoring advantages under matched proposals, vindicating the field's framing for at least a subset of approaches.
fastest_falsification: Two days: matched-proposal re-evaluation of two methods; preserved ranking gaps kill the confound claim.

one_line: What counts as an object is taxonomy leakage: open-world detectors' unknowns are biased toward thing-like categories resembling their known-class inventory, systematically missing stuff-adjacent and functional objects
problem: Open-world systems promise to find any object, but objectness itself was learned from a taxonomy of discrete, bounded, mostly manufactured things; the structural bias in which unknowns get found (and which never do) is unmeasured, though it defines the practical safety envelope of these systems.
core_hypothesis: Unknown-object recall is strongly predicted by the unknown's morphological similarity to the training taxonomy (bounded, convex, canonical-scale things score high; deformable, boundary-ambiguous, or scale-atypical entities like debris, spills, cables score low), so open-world detectors inherit a things-of-familiar-shape prior that no unknown-scoring mechanism corrects.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark of diverse unknowns stratified by morphological similarity to common taxonomies, recall will fall monotonically with dissimilarity across all tested open-world methods, and the deficit will persist even with oracle-generous proposal budgets, locating the bias in learned objectness itself.
why_important: The unknowns that matter for safety (road debris, spills, novel hazards) are exactly the morphologically atypical ones; quantifying the bias defines where open-world claims must not be trusted.
why_possibly_novel: Thing-versus-stuff bias is known in segmentation; its quantification as the shape of open-world detection's blind spot with a similarity-stratified benchmark appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble unknown-object test data spanning a morphological-similarity gradient, evaluate three open-world detectors with generous proposals, fit recall against similarity scores.
main_risk: Morphological similarity is hard to operationalize without circularity; the metric design must be independent of the detectors under test.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Learned objectness generalizes to arbitrary novel objects; unknown recall is limited by scoring, not by an object-shape prior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large-scale class-agnostic pretraining may have diversified objectness enough that the similarity gradient is weak.
fastest_falsification: Two days: recall on ten atypical unknowns (spills, cables, debris) versus ten typical ones at matched size; no gradient kills it.

one_line: Novel-object detection and OOD rejection are mathematically opposed uses of the same uncertainty signal: methods form a single trade-off curve, and claimed wins in both directions are evaluation artifacts
problem: The field wants detectors that both flag unknown objects (high response to novelty) and reject spurious detections under distribution shift (low response to novelty), often evaluating the two goals separately; if both behaviors draw on one underlying novelty score, methods cannot improve both, yet papers implicitly claim to.
core_hypothesis: Across open-world and OOD-aware detection methods, unknown-object recall and false-alarm resistance under shift are negatively coupled along a common trade-off curve when evaluated on matched data, and methods claiming simultaneous wins occupy different operating points rather than better curves; genuinely dominating the curve requires signals beyond scalar novelty (geometry consistency, multi-view agreement).
falsifiable_prediction: Joint evaluation of several methods on a shared benchmark with both unknown-recall and shift-false-alarm axes will place them along one frontier with rank reversals explained by operating point, and ablating any method's novelty scalar into a threshold sweep will reproduce competitors' claimed advantages.
why_important: It would consolidate two subliteratures into one calibrated frontier, stopping double-counted progress claims and pointing research at frontier-shifting signal sources instead of threshold shopping.
why_possibly_novel: The tension is occasionally noted; a joint-frontier evaluation demonstrating that current methods are operating points on one curve appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a joint benchmark pairing unknown-object scenes with shifted no-novelty scenes, evaluate four methods across full threshold sweeps, plot the joint frontier and test for genuine dominance.
main_risk: Constructing shift scenes guaranteed to contain no genuine unknowns requires careful curation; contamination would blur the frontier.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Unknown detection and OOD robustness are separate capabilities that good methods improve independently.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Methods using structurally different signals for the two tasks may already dominate the scalar frontier, disproving the single-curve claim.
fastest_falsification: Two days: joint threshold-sweep evaluation of two methods; clear frontier domination by one method kills it.

one_line: Unknown detections cluster into coherent proto-categories in feature space, and cluster trajectory over deployment time forecasts which novel classes will matter before any human labels them
problem: Deployed open-world systems produce streams of unknown detections that are triaged manually or discarded; whether these unknowns self-organize into stable emergent categories, and whether their growth dynamics predict future taxonomy needs, is unexplored territory between detection and data curation.
core_hypothesis: Feature embeddings of unknown detections form clusters whose purity against post-hoc human labels is high for genuinely novel categories, cluster growth rate and compactness over deployment time predict which clusters correspond to persistent real-world classes versus transient noise, enabling automated vocabulary-expansion proposals ranked by projected importance.
falsifiable_prediction: Retrospective analysis of unknown streams from long-running deployments (or simulated deployments over time-ordered datasets) will show cluster-purity well above chance against later annotation, and growth-rate features will rank persistent classes above noise clusters with strong precision at top ranks.
why_important: It turns the unknown stream from waste into a forecasting instrument for taxonomy management, closing the loop between detection failure and dataset evolution with minimal human effort.
why_possibly_novel: Novel-category discovery is studied on static datasets; the temporal-forecasting formulation on deployment streams with importance ranking appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate deployment by time-ordering a large dataset with held-out classes, collect unknown detections from an open-world detector, cluster and track over time, evaluate purity and persistence-prediction against ground truth.
main_risk: Unknown embeddings from a detector trained on knowns may collapse novel categories toward known prototypes, capping achievable cluster purity.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Unknown detections are unstructured residue useful only after human review; taxonomy expansion is a manual curation decision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Real deployment streams may be dominated by correlated artifacts (lens flares, weather) whose clusters swamp genuine novel categories.
fastest_falsification: Two days: cluster purity of unknowns against held-out classes on one simulated stream; chance-level purity kills it.

one_line: Ensemble disagreement localizes unknown objects better than trained unknown-scoring heads: architecturally diverse detectors disagree most exactly where novel objects sit, a training-free open-world baseline nobody benchmarks
problem: Open-world methods train dedicated machinery to score unknowns, while a simpler signal, structured disagreement between diverse detectors (one fires class A, another class B, a third nothing, all at the same location), plausibly flags novelty without any training, but is absent from open-world baselines and benchmarks.
core_hypothesis: Location-wise disagreement patterns across three or more architecturally diverse detectors (label conflict at high mutual box IoU, or confident-versus-silent splits) concentrate on genuinely novel or mislabeled objects, and a disagreement-based unknown detector will match or beat trained unknown-scoring methods on standard open-world benchmarks at zero training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Regions of structured cross-detector disagreement will overlap held-out unknown-class GT at rates far above chance and above single-model uncertainty baselines, and the disagreement detector will place on the published open-world recall-precision frontier.
why_important: A strong training-free baseline recalibrates the field's progress claims and offers deployments an immediately available unknown-flagging mechanism using models they already run.
why_possibly_novel: Ensemble uncertainty is standard for calibration; structured label-conflict patterns as a localization signal for unknown objects, benchmarked against open-world methods, appears untried.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run three diverse detectors on an open-world benchmark, define disagreement signatures, evaluate unknown recall-precision against published methods and single-model entropy baselines.
main_risk: Detectors trained on the same base datasets may share blind spots so strongly that they agree in silence on exactly the most novel objects.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Detecting unknowns requires dedicated training objectives; ensembles measure uncertainty, not novelty.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shared training data may homogenize failure, making disagreement sparse precisely where all models miss the novel object entirely.
fastest_falsification: One day: disagreement-region overlap with unknown GT on one benchmark; chance-level overlap kills it.

one_line: Suppressed-then-confident detections mined from deployment logs are enriched for annotation errors and novel objects: the NMS discard pile is a free active-learning signal nobody collects
problem: Deployment pipelines discard enormous numbers of suppressed and sub-threshold detections without logging them, on the assumption they are noise; if specific discard patterns (high pre-suppression confidence, repeated across frames or visits) mark annotation gaps and novel objects, pipelines are throwing away their best curation signal.
core_hypothesis: Detections that repeatedly reach high pre-NMS confidence but are suppressed or sub-threshold across multiple observations of the same scene are strongly enriched for missing ground truth, emerging object categories, and systematic model blind spots, making the discard stream a higher-yield active-learning source than standard uncertainty sampling on kept detections.
falsifiable_prediction: Human review of persistence-filtered discarded detections will confirm real-object or novel-category status at rates several times higher than random sub-threshold detections and higher than classic uncertainty-sampled candidates, and annotating them will improve model recall more per label than uncertainty sampling.
why_important: Active learning for detection struggles with what to show annotators; a stronger candidate source using data pipelines already computing (but discarding) would improve label efficiency across the industry.
why_possibly_novel: Active learning samples from kept predictions; systematically mining the suppression discard stream with persistence filters appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument a detector on multi-visit scene data (video or repeated surveys), collect persistence-filtered discards, human-review 300 candidates against random and uncertainty-sampled controls, run one active-learning round comparing label efficiency.
main_risk: Persistent confident discards may be dominated by a few systematic artifact types (reflections, posters), yielding high enrichment but low diversity value for retraining.
territory: Object Detection (failure modes of detectors / open-vocab / foundation-model detection)
default_community_belief: Suppressed and sub-threshold detections are noise; active learning should sample from the model's kept, uncertain predictions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The discard stream may be so artifact-dominated that filtering costs exceed the value of the enriched candidates it yields.
fastest_falsification: Two days: persistence-filtered discard review on one video dataset; enrichment no better than random sub-threshold sampling kills it.
